dan01.kan_en: Nihon Shoki, Book 1 — Age of the Gods (part 1)
dan01.title: The Opening of Heaven and Earth and the Seven Generations of the Age of the Gods (sections 1–3)
dan01.lead: Out of a chaos in which heaven and earth were not yet divided, heaven and earth separate, and from something like a reed shoot the deities are born, beginning with Kuni-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto (国常立尊). Next, paired male and female deities appear, and the generations up to Izanagi-no-Mikoto (伊弉諾尊) and Izanami-no-Mikoto (伊弉冉尊) are called the “Seven Generations of the Age of the Gods” (神世七代).

points.text: The main text of section 1 says that out of an egg-like chaos, what was clear and light became heaven and what was heavy and turbid became earth, and that something like a reed shoot that arose between heaven and earth became a deity, and Kuni-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto (国常立尊) was born. Then Kuni-no-Sazuchi-no-Mikoto (国狭槌尊) and 豊斟渟尊 (reading unconfirmed) were born, and these three deities are described as purely male deities (純男).

In the main text of section 2, four pairs of male and female deities appear (埿土煑尊 and 沙土煑尊, 大戸之道尊 and 大苫辺尊, 面足尊 and 惶根尊 (readings unconfirmed), and Izanagi-no-Mikoto (伊弉諾尊) and Izanami-no-Mikoto (伊弉冉尊)), and the main text of section 3 sums them up as “eight deities”. The generations from Kuni-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto to Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto are called the Seven Generations of the Age of the Gods (神世七代).

Section 1 has six variant accounts, and they do not agree on the first deity. The main text and variant accounts 1, 4 and 5 place Kuni-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto first, but variant accounts 2 and 3 place 可美葦牙彦舅尊 (reading unconfirmed) first, and variant account 6 places Ame-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto (天常立尊) first.
A small note in the original text lays down that the most exalted deities are written with “尊” and the others with “命”, and that both are read “美舉等” (mikoto).

The Kojiki begins with Ame-no-Minakanushi-no-Kami (天之御中主神), who came into being in Takamagahara (高天原), but in the Nihon Shoki the corresponding Ame-no-Minakanushi-no-Kami (天御中主尊), Takamimusubi-no-Kami (高皇産霊尊) and 神皇産霊尊 (reading unconfirmed) appear only in the “又曰” (“it is also said”) part of variant account 4 of section 1.

Kokugakuin University’s database of deity names introduces the view that the Nihon Shoki makes Kuni-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto the first deity because its compilers were more interested in the beginning of the land than in the heavenly realm. It also notes that the tradition of the three deities, such as Ame-no-Minakanushi-no-Kami (天御中主尊), is thought to be a part added later than the other traditions.

story.text: Long ago, heaven and earth were not yet divided, nor were yin and yang separated. Their state was mixed together like a hen’s egg, vague and yet holding a germ. In time, what was clear and bright thinly trailed out and became heaven, and what was heavy and turbid settled and became earth. Because what is pure gathers easily and what is heavy and turbid hardens with difficulty, heaven was formed first and earth was fixed afterwards. After that, it is said, deities were born within it.

At the beginning, when heaven and earth opened, the land drifted like a fish floating on water. At that time something shaped like a reed shoot arose between heaven and earth, and it became a deity just as it was. This was Kuni-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto (国常立尊); next were born Kuni-no-Sazuchi-no-Mikoto (国狭槌尊) and 豊斟渟尊 (reading unconfirmed). The original text explains that these three deities came into being by the way of 乾 (Heaven) alone, and were therefore purely male deities.

Next, deities appeared in male and female pairs: 埿土煑尊 and 沙土煑尊, 大戸之道尊 and 大苫辺尊, 面足尊 and 惶根尊 (readings unconfirmed), and Izanagi-no-Mikoto (伊弉諾尊) and Izanami-no-Mikoto (伊弉冉尊). Small notes add many other names for each of these deities (such as 埿土根尊 and 沙土根尊, 大戸摩彦尊 and 大戸摩姫尊, and 青橿城根尊; readings unconfirmed).

The main text of section 3 counts these together as eight deities, and says that because they came into being through the interaction of the ways of 乾 (Heaven) and 坤 (Earth), they became male and female deities. It concludes by saying that the generations from Kuni-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto to Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto are called the Seven Generations of the Age of the Gods (神世七代).

quotes.note: The chaotic state was like a hen’s egg, vague and yet holding a germ.
The most exalted deities are written “尊” and the others “命”, and both are read “mikoto” (a small note in the original text).
The generations from Kuni-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto to Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto are called the Seven Generations of the Age of the Gods.
The deity born in Takamagahara (高天原) is named Ame-no-Minakanushi-no-Kami (天御中主尊) (the “又曰” part of variant account 4).

figures.name: 豐斟渟尊 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: The third deity, born after Kuni-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto and Kuni-no-Sazuchi-no-Mikoto in the main text of section 1.

figures.name: 可美葦牙彥舅尊 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: A deity found in variant accounts 2, 3 and 6 of section 1; in variant accounts 2 and 3 he is the first deity to be born (a reading note says that “可美” is read 于麻時 and “彦舅” is read 比古尼).

figures.name: 神皇產靈尊 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: In the “又曰” part of variant account 4 of section 1, the third deity born in Takamagahara (a reading note says that “皇産霊” is read 美武須毗).

figures.name: 埿土煑尊 and 沙土煑尊 (readings unconfirmed)
figures.role: The first male-and-female pair of deities to appear in the Seven Generations of the Age of the Gods (a reading note says that “埿土” is read 于毗尼 and “沙土” is read 須毗尼).

figures.name: 大戶之道尊 and 大苫邊尊 (readings unconfirmed)
figures.role: The second male-and-female pair of deities to appear in the main text of section 2.

figures.name: 面足尊 and 惶根尊 (readings unconfirmed)
figures.role: The male-and-female pair of deities that appears just before Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto in the main text of section 2.

figures.name: 角樴尊 and 活樴尊 (readings unconfirmed)
figures.role: A male-and-female pair of deities found only in variant account 1 of section 3 (a small note says that “樴” means 橛 (kui), a stake).

figures.name: 天鏡尊, 天萬尊 and 沫蕩尊 (readings unconfirmed)
figures.role: Deities placed in the line of descent from Kuni-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto to Izanagi-no-Mikoto in variant account 2 of section 2 (a reading note says that “沫蕩” is read 阿和那伎).

compare.where: Kojiki, Part 1, opening (the beginning of heaven and earth; the Separate Heavenly Deities)
compare.text: The Kojiki begins with Ame-no-Minakanushi-no-Kami (天之御中主神), Takamimusubi-no-Kami (高御産巣日神) and 神産巣日神 (reading unconfirmed), who came into being in Takamagahara (高天原) when heaven and earth first opened. The main text of the Nihon Shoki does not mention these three deities and begins with Kuni-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto (国常立尊).

compare.where: Kojiki, Part 1, opening (the Seven Generations of the Age of the Gods)
compare.text: The Kojiki’s Seven Generations of the Age of the Gods consist of two solitary deities (独神), Kuni-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto (国之常立神) and 豊雲野神 (reading unconfirmed), and five male-and-female pairs, including the pair 角杙神 and 妹活杙神 (readings unconfirmed). The main text of the Nihon Shoki makes up the seven generations from three purely male deities and four male-and-female pairs, and 角樴尊 and 活樴尊 (readings unconfirmed) appear only in variant account 1 of section 3.

compare.where: Kojiki, Part 1, opening (the Separate Heavenly Deities)
compare.text: The Kojiki says that when the land was young and drifting like floating oil, 宇摩志阿斯訶備比古遅神 (reading unconfirmed) came into being from something that sprouted up like a reed shoot, and counts him, together with Ame-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto (天之常立神), among the Separate Heavenly Deities (別天神). In the Nihon Shoki a similar description is found in variant account 2, where 可美葦牙彦舅尊 (reading unconfirmed) is the first deity.

variants.name: Section 1, variant account 1
variants.text: When heaven and earth divided, there was within the void a thing whose form was hard to describe, and from it were born Kuni-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto (国常立尊; also called 国底立尊), Kuni-no-Sazuchi-no-Mikoto (国狭槌尊; also called 国狭立尊) and 豊国主尊 (readings unconfirmed). It makes the third deity 豊国主尊 rather than 豊斟渟尊, and lists many other names such as 豊組野尊, 葉木国野尊 and 見野尊 (readings unconfirmed).

variants.name: Section 1, variant account 2
variants.text: When the land and the earth were young and drifting like floating oil, 可美葦牙彦舅尊 (reading unconfirmed) was born from a thing that arose like a reed shoot sprouting forth, and next were born Kuni-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto and Kuni-no-Sazuchi-no-Mikoto. It makes the first deity 可美葦牙彦舅尊 rather than Kuni-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto.

variants.name: Section 1, variant account 3
variants.text: When heaven and earth were mixed together, there was first a “神人” (divine person), named 可美葦牙彦舅尊 (reading unconfirmed) and next 国底立尊 (reading unconfirmed). It lists only two deities.

variants.name: Section 1, variant account 4
variants.text: It lists Kuni-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto and Kuni-no-Sazuchi-no-Mikoto as the deities born together when heaven and earth divided. It further records, under “又曰” (“it is also said”), that the deities born in Takamagahara (高天原) were named Ame-no-Minakanushi-no-Kami (天御中主尊), Takamimusubi-no-Kami (高皇産霊尊) and 神皇産霊尊 (reading unconfirmed).

variants.name: Section 1, variant account 5
variants.text: Before heaven and earth came into being, there was a state like rootless snow floating on the sea, and within it arose a thing like a reed shoot first sprouting from the mud. It became a “人” (person) and was named Kuni-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto; this account lists only one deity.

variants.name: Section 1, variant account 6
variants.text: When heaven and earth divided, a thing like a reed shoot arose in the sky and became Ame-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto (天常立尊), and next 可美葦牙彦舅尊 (reading unconfirmed). A thing like floating oil also arose in the sky and became Kuni-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto; this account puts Ame-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto first.

variants.name: Section 2, variant account 1
variants.text: It says that the two deities Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto are the children of 青橿城根尊 (reading unconfirmed). In the main text, 青橿城根尊 appears in a small note as one of the other names of 惶根尊 (reading unconfirmed).

variants.name: Section 2, variant account 2
variants.text: It gives the tradition as a parent-to-child line of descent: Kuni-no-Tokotachi-no-Mikoto begat 天鏡尊, 天鏡尊 begat 天萬尊, 天萬尊 begat 沫蕩尊 (readings unconfirmed), and 沫蕩尊 begat Izanagi-no-Mikoto. This is a different form from the sequence of male-and-female pairs in the main text.

variants.name: Section 3, variant account 1
variants.text: It lists four pairs as the deities born in male-and-female pairs: 埿土煑尊 and 沙土煑尊, 角樴尊 and 活樴尊, 面足尊 and 惶根尊 (readings unconfirmed), and Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto. 角樴尊 and 活樴尊 take the place of the main text’s 大戸之道尊 and 大苫辺尊 (readings unconfirmed).

dan04.kan_en: Nihon Shoki, Book 1 — Age of the Gods (part 1)
dan04.title: The Birth of the Land (section 4)
dan04.lead: Izanagi-no-Mikoto (伊弉諾尊) and Izanami-no-Mikoto (伊弉冉尊) probe the sea with a spear from the Floating Bridge of Heaven (天浮橋) and obtain Onogoro Island (磤馭慮島), where they descend and become husband and wife. Taking Awaji Island (淡路洲) as the afterbirth (胞), the two deities give birth to 大日本豊秋津洲 (reading unconfirmed) and other islands, and the name “Land of the Great Eight Islands” (大八洲国) arises.

points.text: In the main text, Izanagi-no-Mikoto (伊弉諾尊) and Izanami-no-Mikoto (伊弉冉尊) stand on the Floating Bridge of Heaven (天浮橋) and consult together, “Might there not be a land below?”; when they probe with the Jewelled Spear of Heaven (天之瓊矛), the brine that drips from the spear’s tip hardens and becomes Onogoro Island (磤馭慮島). The main text does not record any command from the heavenly deities (天神).

When the two deities went round the island, taken as the central pillar of the land, in opposite directions, the female deity (陰神) spoke first, so the male deity (陽神), saying that the man ought to speak first, had them go round again; the second time the male deity spoke first, and they became husband and wife.

When it came to giving birth, they first took Awaji Island (淡路洲) as the afterbirth (胞, e), and then gave birth to 大日本豊秋津洲, 伊予二名洲 (readings unconfirmed), Tsukushi Island (筑紫洲), Oki Island (隠岐洲) and Sado Island (佐度洲) (as twins), Koshi (越洲), 大洲 and 吉備子洲 (readings unconfirmed), and so the name “Land of the Great Eight Islands” (大八洲国) arose. Tsushima (対馬島), Iki (壱岐島) and the small islands are said to have formed from hardened foam of the brine.

In variant account 1, the heavenly deities (天神) give the two deities the Jewelled Spear of Heaven (天瓊戈) with a command; their first child, 蛭児 (Hiruko), is set adrift in a reed boat, and 淡洲 (reading unconfirmed) too is not counted among their children. When the two deities return to heaven and report, the heavenly deities divine by 太占 (reading unconfirmed) and tell them that it happened because the woman’s words came first, and have them do it again.

There are ten variant accounts, and their traditions of how the islands were born vary. Some take Awaji Island (淡路洲) and 淡洲 (reading unconfirmed) as the afterbirth (variant account 6), and one takes 磤馭慮嶋 (Onogoro Island) as the afterbirth and gives birth to Awaji Island (variant account 8); variant account 7 counts Iki (壱岐洲) and Tsushima (対馬洲) among the islands born.

Kokugakuin University’s database of deity names notes that there is a tradition in which an island forms from drops from the spear’s tip hardening, as in the main text and variant account 1, and a tradition in which the island is obtained by probing with the spear, as in variant accounts 2 to 4, and that there is a view that the latter is the older form. It also cites a view that old elements of Awaji traditions survive in variant account 8, in which Awaji Island is born first with 磤馭慮島 (Onogoro Island) as the afterbirth.

story.text: Izanagi-no-Mikoto (伊弉諾尊) and Izanami-no-Mikoto (伊弉冉尊) stood on the Floating Bridge of Heaven (天浮橋) and consulted together, “How could there be no land below this?” So they thrust the Jewelled Spear of Heaven (天之瓊矛; 瓊 means jewel) downward and probed, and struck the blue sea. The brine that dripped from the tip of the spear hardened into an island, which was named Onogoro Island (磤馭慮島).

The two deities descended to the island and dwelt there, and thought to become husband and wife and give birth to lands. Taking Onogoro Island as the central pillar of the land, the male deity (陽神) went round the pillar from the left and the female deity (陰神) from the right, and they met at the same place. Then the female deity spoke first: “Oh, how delightful! I have met a lovely young man.” The male deity was displeased and said, “I am a man, so it is right that I should speak first. It is not good that the woman spoke first, so let us go round again.”

The two deities went round once more and met, and this time the male deity spoke first: “Oh, how delightful! I have met a lovely young woman.” The male deity and the female deity examined each other’s bodies, and here for the first time they were joined as husband and wife.

When the time came to give birth, they first took Awaji Island (淡路洲) as the afterbirth (胞, e), but because it did not satisfy them, the original text records, they named it Awaji Island. Then they gave birth to 大日本豊秋津洲, 伊予二名洲 (readings unconfirmed) and Tsukushi Island (筑紫洲), and gave birth to Oki Island (隠岐洲) and Sado Island (佐度洲) as twins. The original text adds that the twins sometimes born among people follow this precedent. They further gave birth to Koshi (越洲), 大洲 and 吉備子洲 (readings unconfirmed).

In this way the name “Land of the Great Eight Islands” (大八洲国) first arose. Tsushima (対馬島), Iki (壱岐島) and the small islands in various places are all said to have formed from hardened foam of the brine (or foam of the water).

quotes.note: How could there be no land below this? (the words of the two deities as they consulted)
I am a man, so it is right that I should speak first; why did the woman speak first? (the words of the male deity)
By this the name “Land of the Great Eight Islands” (大八洲国) first arose.
Then a wagtail (鶺鴒) flew up and shook its head and tail (variant account 5).

figures.name: Onogoro-shima (磤馭慮島)
figures.role: The island formed when the brine that dripped from the spear’s tip hardened; the two deities descended and dwelt there and made it the central pillar of the land.

figures.name: Jewelled Spear of Heaven (天之瓊矛)
figures.role: The spear the two deities used to probe the sea from the Floating Bridge of Heaven (a small note says that “瓊” means jewel and is read 努). In variant account 1 it is the Jewelled Spear of Heaven (天瓊戈) bestowed by the heavenly deities.

figures.name: Hiruko (蛭兒)
figures.role: The child born first in variant account 1 and set adrift in a reed boat. In variant account 10 he is born after Awaji Island. He does not appear in the main text of section 4.

figures.name: Awaji Island (淡路洲)
figures.role: The island taken as the afterbirth in the main text. It is recorded that because it did not satisfy them it was named Awaji Island.

figures.name: 大日本豐秋津洲 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: In the main text, the first island born after Awaji Island, the afterbirth (a reading note says that “日本” is read 耶麻騰).

figures.name: 淡洲 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: An island that in variant account 1 is not counted among the children, and in variant account 6 is taken as the afterbirth together with Awaji Island.

figures.name: Wagtail (鶺鴒)
figures.role: The bird in variant account 5 that, by shaking its head and tail, taught the two deities the way of union.

compare.where: Kojiki, Part 1 (the section on 淤能碁呂島 (reading unconfirmed) and the making firm of the land)
compare.text: In the Kojiki, the heavenly deities command the two deities to put the land in order and make it firm, and bestow on them the Jewelled Spear of Heaven (天沼矛). In the main text of the Nihon Shoki there is no command from the heavenly deities, and the two deities lower the spear after consulting between themselves (the command of the heavenly deities is in variant account 1).

compare.where: Kojiki, Part 1 (水蛭子 and 淡嶋 (readings unconfirmed); consulting the heavenly deities)
compare.text: In the Kojiki, the female deity speaks first and 水蛭子 (reading unconfirmed) is born, who is put in a reed boat and set adrift; 淡嶋 (reading unconfirmed) too is not counted among their children, and they do it again following the heavenly deities’ divination by 太占 (reading unconfirmed). In the main text of the Nihon Shoki, 蛭児 (Hiruko) does not appear in section 4, and it is the male deity himself who proposes going round again, so the account closest to the Kojiki is variant account 1.

compare.where: Kojiki, Part 1 (the formation of the Land of the Great Eight Islands, 大八嶋国)
compare.text: The Kojiki begins the births with 淡道之穂之狭別嶋 (reading unconfirmed) and calls the eight islands, including 伊伎嶋 (reading unconfirmed) and 津嶋 (Tsushima), the Land of the Great Eight Islands (大八嶋国), after which six more islands, such as 吉備児嶋 (reading unconfirmed), are born. The main text of the Nihon Shoki takes Awaji Island (淡路洲) as the afterbirth, begins the births with 大日本豊秋津洲 (reading unconfirmed), and says that Tsushima and Iki were formed from hardened foam of the brine.

variants.name: Variant account 1
variants.text: The heavenly deities (天神) command the two deities to go to “豊葦原千五百秋瑞穂之地” (reading unconfirmed) and bestow on them the Jewelled Spear of Heaven (天瓊戈), and the two deities set up a hall eight fathoms long (八尋之殿) and a heavenly pillar (天柱) on the island. At first the female deity goes round from the left and the male deity from the right, and the female deity speaks first; 蛭児 (Hiruko; set adrift in a reed boat) and 淡洲 (reading unconfirmed) are born, but they are not counted as children. Following the teaching of the heavenly deities, obtained by divination with 太占 (reading unconfirmed), the male deity goes round from the left and speaks first again. The islands born are 大日本豊秋津洲 (reading unconfirmed), Awaji Island (淡路洲), 伊予二名洲 (reading unconfirmed), Tsukushi Island (筑紫洲), 隠岐三子洲 (reading unconfirmed), Sado Island (佐度洲), Koshi (越洲) and 吉備子洲 (reading unconfirmed), and these are called the Land of the Great Eight Islands (大八洲国).

variants.name: Variant account 2
variants.text: The two deities stood in the mist of heaven (天霧) and said, “We wish to obtain a land,” and thrusting down the Jewelled Spear of Heaven (天瓊矛) they probed and obtained Onogoro Island (磤馭慮島). It says that they drew out the spear and rejoiced, “How good, there was a land,” and there is no story of drops hardening.

variants.name: Variant account 3
variants.text: The two deities, who were in Takamagahara (高天原), said, “There must be a land,” and with the Jewelled Spear of Heaven (天瓊矛) produced Onogoro Island (磤馭慮島) as if drawing it.

variants.name: Variant account 4
variants.text: The two deities talked together: “There is a thing like floating oil. Might there not be a land within it?” They probed with the Jewelled Spear of Heaven (天瓊矛), made an island, and named it Onogoro Island (磤馭慮嶋).

variants.name: Variant account 5
variants.text: That the female deity spoke first, which was taken as inauspicious, and that they went round again, is the same as in the main text; but afterwards the two deities did not know how to unite. Then a wagtail (鶺鴒) flew up and shook its head and tail, and by copying it the two deities learned the way of union, according to this account.

variants.name: Variant account 6
variants.text: It says that, taking Awaji Island (淡路洲) and 淡洲 (reading unconfirmed) as the afterbirth, they gave birth to 大日本豊秋津洲 (reading unconfirmed), and then to 伊予洲 (reading unconfirmed), Tsukushi Island (筑紫洲), Oki Island (隠岐洲) and Sado Island (佐度洲) (twins), Koshi (越洲), 大洲 and 子洲 (readings unconfirmed).

variants.name: Variant account 7
variants.text: There is no story of the afterbirth; it says that they first gave birth to Awaji Island (淡路洲), and then to 大日本豊秋津洲, 伊予二名洲 (readings unconfirmed), Oki Island (隠岐洲), Sado Island (佐度洲), Tsukushi Island (筑紫洲), Iki (壱岐洲) and Tsushima (対馬洲). Iki and Tsushima, which in the main text formed from the foam of the brine, are included among the islands born.

variants.name: Variant account 8
variants.text: It says that, taking Onogoro Island (磤馭慮嶋) as the afterbirth, they gave birth to Awaji Island (淡路洲), and then to 大日本豊秋津洲, 伊予二名洲 (readings unconfirmed), Tsukushi Island (筑紫洲), 吉備子洲 (reading unconfirmed), Oki Island (隠岐洲) and Sado Island (佐度洲) (twins), and Koshi (越洲).

variants.name: Variant account 9
variants.text: It says that, taking Awaji Island (淡路洲) as the afterbirth, they gave birth to 大日本豊秋津洲 (reading unconfirmed), and then to 淡洲, 伊予二名洲, 隠岐三子洲 (readings unconfirmed), Sado Island (佐度洲), Tsukushi Island (筑紫洲), 吉備子洲 and 大洲 (readings unconfirmed).

variants.name: Variant account 10
variants.text: It says that the female deity spoke first, “Ah, what a dear young man!”, took the male deity’s hand, and they became husband and wife, and gave birth to Awaji Island (淡路洲) and next to 蛭児 (Hiruko). There is no story of going round again.

dan05.kan_en: Nihon Shoki, Book 1 — Age of the Gods (part 1)
dan05.title: The Birth of the Three Noble Children, the Birth of the Deities, and Yomi (Section 5)
dan05.lead: In the main text, Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto together give birth to the sea, rivers, mountains, and trees and grasses, and then to the Sun Deity, the Moon Deity, Hiruko, and Susanoo-no-Mikoto. The birth of the fire deity and the death of Izanami-no-Mikoto, the visit to the land of Yomi, the birth of the three deities through purification, and the story of Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto and Ukemochi-no-Kami are transmitted in the eleven variant accounts.

points.text: In the main text, after the two deities together gave birth to the sea, rivers, mountains, the ancestor of trees, and the ancestor of grasses, they sought to produce a ruler of all under heaven and gave birth to the Sun Deity (Ōhirume-no-Muchi, 大日孁貴), whom they sent up to heaven. They next sent the Moon Deity to heaven as well; Hiruko, who could not stand on its legs even at the age of three, was set adrift in a boat; and Susanoo-no-Mikoto was driven away to the Root Land (根国) for his lawlessness.

The main text of section 5 does not record the birth of the fire deity or the death of Izanami-no-Mikoto. The story of Izanami-no-Mikoto dying after giving birth to the fire deity (Kagutsuchi, 軻遇突智; Homusubi, 火産霊) is transmitted in variant accounts 2, 3, 5, and 6, each in a slightly different form, and variant account 4 relates that Kanayamahiko and others were born from her suffering in giving birth to the fire deity.

Variant account 6 relates how Izanagi-no-Mikoto saw Izanami-no-Mikoto's appearance in Yomi and fled back, blocked 泉津平坂 (reading unconfirmed) with a rock and exchanged vows of separation, and purified himself at 檍原 (reading unconfirmed) in Hyūga. When he washed his left eye Amaterasu-Ōmikami was born, from his right eye Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto (月読尊), and from his nose Susanoo-no-Mikoto, and they were entrusted with ruling the High Plain of Heaven (高天原), the sea, and the realm under heaven, respectively.

In variant account 11, Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto (月夜見尊) visits Ukemochi-no-Kami (保食神) on Amaterasu-Ōmikami's orders but, angered at being entertained with food brought out of the deity's mouth, kills it. Amaterasu-Ōmikami, angered, came to live separated from Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto by one day and one night, and the account holds that the millet, barnyard millet, rice, wheat, beans, and silkworms that arose from Ukemochi-no-Kami's body became the origin of the seeds for fields and of sericulture.

In the Kojiki, the three noble children are born when Izanagi-no-Mikoto (伊耶那岐命) performs purification after returning from Yomi, and Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto (月読命) is entrusted with the realm of the night (夜之食國) and Susanoo-no-Mikoto with the sea plain. In the Nihon Shoki the traditions are divided: in the main text they are born of the two deities, in variant account 1 by means of white copper mirrors, and in variant account 6 through purification.

The deity-name database of Kokugakuin University explains that the Kojiki's story of the fire deity is structured as though it had gathered and organized the various traditions of the Nihon Shoki. For example, it states that deities coming into being from what Izanami-no-Mikoto (伊耶那美神) vomited and excreted corresponds to variant account 4, 泣沢女神 (reading unconfirmed) coming into being from tears to variant account 6, the burial to variant account 5, and deities coming into being when the fire deity is cut down to variant accounts 6 to 8.

story.text: Izanagi-no-Mikoto and Izanami-no-Mikoto next gave birth to the sea, then to the rivers, then to the mountains. They further gave birth to 句句迺馳 (reading unconfirmed), the ancestor of trees, and to 草野姫 (reading unconfirmed; also called 野槌), the ancestor of grasses. The two deities then consulted together, saying, “We have already given birth to the Land of the Great Eight Islands (大八洲国) and to the mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees. How can we not give birth to one who will be ruler of all under heaven?”

So the two deities together gave birth to the Sun Deity and named it Ōhirume-no-Muchi (大日孁貴) (according to a small note, one writing also calls it Amaterasu-Ōmikami (天照大神) or 天照大日孁尊 (reading unconfirmed)). This child shone with beautiful, radiant light and illuminated everything within heaven, earth, and the four directions. The two deities rejoiced and said, “Though we have many children, none is as wondrous as this one. It should not be kept long in this land; let us quickly send it to heaven and entrust it with the affairs of heaven.” It is said that because heaven and earth were not yet far apart at this time, they raised the child up to heaven by way of the pillar of heaven (天柱).

Next they gave birth to the Moon Deity (a small note says it is also called 月弓尊 (reading unconfirmed), 月夜見尊, or 月読尊, that is, Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto). Its light was second only to the sun's, and since it was fit to rule alongside the sun, it too was sent to heaven. Next they gave birth to Hiruko, but since the child could not stand on its legs even at the age of three, they placed it in the heavenly rock-camphor boat (天磐櫲樟船) and cast it away to drift as the wind took it.

Next they gave birth to Susanoo-no-Mikoto (a small note says he is also called 神素戔嗚尊 or 速素戔嗚尊, readings unconfirmed). This deity was brave and fierce, did cruel things without hesitation, and was always crying and wailing. Because of this, many of the people of the land died young, and the green mountains withered. The two parent deities commanded, “You are utterly lawless, so you cannot reign over the universe. Go far away to the Root Land,” and drove Susanoo-no-Mikoto away.

quotes.note: How can we not give birth to one who will be ruler of all under heaven? (the two deities' consultation).
This child shone with beautiful, radiant light and illuminated everything within heaven, earth, and the four directions (the birth of the Sun Deity).
I will strangle to death a thousand of the people of the land you rule each day (Izanami-no-Mikoto's words in variant account 6).
These are things that the people of this world should eat in order to live (Amaterasu-Ōmikami's words in variant account 11).

figures.name: Ōhirume-no-Muchi (大日孁貴)
figures.role: The name of the Sun Deity whom the two deities produced as ruler of all under heaven in the main text (a gloss says it is read 「於保比屢咩能武智」).

figures.name: Hiruko (蛭兒)
figures.role: In the main text, the child born after the Sun Deity and the Moon Deity who could not stand on its legs even at the age of three and was set adrift in the heavenly rock-camphor boat (天磐櫲樟船).

figures.name: 句句迺馳 and 草野姬 (野槌) (readings unconfirmed)
figures.role: The ancestor of trees and the ancestor of grasses, produced by the two deities in the main text.

figures.name: Kagutsuchi (軻遇突智)
figures.role: The fire deity appearing in variant accounts 2, 4, 6, and others; Izanami-no-Mikoto is burned and dies in giving birth to this deity.

figures.name: 罔象女 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: The water deity born from Izanami-no-Mikoto in variant accounts 2 to 4 (a gloss says that 「罔象」 is read 美都波).

figures.name: 啼澤女命 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: In variant account 6, the deity that came into being from the tears Izanagi-no-Mikoto shed in grief at his wife's death.

figures.name: Yomotsu-shikome (泉津醜女)
figures.role: In variant account 6, the women of Yomi (eight of them) whom Izanami-no-Mikoto sent to pursue the fleeing Izanagi-no-Mikoto.

figures.name: Funato-no-Kami (岐神)
figures.role: In variant accounts 6 and 9, the deity that came into being from the staff Izanagi-no-Mikoto threw (the reading follows the gloss 「布那斗能加微」 at the end of variant account 7).

figures.name: 泉守道者 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: In variant account 10, the one who conveyed Izanami-no-Mikoto's words to Izanagi-no-Mikoto at 泉平坂 (reading unconfirmed).

figures.name: 天熊人 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: In variant account 11, the one sent by Amaterasu-Ōmikami who brought back the things that arose from Ukemochi-no-Kami's corpse.

compare.where: Kojiki, Part 1 (purification and the birth of the three noble children)
compare.text: In the Kojiki, Izanagi-no-Mikoto returns from Yomi and purifies himself; when he washes his left eye Amaterasu-Ōmikami comes into being, from his right eye Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto, and from his nose Susanoo-no-Mikoto. In the main text of the Nihon Shoki, the two deities, as husband and wife, give birth to the Sun Deity, the Moon Deity, and Susanoo-no-Mikoto; birth through purification is the tradition of variant account 6.

compare.where: Kojiki, Part 1 (the division of rule among the three noble children)
compare.text: In the Kojiki, Amaterasu-Ōmikami is entrusted with the High Plain of Heaven, Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto with the realm of the night (夜之食國), and Susanoo-no-Mikoto with the sea plain. In the Nihon Shoki, variant account 6 entrusts Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto (月読尊) with the sea plain and Susanoo-no-Mikoto with the realm under heaven, while variant account 11 entrusts Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto (月夜見尊) with the affairs of heaven alongside the sun and Susanoo-no-Mikoto with the sea plain.

compare.where: Kojiki, Part 1 (the banishment of Susanoo-no-Mikoto and Ōgetsuhime-no-Kami)
compare.text: In the Kojiki, it is Susanoo-no-Mikoto who kills Ōgetsuhime-no-Kami (大宜津比売神), who had entertained him with food brought out of her mouth and rear, and this story comes after the episode of the Heavenly Rock Cave (天石屋戸). In the Nihon Shoki, in variant account 11 Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto (月夜見尊) kills Ukemochi-no-Kami, and for that reason the sun and moon came to be separated by one day and one night.

variants.name: Variant account 1
variants.text: Izanagi-no-Mikoto, alone, wishing to produce a noble child to rule the world, took a white copper mirror in his left hand, whereupon Ōhirume-no-Mikoto (大日孁尊) appeared; when he took one in his right hand, 月弓尊 (reading unconfirmed) appeared; and while he turned his head to look back, Susanoo-no-Mikoto (素戔鳴尊) appeared. The two deities of sun and moon were given the role of illuminating heaven and earth, and Susanoo-no-Mikoto, cruel by nature, was given the role of ruling the Root Land.

variants.name: Variant account 2
variants.text: It explains that Hiruko, born after the sun and moon, could not stand even at the age of three because, when the deities went around the pillar, the female deity spoke words of joy first and so went against the principle of yin and yang; the child was placed in the 鳥磐櫲樟橡船 (a rock-camphor boat) and set adrift. Next Izanami-no-Mikoto gave birth to the fire deity Kagutsuchi, was burned and died, and as she was dying gave birth to the earth deity Haniyamahime (埴山姫) and the water deity 罔象女 (reading unconfirmed). Kagutsuchi took Haniyamahime as wife and 稚産霊 (reading unconfirmed) was born, and the account holds that silkworms and mulberry arose on top of this deity's head and the five grains within its navel.

variants.name: Variant account 3
variants.text: When Izanami-no-Mikoto gave birth to Homusubi (火産霊), she was burned by the child and “withdrew as a deity” (神退; also written 神避). The account holds that as she withdrew she gave birth to the water deity 罔象女 (reading unconfirmed), the earth deity Haniyamahime, and further to 天吉葛 (reading unconfirmed).

variants.name: Variant account 4
variants.text: The account holds that when Izanami-no-Mikoto was giving birth to Kagutsuchi, suffering from the heat, what she vomited became Kanayamahiko (金山彦), her urine became 罔象女 (reading unconfirmed), and her feces became Haniyamahime.

variants.name: Variant account 5
variants.text: Izanami-no-Mikoto gave birth to the fire deity, was burned and died, and was buried at the village of 有馬村 (reading unconfirmed) in Kumano, in the province of Kii. It is said that the people of that place worship this deity's spirit with flowers in the flowering season, and worship it with singing and dancing, using drums, flutes, and banners.

variants.name: Variant account 6
variants.text: Izanagi-no-Mikoto gave birth to many deities, among them the wind deity 級長戸辺命 (reading unconfirmed), born from the breath with which he blew away the morning mist; after this Izanami-no-Mikoto died through the birth of the fire deity. From his tears Izanagi-no-Mikoto produced 啼沢女命 (reading unconfirmed), and he cut Kagutsuchi into three pieces with his ten-span sword, and from the blood arose deities such as 甕速日神 (reading unconfirmed) and Takemikazuchi (武甕槌神). Visiting Yomi, Izanagi-no-Mikoto peered at the form he had been told not to look at and fled; pursued by the Yomotsu-shikome (泉津醜女), he blocked 泉津平坂 (reading unconfirmed) with a rock that would take a thousand people to pull, and when Izanami-no-Mikoto said she would kill a thousand people a day, he answered that he would cause fifteen hundred to be born. He purified himself at 筑紫日向小戸橘之檍原 (reading unconfirmed) and produced 八十枉津日神 (reading unconfirmed), the Sumiyoshi Great Deities (住吉大神), and others; Amaterasu-Ōmikami was born from his left eye, Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto (月読尊) from his right eye, and Susanoo-no-Mikoto from his nose, and they were entrusted with the High Plain of Heaven, the sea plain, and the realm under heaven, respectively; but Susanoo-no-Mikoto wept, wishing to go to the Root Land where his mother was, and was driven out.

variants.name: Variant account 7
variants.text: The account holds that when Izanagi-no-Mikoto cut Kagutsuchi into three pieces, they became, respectively, a thunder deity, Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami (大山祇神), and Takaokami (高龗). The blood from the cutting also dyed the five hundred rocks of the 天八十河 (reading unconfirmed), giving rise to deities such as 磐裂神 and 根裂神 (readings unconfirmed), and that lineage leads down to Futsunushi-no-Kami (経津主神). In the latter half, glosses showing the readings of words in variant account 6 are placed together.

variants.name: Variant account 8
variants.text: The account holds that when Izanagi-no-Mikoto cut Kagutsuchi into five pieces, the head, trunk, hands, waist, and feet became five mountain deities: Ōyamatsumi (大山祇), 中山祇, 麓山祇, 正勝山祇, and 䨄山祇 (readings unconfirmed), respectively. It is said that the blood that spattered at that time dyed the rocks, grasses, and trees, and that this is why grasses, trees, and rocks came to contain fire.

variants.name: Variant account 9
variants.text: Izanagi-no-Mikoto went to the place of temporary enshrinement (殯斂) to see his wife; he was told not to look, but he lit a light and looked, and Izanami-no-Mikoto's body was swollen, with eight kinds of thunder upon it. Fleeing, Izanagi-no-Mikoto hid beneath a large peach tree and drove off the thunders by throwing peaches, and the account holds that this is the origin of warding off demons with peaches. He threw down his staff, saying, “Beyond here the thunders cannot come,” and it became Funato-no-Kami (岐神; originally named 来名戸之祖神, reading unconfirmed).

variants.name: Variant account 10
variants.text: Izanami-no-Mikoto, whose form had been seen when she had said not to look, said resentfully, “You have seen my heart, so I too have seen yours.” From the spittle that the departing Izanagi-no-Mikoto spat out as he swore was born Hayatama-no-O (速玉之男), and from what he swept away was born Yomotsu-Kotosaka-no-O (泉津事解之男). At 泉平坂 (reading unconfirmed), 泉守道者 (reading unconfirmed) conveyed Izanami-no-Mikoto's words, and Kukuri-hime-no-Kami (菊理媛神) also said something, which Izanagi-no-Mikoto praised before leaving; he then purified himself at 橘之小門 (reading unconfirmed) and produced 磐土命, 大直日神, 底土命, 大綾津日神, 赤土命 (readings unconfirmed), and others.

variants.name: Variant account 11
variants.text: Izanagi-no-Mikoto appointed Amaterasu-Ōmikami (天照太神) to rule 高天之原 (the High Plain of Heaven), Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto (月夜見尊) to rule the affairs of heaven alongside the sun, and Susanoo-no-Mikoto to rule the sea plain. Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto killed Ukemochi-no-Kami, who had entertained him with food brought out of its mouth, and came to live separated by one day and one night from the angered Amaterasu-Ōmikami. Cattle and horses, millet, silkworms, barnyard millet, rice, wheat, and beans arose from Ukemochi-no-Kami's body; the account holds that Amaterasu-Ōmikami made these the food of people, designating them as seeds for dry fields and paddy fields, planted rice in 天狭田 and 長田 (readings unconfirmed), and, drawing thread from a cocoon held in her mouth, began the way of sericulture.

dan06.kan_en: Nihon Shoki, Book 1 — Age of the Gods (part 1)
dan06.title: Susanoo-no-Mikoto's Ascent to Heaven and the Pledge (Section 6)
dan06.lead: Susanoo-no-Mikoto ascends to heaven to see his elder sister before going to the Root Land, and Amaterasu-Ōmikami, suspecting that he has come to seize her land, meets him armed. The two deities make a pledge (ukei) and produce children; the five male deities born from the jewels are determined to be Amaterasu-Ōmikami's children, and the three goddesses born from the sword to be Susanoo-no-Mikoto's children.

points.text: In the main text, Susanoo-no-Mikoto himself proposes the terms of the pledge, “if a female is born, an impure heart; if a male is born, a pure heart,” and Amaterasu-Ōmikami produces three goddesses from Susanoo-no-Mikoto's ten-span sword, while Susanoo-no-Mikoto produces five male deities from Amaterasu-Ōmikami's string of Yasakani jewels (八坂瓊之御統).

The children's affiliation is determined by the owner of the “original object” (物根). Since the jewels were Amaterasu-Ōmikami's, the five male deities are regarded as Amaterasu-Ōmikami's children, and since the sword was Susanoo-no-Mikoto's, the three goddesses are regarded as Susanoo-no-Mikoto's children; the three goddesses are recorded as the deities worshipped by the 胸肩君 (reading unconfirmed) and others of Tsukushi.

The three variant accounts each differ in the terms of the pledge, the objects used, and the names and order of the deities born. In variant accounts 1 and 3, Amaterasu-Ōmikami eats her own swords (of ten, nine, and eight spans) to produce the three goddesses, and in variant account 3 Susanoo-no-Mikoto produces six male deities.

In variant account 1 the three goddesses are sent down to the island of Tsukushi (筑紫洲) and commanded to stay “on the way” (道中) and assist the Heavenly Grandson; variant account 3 records that they descended to 宇佐嶋 (reading unconfirmed) in the Central Land of Reed Plains (葦原中国), and that they are now on the 海北道中 (the way north across the sea) and are called 道主貴 (reading unconfirmed).

The deity-name database of Kokugakuin University tabulates how the names and birth order of the three goddesses differ between the main text and each variant account, and introduces a theory that sees the command in variant account 1 to “assist the Heavenly Grandson” as reflecting a history in which rituals for the sea route to the Korean Peninsula were held in high regard.

In the Kojiki, Susanoo-no-Mikoto (須佐之男命) does not state terms in advance, and declares his own victory on the grounds that the children born were “graceful maidens” (手弱女). Terms like those of the main text of the Nihon Shoki, “if male, a pure heart,” are not found in the Kojiki.

story.text: Susanoo-no-Mikoto asked to be allowed, before going to the Root Land, to go for a while to the High Plain of Heaven to see his elder sister and then depart forever; this was permitted, and he ascended to heaven. After this, Izanagi-no-Mikoto, his work completed, built a hidden palace (幽宮) on the island of Awaji (淡路洲) and quietly withdrew there. As another version, it is also recorded that he ascended to heaven to report and remained in the Little Palace of the Sun (日之少宮, wakamiya).

When Susanoo-no-Mikoto ascended, the sea heaved and the mountains roared. Amaterasu-Ōmikami had long known that her younger brother was violent, and, alarmed that he might intend to seize her land, she bound up her hair into topknots and tied up her skirt to make trousers. She wound the string of five hundred Yasakani jewels (八坂瓊之五百箇御統, misumaru) around her topknots and arms, slung on her back quivers holding a thousand arrows and five hundred arrows, put on a high arm-guard (高鞆), brandished her bow, grasped the hilt of her sword, stamped into the hard ground up to her thighs, and, raising a war cry, questioned him.

Susanoo-no-Mikoto answered that he had never had a black heart, and had come only because he wished to see his elder sister before going to the Root Land at his parents' command. When Amaterasu-Ōmikami asked how he would prove the purity of his heart, Susanoo-no-Mikoto said that he and his sister should make a pledge and produce children, and offered that if what was born was female it would mean an impure heart, and if male a pure heart.

Amaterasu-Ōmikami took Susanoo-no-Mikoto's ten-span sword, broke it into three pieces, rinsed them in the 天真名井 (reading unconfirmed), and crunched them, and from the mist of the breath she blew out were born three goddesses: Takori-hime (田心姫), Takitsu-hime (湍津姫), and Ichikishima-hime (市杵嶋姫). Next Susanoo-no-Mikoto took the string of five hundred Yasakani jewels wound around Amaterasu-Ōmikami's topknots and arms and did the same, and five male deities were born: 正哉吾勝勝速日天忍穂耳尊 (reading unconfirmed), Ame-no-Hohi-no-Mikoto (天穂日命), Amatsuhikone-no-Mikoto (天津彦根命), Ikutsuhikone-no-Mikoto (活津彦根命), and Kumanokusubi-no-Mikoto (熊野橡樟日命).

Amaterasu-Ōmikami said that, tracing the original objects, the jewel string was hers, so the five male deities were all her children, and she took them and raised them. She also said that since the ten-span sword was Susanoo-no-Mikoto's, the three goddesses were Susanoo-no-Mikoto's children, and gave them to Susanoo-no-Mikoto. These three goddesses are the deities worshipped by the 胸肩君 (reading unconfirmed) and others of Tsukushi. A small note states that Ame-no-Hohi-no-Mikoto is the ancestor of the 出雲臣, the 土師連, and others, and Amatsuhikone-no-Mikoto the ancestor of the 凡川内直, the 山代直, and others (readings unconfirmed).

quotes.note: I have never had a black (evil) heart. By my parents' strict command, I am now about to go forever to the Root Land: Susanoo-no-Mikoto's defense of himself.
If the child I produce is female, regard me as having an impure heart; if male, regard me as having a pure heart: the terms of the pledge.
The Yasakani jewel string is mine, so the five male deities are all my children: the words of Amaterasu-Ōmikami.
You three deities, descend and stay on the way, assist the Heavenly Grandson, and be worshipped by the Heavenly Grandson: the Sun Deity's instruction in variant account 1.

figures.name: Susanoo-no-Mikoto (素戔嗚尊)
figures.role: Ascends to heaven to see his elder sister before going to the Root Land, and shows the purity of his heart by producing male deities through the pledge.

figures.name: Amaterasu-Ōmikami (天照大神)
figures.role: Suspecting that her younger brother has come to seize her land, she meets him armed, and makes the five male deities born of the pledge her own children.

figures.name: Izanagi-no-Mikoto (伊弉諾尊)
figures.role: His work completed, he withdrew into the hidden palace on the island of Awaji (in another version, he ascended to heaven and remained in the Little Palace of the Sun).

figures.name: Takori-hime (田心姫)
figures.role: One of the three goddesses Amaterasu-Ōmikami produced from the ten-span sword (born first in the main text).

figures.name: Takitsu-hime (湍津姫)
figures.role: One of the three goddesses.

figures.name: Ichikishima-hime (市杵嶋姫)
figures.role: One of the three goddesses. In variant account 2 she is regarded as the deity of the distant sea (遠瀛).

figures.name: Okitsushima-hime (瀛津嶋姫)
figures.role: The goddess born first in variant accounts 1 and 3. In variant account 3 this name is regarded as another name of Ichikishima-hime-no-Mikoto.

figures.name: 正哉吾勝勝速日天忍穂耳尊 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: The first male deity Susanoo-no-Mikoto produced from Amaterasu-Ōmikami's jewel string; regarded as Amaterasu-Ōmikami's child.

figures.name: Ame-no-Hohi-no-Mikoto (天穂日命)
figures.role: One of the five male deities. In the small note of the main text he is regarded as the ancestor of the 出雲臣, the 土師連, and others (readings unconfirmed).

figures.name: Amatsuhikone-no-Mikoto (天津彦根命)
figures.role: One of the five male deities. In the small note he is regarded as the ancestor of the 凡川内直, the 山代直, and others (readings unconfirmed).

figures.name: Ikutsuhikone-no-Mikoto (活津彦根命)
figures.role: One of the five male deities.

figures.name: Kumanokusubi-no-Mikoto (熊野橡樟日命)
figures.role: One of the five male deities (in the variant accounts he appears under names such as 熊野忍蹈命 and 熊野樟日命, readings unconfirmed).

figures.name: 羽明玉 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: In variant account 2, the deity who met the ascending Susanoo-no-Mikoto and presented him with the 瑞八坂瓊 curved jewel.

compare.where: Kojiki, Part 1 — the pledge (after the pledge between Amaterasu-Ōmikami and Susanoo-no-Mikoto)
compare.text: In the Kojiki, Susanoo-no-Mikoto says only “各宇氣比而，生子” without stating terms beforehand, and declares his own victory on the grounds that those born were female. The main text of the Nihon Shoki sets the terms first, “if female, an impure heart; if male, a pure heart,” so the way the result is read is reversed.

compare.where: Kojiki, Part 1 — the pledge
compare.text: The point that the children's affiliation is divided according to the “original object” is the same, but the Kojiki specifically records that the three goddesses dwell respectively in the offshore shrine (奥津宮), middle shrine (中津宮), and shore shrine (辺津宮) of Munakata (胸形, 宗像), and names the first goddess 多紀理毗賣命 (reading unconfirmed).

compare.where: Kojiki, Part 1 — end of the section on the division of rule among the three noble children
compare.text: Regarding Izanagi-no-Mikoto's end, which is recorded before the pledge, the main text of the Nihon Shoki says that he withdrew into the hidden palace on the island of Awaji, whereas the Kojiki records that he dwells at 多賀 (reading unconfirmed) in Ōmi (淡海).

variants.name: Variant account 1
variants.text: The Sun Deity (Amaterasu-Ōmikami) met him wearing three swords of her own, of ten, nine, and eight spans, and the pledge is that “if the heart is pure, males will be born.” The Sun Deity ate her own swords and produced Okitsushima-hime (瀛津嶋姫), Takitsu-hime, and Takori-hime, and Susanoo-no-Mikoto produced five male deities from the jewels of the string hung around his neck and obtained the sign of victory. The Sun Deity sent the three goddesses down to the island of Tsukushi and instructed them to stay on the way, assist the Heavenly Grandson, and be worshipped by the Heavenly Grandson.

variants.name: Variant account 2
variants.text: As Susanoo-no-Mikoto was ascending, a deity named 羽明玉 (reading unconfirmed) presented him with the 瑞八坂瓊 curved jewel (曲玉). Amaterasu-Ōmikami and Susanoo-no-Mikoto exchanged sword and curved jewel; Amaterasu-Ōmikami bit the curved jewel and produced Ichikishima-hime-no-Mikoto (the distant sea, 遠瀛), Takori-hime-no-Mikoto (the middle sea, 中瀛), and Takitsu-hime-no-Mikoto (the seashore, 海浜), and Susanoo-no-Mikoto bit the sword and produced five male deities, Ame-no-Hohi-no-Mikoto and the others. The terms are “if female, a black heart; if male, a red heart,” and no conclusion about victory or defeat is recorded.

variants.name: Variant account 3
variants.text: The two deities faced each other across the 天安河 (reading unconfirmed), and the Sun Deity pledged, “If males are born, I will make them my children and have them rule the Heavenly Plain (天原).” The Sun Deity ate her own sword and produced three goddesses, and Susanoo-no-Mikoto held in his mouth the jewels hung on his topknot and around his neck and produced six male deities from his palms, arms, and feet. The Sun Deity made those six males her own children and had them rule the Heavenly Plain; the account records that the three goddesses descended to 宇佐嶋 (reading unconfirmed) in the Central Land of Reed Plains, are now on the 海北道中 (the way north across the sea) and are called 道主貴 (reading unconfirmed), and are worshipped by the 水沼君 (reading unconfirmed) and others of Tsukushi.

dan07.kan_en: Nihon Shoki, Book 1 — Age of the Gods (part 1)
dan07.title: The Heavenly Rock Cave (Section 7)
dan07.lead: Amaterasu-Ōmikami, alarmed and wounded by Susanoo-no-Mikoto's violent deeds, shuts herself in the Heavenly Rock Cave, and the world falls into a darkness with neither day nor night. The eight hundred thousand deities hold a ritual following the plan of Omoikane-no-Kami and bring Amaterasu-Ōmikami out, and they make Susanoo-no-Mikoto bear restitution for his offenses and banish him from heaven.

points.text: In the main text, Susanoo-no-Mikoto sows seed over seed in Amaterasu-Ōmikami's fields, breaks down the ridges between them, defecates in the new palace at the time of the first-fruits festival (新嘗), and makes a hole in the roof of the hall of sacred garments (斎服殿) and throws in a flayed heavenly piebald colt (天斑駒). Amaterasu-Ōmikami, startled, wounds herself with a shuttle (梭, hi), and in anger shuts herself in the Heavenly Rock Cave (天石窟).

When Amaterasu-Ōmikami closes the rock door, everything “within the six directions” (六合之内) is always dark, and there is no longer any distinction between day and night. The deities gather on the bank of the 天安河 (reading unconfirmed); Omoikane-no-Kami has the long-crying birds cry, Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto and Futodama-no-Mikoto (太玉命) hang a jewel string (御統), the Yata mirror (八咫鏡), and nikite offerings (和幣) on a sakaki tree (真坂樹) of Mount Ame-no-Kagoyama (天香山) and pray, and Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto performs (wazaoki, 俳優) before the door.

When Amaterasu-Ōmikami opens the door a crack and peers out, Tajikarao-no-Kami (手力雄神) takes her hand and draws her out, and the Nakatomi deity (中臣神) and the 忌部 (reading unconfirmed) deity stretch a shirikume rope (端出之縄) and beg her, “Please do not go back again.” Afterward the deities made Susanoo-no-Mikoto bear restitution in the form of a thousand tables of offerings (千座置戸), had his hair (or the nails of his hands and feet) pulled out, and banished him.

The story of the mirror differs from one variant account to another. In variant account 1, Ishikoridome (石凝姥) makes an image of a deity from the metal of Mount Ame-no-Kagoyama, and it is regarded as the Hinokuma deity (日前神) of the province of Kii. In variant account 2, Ame-no-Nukado (天糠戸) makes a mirror, and the mirror placed in the cave, which still bears a small flaw from touching the door, is regarded as the 伊勢崇秘之大神 (reading unconfirmed). In variant account 3, 石凝戸辺 (reading unconfirmed) makes the Yata mirror.

Variant account 3 presents the making of restitution with the nails of the hands and feet as “nails of good riddance and nails of ill riddance” (吉爪棄物, 凶爪棄物) as the reason why people dispose of their own nails with care, and presents the banished Susanoo-no-Mikoto being refused lodging while wearing a hat and straw cape as the reason why entering another's house in a hat and straw cape is shunned. It also includes a story in which Susanoo-no-Mikoto ascends to heaven once more, makes a pledge, and produces six male deities.

The deity-name database of Kokugakuin University cites a theory that, based on the Nihon Shoki's spelling 「思兼神」, interprets the name of Omoikane-no-Kami as “a deity combining many thoughts,” and also notes that the Nihon Shoki describes him with the phrases “deeply plotting and thinking far ahead” and “wisdom of deliberation.” Variant account 1 makes Omoikane-no-Kami the child of Takamimusubi (高皇産霊).

story.text: After the pledge, Susanoo-no-Mikoto's conduct became extremely violent. Amaterasu-Ōmikami had made 天狭田 and 長田 (readings unconfirmed) her sacred fields, but in spring Susanoo-no-Mikoto sowed seed over seed and broke down the ridges between the fields, and in autumn he let loose the heavenly piebald colt and made it lie down in the fields. When Amaterasu-Ōmikami was holding the first-fruits festival, he secretly defecated in the new palace, and when Amaterasu-Ōmikami was weaving the garments of the deities in the hall of sacred garments, he flayed the heavenly piebald colt, made a hole in the roof of the hall, and threw it in.

Amaterasu-Ōmikami, startled, wounded herself with the shuttle, and in anger entered the Heavenly Rock Cave, closed the rock door, and shut herself in. Because of this, everything within the six directions was always dark, and the alternation of day and night could no longer be told.

The eight hundred thousand deities gathered on the bank of the 天安河 (reading unconfirmed) and discussed how they should pray. Omoikane-no-Kami, plotting deeply, gathered the long-crying birds of the Eternal Land (常世) and made them cry at length, and had Tajikarao-no-Kami stand beside the rock door. Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto, distant ancestor of the Nakatomi no Muraji (中臣連), and Futodama-no-Mikoto, distant ancestor of the 忌部 (reading unconfirmed), dug up by the roots five hundred sakaki trees (五百箇真坂樹) of Mount Ame-no-Kagoyama, hung the string of five hundred Yasakani jewels (八坂瓊之五百箇御統) on the upper branches, the Yata mirror on the middle branches, and blue and white nikite offerings (青和幣, 白和幣) on the lower branches, and prayed together.

Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto, distant ancestor of the 猿女君 (reading unconfirmed), held in her hand a spear wound with miscanthus grass, stood before the door of the Heavenly Rock Cave, and performed skillfully. She made a headdress of the sakaki of Mount Ame-no-Kagoyama and a sash (tasuki, 手繦) of hikage moss (蘿), lit fires, set an overturned tub (覆槽, uke) in place, and spoke words of divine possession.

Hearing this, Amaterasu-Ōmikami said that since she had shut herself away, the Central Land of Plentiful Reed Plains (豊葦原中国) should be in long night, so why was Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto making merry like this? She opened the rock door a crack with her hand and peered out. At that moment Tajikarao-no-Kami took her hand and drew her out. The Nakatomi deity and the 忌部 (reading unconfirmed) deity stretched the shirikume rope (端出之縄) all around and begged her not to go back again.

Afterward the deities laid the guilt on Susanoo-no-Mikoto, imposed on him a thousand tables of restitution (千座置戸), and had his hair pulled out to atone for his offenses. It is also said that they had the nails of his hands and feet pulled out. Thus Susanoo-no-Mikoto was at last driven out of heaven.

quotes.note: Because she closed the rock door and shut herself in, the whole world was always dark, and the alternation of day and night could no longer be told.
At that moment Tajikarao-no-Kami took Amaterasu-Ōmikami's hand and drew her out.
Afterward the deities laid the guilt on Susanoo-no-Mikoto and imposed on him a thousand tables of restitution (千座置戸, a great quantity of articles of atonement).
Lately many have made petitions, but there have never been words as beautiful as these: the Sun Deity's words in variant account 3.

figures.name: Susanoo-no-Mikoto (素戔嗚尊)
figures.role: Commits one violent deed after another in heaven, causes Amaterasu-Ōmikami to shut herself in the cave, and is made to pay restitution and banished.

figures.name: Amaterasu-Ōmikami (天照大神)
figures.role: Startled and wounded by Susanoo-no-Mikoto's deeds, she shuts herself in the Heavenly Rock Cave, but, drawn by the deities' ritual, opens the door.

figures.name: Omoikane-no-Kami (思兼神)
figures.role: The deity who, at the deities' council, deeply planned the means of drawing Amaterasu-Ōmikami out. In variant account 1, the child of Takamimusubi.

figures.name: Ame-no-Tajikarao-no-Kami (天手力雄神)
figures.role: The deity who stood beside the rock door and took Amaterasu-Ōmikami's hand to draw her out (called Tajikarao-no-Kami, 手力雄神, in the main text).

figures.name: Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto (天兒屋命)
figures.role: Distant ancestor of the Nakatomi no Muraji. He decorates the sakaki tree and prays, and in variant accounts 2 and 3 recites the ritual words.

figures.name: Futodama-no-Mikoto (太玉命)
figures.role: Distant ancestor of the 忌部 (reading unconfirmed). He prays together with Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto, and in variant account 3 holds up the decorated sakaki tree.

figures.name: Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto (天鈿女命)
figures.role: Distant ancestor of the 猿女君 (reading unconfirmed). She performed before the door of the cave and spoke words of divine possession.

figures.name: Wakahirume-no-Mikoto (稚日女尊)
figures.role: In variant account 1, the deity who was weaving the garments of the deities in the hall of sacred garments and died, startled by the piebald colt thrown in.

figures.name: Ishikoridome (石凝姥)
figures.role: In variant account 1, the smith who used the metal of Mount Ame-no-Kagoyama to make the image that became the Hinokuma deity (gloss: 「伊之居梨度咩」).

figures.name: Ame-no-Nukado (天糠戶)
figures.role: In variant account 2, the distant ancestor of the mirror-makers' guild, who made the mirror.

figures.name: 天明玉 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: In variant account 3, the distant ancestor of the jewel-makers who made the Yasakani curved jewels; regarded as a child of Izanagi-no-Mikoto.

figures.name: Kogotomusubi (興台產靈)
figures.role: In variant account 3, regarded as the father of Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto (gloss: 「許語等武須毘」).

compare.where: Kojiki, Part 1 — Susanoo-no-Mikoto's misdeeds (after the pledge)
compare.text: In the Kojiki, the one who dies in the incident at the hall of sacred garments is a heavenly weaving maiden (天衣織女), who strikes her genitals on a shuttle and dies. In the main text of the Nihon Shoki, Amaterasu-Ōmikami herself wounds herself with the shuttle, and in variant account 1 Wakahirume-no-Mikoto dies.

compare.where: Kojiki, Part 1 — the Heavenly Rock Cave (天石屋)
compare.text: In the Kojiki, the eight million deities laugh, and Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto and Futodama-no-Mikoto (布刀玉命) hold out the mirror to show it to Amaterasu-Ōmikami; when she comes out wondering, Tajikarao-no-Kami (手力男神) draws her out. The main text of the Nihon Shoki has neither the scene of showing the mirror nor the laughter of the deities; Amaterasu-Ōmikami opens the door herself after hearing the merry voice of Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto.

compare.where: Kojiki, Part 1 — the banishment of Susanoo-no-Mikoto and Ōgetsuhime
compare.text: In the Kojiki, right after the banishment comes the story of Susanoo-no-Mikoto killing Ōgetsuhime-no-Kami (大気津比売神), from whose body the five grains and other things arise, but no corresponding passage could be confirmed in the main text or the variant accounts of section 7 of the Nihon Shoki (a similar story appears in section 5, variant account 11, as the story of Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto (月夜見尊) and Ukemochi-no-Kami).

variants.name: Variant account 1
variants.text: It was Wakahirume-no-Mikoto (稚日女尊) who was weaving the garments of the deities in the hall of sacred garments; startled by the piebald colt thrown in, she fell from the loom, wounded her body with the shuttle, and died (神退). Amaterasu-Ōmikami tells Susanoo-no-Mikoto, “You still have a black heart,” and shuts herself in the cave. The deities gather at 天高市 (reading unconfirmed), and on the proposal of Omoikane-no-Kami, child of Takamimusubi, Ishikoridome (石凝姥) makes an image of a deity using the metal of Mount Ame-no-Kagoyama and a bellows of deerskin. This is said to be the Hinokuma deity (日前神) of the province of Kii; the scene in which Amaterasu-Ōmikami comes out is not recorded.

variants.name: Variant account 2
variants.text: The Sun Deity had forgiven Susanoo-no-Mikoto's ravaging of the fields and his throwing in of the piebald colt, without anger or resentment, but at the first-fruits festival he secretly placed feces beneath her seat; she sat down without knowing it, fell ill, and shut herself in the cave. Ame-no-Nukado (天糠戸), distant ancestor of the mirror-makers' guild (鏡作部), makes a mirror; Futodama (太玉), distant ancestor of the 忌部 (reading unconfirmed), makes offerings; 豊玉 (reading unconfirmed), distant ancestor of the jewel-makers' guild (玉作部), makes jewels; and when Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto recites divine blessings, the Sun Deity comes out. The flaw made when the mirror placed in the cave touched the door remains, and this is said to be the 伊勢崇秘之大神 (reading unconfirmed). Susanoo-no-Mikoto is made to give up things from his hands and feet and his spittle and nasal mucus as articles of purification, and is banished.

variants.name: Variant account 3
variants.text: Through the contrast between the Sun Deity's good fields and Susanoo-no-Mikoto's poor fields, Susanoo-no-Mikoto, jealous, ravages the fields. Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto hangs on a sakaki tree (真坂木) the Yata mirror of 石凝戸辺 (reading unconfirmed), the curved jewels of 天明玉 (reading unconfirmed), and the bark-cloth of 天日鷲 (reading unconfirmed); when Futodama-no-Mikoto holds it up and prays, the Sun Deity says, “There have never been words as beautiful as these,” and opens the door, and Ame-no-Tajikarao-no-Kami (天手力雄神) pulls it open and light fills everything. The account tells the purification by nails and the story of being refused when asking for lodging in a hat and straw cape as the origins of customs, and continues on to a story in which Susanoo-no-Mikoto ascends to heaven again, makes a pledge, produces six male deities and presents them to his elder sister, and goes down to the Root Land.

dan08.kan_en: Nihon Shoki, Book 1 — Age of the Gods (part 1)
dan08.title: Yamata-no-Orochi and Ōanamuchi-no-Kami (Section 8)
dan08.lead: Susanoo-no-Mikoto, driven out of heaven, slays Yamata-no-Orochi upstream on the 簸 River (reading unconfirmed) in Izumo and saves Inada-hime (奇稲田姫); he presents the Kusanagi Sword, which came out of the serpent's tail, to the heavenly deities, builds a palace at Suga (清地), and fathers Ōanamuchi-no-Kami (大己貴神). The six variant accounts transmit separately such matters as the setting, the names of the swords, the counting of generations of descendants, the tree-planting of Itakeru-no-Kami (五十猛神), and the making of the land by Ōanamuchi-no-Mikoto and Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto.

points.text: In the main text, Susanoo-no-Mikoto meets the earthly deities Ashinazuchi (脚摩乳) and Tenazuchi (手摩乳) and their daughter Inada-hime upstream on the 簸 River (reading unconfirmed) in the province of Izumo. Since their daughters had been swallowed by Yamata-no-Orochi year after year, Susanoo-no-Mikoto changed the maiden into a many-toothed comb (湯津爪櫛) and stuck it in his topknot, filled eight vats with eight-times-brewed sake (八醞酒) to make the serpent drunk, and cut it down with his ten-span sword.

When he cut the serpent's tail, the edge of his sword was slightly chipped, and when he split the tail open there was a sword inside. This is the Kusanagi Sword (草薙剣), and a writing quoted in a small note records that its original name was 天叢雲剣 (reading unconfirmed) and that it was renamed the Kusanagi Sword in the time of Prince Yamato Takeru (日本武皇子). Susanoo-no-Mikoto said, “I cannot make this my own,” and presented it to the heavenly deities.

In the main text, Susanoo-no-Mikoto says, “My heart is refreshed (sugasugashi),” at Suga (清地) in Izumo and builds a palace there, and with Inada-hime he begets Ōanamuchi-no-Kami. Ashinazuchi and Tenazuchi are made chiefs of the palace and given the name 稲田宮主神 (reading unconfirmed), and Susanoo-no-Mikoto afterward goes to the Root Land.

In the variant accounts, the setting, the names of the swords, and where the swords are kept differ. In variant account 2 the setting is upstream on the 可愛 River (reading unconfirmed) in the province of Aki, and the account holds that the Kusanagi Sword is at 吾湯市村 (reading unconfirmed) in the province of Owari (in the charge of the priests of Atsuta), and that the sword that cut the serpent, 蛇之麁正 (reading unconfirmed), is at 石上 (reading unconfirmed). In variant account 3 the sword that cut the serpent is the 蛇韓鋤之剣 (reading unconfirmed) and is with the 神部 of Kibi, and in variant account 4 the serpent is cut with the 天蝿斫之剣 (reading unconfirmed), and Susanoo-no-Mikoto crosses from 曾尸茂梨 (reading unconfirmed) in Silla to Izumo in a boat of clay.

Variant accounts 4 and 5 transmit that Itakeru-no-Kami (or -no-Mikoto) brought back the seeds of trees and planted them from Tsukushi throughout the Land of the Great Eight Islands, making the mountains green, and that Susanoo-no-Mikoto pulled out his hairs and turned them into cryptomeria, cypress, and other trees. Variant account 6 records that Ōanamuchi-no-Mikoto and Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto joined forces to make the land, established methods of curing illness and rites of spell-casting, and that the 幸魂 and 奇魂 (sakimitama and kushimitama) of Ōanamuchi-no-Kami, which appeared lighting up the sea, came to dwell on Mount 三諸山 (reading unconfirmed) and became the deity of 大三輪 (reading unconfirmed).

The deity-name database of Kokugakuin University introduces both a theory that regards variant account 1, which tells only of the marriage without the slaying of the serpent, as the oldest form and holds that the serpent-slaying was added later, and the opinion that the serpent-slaying was simply omitted because variant account 1 extracted only the parts that differ from the main text.

story.text: Susanoo-no-Mikoto descended from heaven and arrived upstream on the 簸 River (reading unconfirmed) in the province of Izumo. Hearing the sound of weeping from upstream, he went to see, and found an old man and an old woman weeping as they stroked a young girl placed between them. When Susanoo-no-Mikoto asked who they were, the old man answered that he was the earthly deity Ashinazuchi, that his wife was Tenazuchi, and that this daughter was Inada-hime (奇稲田姫).

They said the reason they were weeping was that they had once had eight daughters, but each year one had been swallowed by Yamata-no-Orochi, and now this daughter too was about to be swallowed, and there was no way to escape. When Susanoo-no-Mikoto asked whether they would give the daughter to him, the two answered that they would offer her as he wished. Susanoo-no-Mikoto changed Inada-hime into a many-toothed comb and stuck it in his own topknot, had Ashinazuchi and Tenazuchi brew eight-times-brewed sake, made eight temporary platforms (sazuki, 棚), placed on each one a vat filled with sake, and waited.

When the time came, the serpent did indeed appear. Its head and tail were each divided into eight, its eyes were like red ground-cherries (akakagachi, 赤酸醤), pines and oaks (柏) grew on its back, and it stretched across eight hills and eight valleys. The serpent put each of its heads into a vat, drank the sake, became drunk, and fell asleep. Susanoo-no-Mikoto drew the ten-span sword he wore and hacked the serpent to pieces.

When he cut the tail, the edge of his sword was slightly chipped, so he split the tail open to look, and inside there was a sword. This is the so-called Kusanagi Sword (kusanagi no tsurugi). A writing quoted in a small note records that its original name was 天叢雲剣 (reading unconfirmed), probably because there were always clouds above where the serpent was, and that it was renamed the Kusanagi Sword in the time of Prince Yamato Takeru. Susanoo-no-Mikoto said that this was a divine sword and that he could not make it his own, and presented it to the heavenly deities.

After that, Susanoo-no-Mikoto looked for a place to marry and arrived at Suga (清地) in Izumo, where he said, “My heart is refreshed,” and built a palace there. A small note records a song beginning 「夜句茂多菟」 as one that Susanoo-no-Mikoto composed at that time. Susanoo-no-Mikoto was united with Inada-hime and begot Ōanamuchi-no-Kami, and he made Ashinazuchi and Tenazuchi chiefs of the palace and gave them the name 稲田宮主神 (reading unconfirmed). After this, Susanoo-no-Mikoto departed for the Root Land.

quotes.note: The serpent's appearance: its head and tail were each divided into eight, and its eyes were like red ground-cherries (赤酸醤).
“This is a divine sword. How could I dare make it my own?” he said, and presented it to the heavenly deities.
Arriving at Suga (清地), he said, “My heart is refreshed.” This is regarded as the origin of the place name Suga (清).
“I am your sakimitama and kushimitama (幸魂, 奇魂)”: the words with which the deity who appeared from the sea answered Ōanamuchi-no-Kami (variant account 6).

figures.name: Susanoo-no-Mikoto (素戔嗚尊)
figures.role: Cuts down Yamata-no-Orochi upstream on the 簸 River (reading unconfirmed) in Izumo, presents the Kusanagi Sword to the heavenly deities, and builds a palace at Suga.

figures.name: Ashinazuchi (脚摩乳)
figures.role: An earthly deity of Izumo and father of Inada-hime. He is later made chief of the palace and given the name 稲田宮主神 (reading unconfirmed).

figures.name: Tenazuchi (手摩乳)
figures.role: Wife of Ashinazuchi and mother of Inada-hime.

figures.name: Inada-hime (奇稻田姬)
figures.role: The daughter who was about to be swallowed by Yamata-no-Orochi. She is changed into a many-toothed comb and later becomes Susanoo-no-Mikoto's wife (in the variant accounts, 稲田媛 and 真髪触奇稲田媛).

figures.name: Yamata-no-Orochi (八岐大蛇)
figures.role: A great serpent whose head and tail are divided into eight. It swallowed a daughter every year, but is cut down while drunk on sake.

figures.name: Ōanamuchi-no-Kami (大己貴神)
figures.role: In the main text, the child of Susanoo-no-Mikoto and Inada-hime. In variant account 6 he makes the land together with Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto (the reading follows the gloss 「於褒婀娜武智」 in variant account 2).

figures.name: Itakeru-no-Kami (五十猛神)
figures.role: A child of Susanoo-no-Mikoto who appears in variant accounts 4 and 5. He planted the seeds of trees throughout the Land of the Great Eight Islands and is regarded as the great deity who dwells in the province of Kii.

figures.name: Ōyatsuhime-no-Mikoto (大屋津姬命)
figures.role: In variant account 5, regarded as a younger sister of Itakeru-no-Mikoto; a deity who spread the seeds of trees.

figures.name: Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto (少彥名命)
figures.role: In variant account 6, the small deity who made the land with Ōanamuchi-no-Mikoto. He is a child of Takamimusubi-no-Mikoto and later departs for the Eternal Land.

figures.name: Ōmononushi-no-Kami (大物主神)
figures.role: In variant account 6, listed as one of the other names of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami; also, the sakimitama and kushimitama of Ōanamuchi-no-Kami come to dwell on Mount 三諸山 (reading unconfirmed) and become the deity of 大三輪 (reading unconfirmed).

figures.name: Kotoshironushi-no-Kami (事代主神)
figures.role: In an alternative tradition in variant account 6, he is said to have become an eight-fathom bear-wani, visited 三嶋溝樴姫 (reading unconfirmed), and begotten Himetatara-isuzu-hime-no-Mikoto.

figures.name: Himetatara-isuzu-hime-no-Mikoto (姬蹈鞴五十鈴姬命)
figures.role: Child of the deity of 大三輪 (reading unconfirmed) (or of Kotoshironushi-no-Kami), and consort of Emperor 神日本磐余彦火火出見 (reading unconfirmed). A gloss says 「蹈鞴。此云多多羅」.

compare.where: Kojiki, Part 1 — the slaying of Yamata-no-Orochi
compare.text: In the Kojiki, Susanoo-no-Mikoto presents the sword obtained from the serpent's tail to “Amaterasu-Ōmikami,” but the main text of the Nihon Shoki records the recipient only as “the heavenly deities.” In addition, the Kojiki makes Ashinazuchi (足名椎) a child of Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami (大山津見神), and places the setting at 鳥髪 (reading unconfirmed) upstream on the 肥 River (reading unconfirmed).

compare.where: Kojiki, Part 1 — the palace at Suga and the genealogy of Susanoo-no-Mikoto
compare.text: In the Kojiki, the child of Susanoo-no-Mikoto and 櫛名田比売 (reading unconfirmed) is 八嶋士奴美神 (reading unconfirmed), and Ōkuninushi-no-Kami is born in a later generation of that lineage. In the main text of the Nihon Shoki, the child of the two deities is directly Ōanamuchi-no-Kami; variant account 1 makes him a descendant in the fifth generation, and variant account 2 in the sixth generation.

compare.where: Kojiki, Part 1 — Sukunahikona-no-Kami and the deity of 御諸山 (reading unconfirmed)
compare.text: In the Kojiki, 神産巣日神 (reading unconfirmed) says that Sukunahikona-no-Kami (少名毗古那神) is a child who slipped through the fingers of that deity's hand, and the deity who came lighting up the sea says to worship it on the mountain east of the green fence of Yamato (倭). In variant account 6 of the Nihon Shoki, the parent of Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto is Takamimusubi-no-Mikoto, and the deity who came from the sea dwells on Mount 三諸山 (reading unconfirmed) as Ōanamuchi-no-Kami's own sakimitama and kushimitama.

variants.name: Variant account 1
variants.text: The slaying of the serpent is not told. Upstream on the 簸 River (reading unconfirmed), Susanoo-no-Mikoto meets and is united with 稲田媛 (Inada-hime), daughter of 稲田宮主簀狭之八箇耳 (reading unconfirmed), and begets 清之湯山主三名狭漏彦八嶋篠 (reading unconfirmed; two other names are also given). The account holds that the descendant of this deity in the fifth generation is Ōkuninushi-no-Kami (大国主神).

variants.name: Variant account 2
variants.text: The setting is upstream on the 可愛 River (reading unconfirmed) in the province of Aki; 稲田宮主簀狭之八箇耳 (reading unconfirmed), the wife of 脚摩手摩 (reading unconfirmed), is pregnant and fears that the child to be born will again be swallowed by the serpent. Susanoo-no-Mikoto has sake brewed from fruit in eight jars, calls out to the serpent, “You are a deity to be held in awe,” makes it drink, and cuts it down. The account holds that the Kusanagi Sword is now at 吾湯市村 (reading unconfirmed) in the province of Owari, in the charge of the priests of Atsuta, and that the sword that cut the serpent, 蛇之麁正 (reading unconfirmed), is at 石上 (reading unconfirmed). The child born, 真髪触奇稲田媛 (reading unconfirmed), is raised upstream on the 簸 River in Izumo and becomes his consort, and her descendant in the sixth generation is said to be Ōanamuchi-no-Mikoto (大己貴命, ōanamuchi).

variants.name: Variant account 3
variants.text: Ashinazuchi and Tenazuchi ask that, if he is to marry their daughter, he first kill the serpent. The serpent was a fearsome thing, with a rock-pine (石松) on each head and mountains on both flanks. Susanoo-no-Mikoto makes it drink poisoned sake and cuts its heads and belly with the 蛇韓鋤之剣 (reading unconfirmed). The account holds that the Kusanagi Sword that came out of the tail is now in the province of Owari and that the sword that did the cutting is now with the 神部 of Kibi, and it places the setting on a mountain upstream on the 簸 River in Izumo.

variants.name: Variant account 4
variants.text: The banished Susanoo-no-Mikoto takes his child Itakeru-no-Kami and descends to 曾尸茂梨 (reading unconfirmed) in the land of Silla, but, saying he does not wish to live there, crosses eastward in a boat of clay and arrives at the peak of 鳥上 (reading unconfirmed) upstream on the 簸 River in Izumo. He cuts down a man-swallowing serpent with the 天蝿斫之剣 (reading unconfirmed), and has his descendant in the fifth generation, 天之葺根神 (reading unconfirmed), present the sword that came out of its tail to heaven. Itakeru-no-Kami descended carrying the seeds of many trees, and, without planting them in the land of 韓 (reading unconfirmed), planted them from Tsukushi throughout the Land of the Great Eight Islands, making the mountains green; for this reason he is regarded as a deity of merit, and the account holds that he is the great deity who dwells in the province of Kii.

variants.name: Variant account 5
variants.text: Susanoo-no-Mikoto said that the islands of 韓郷 (reading unconfirmed) have gold and silver, and that it would not be good if the land ruled by his child had no floating treasures (浮宝); he pulled out his beard and turned it into cryptomeria (杉), his chest hair into cypress (桧), the hair of his buttocks into podocarpus (柀), and his eyebrows into camphor trees (櫲樟), and fixed their respective uses (floating treasures, timber for palaces, and things on which people lie). Itakeru-no-Mikoto and his younger sisters Ōyatsuhime-no-Mikoto (大屋津姫命) and 採津姫命 (reading unconfirmed) spread the seeds of the trees and crossed over to the province of Kii. Susanoo-no-Mikoto lived on the peak of 熊成峯 (reading unconfirmed) and later entered the Root Land.

variants.name: Variant account 6
variants.text: It records the many other names of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami (Ōmononushi-no-Kami (大物主神), 国作大己貴命, 葦原醜男, 八千戈神 (readings unconfirmed), Ōkunitama-no-Kami (大国玉神), and Utsushikunitama-no-Kami (顕国玉神)), and that he had one hundred and eighty-one children.
