He could hear the petitions of ten people at once and distinguish them without error.
In heaven above there are gods, and on earth below there is the emperor (words from the memorial of Silla and Mimana).

figures.name: 豊御食炊屋姫天皇 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Empress Suiko. Empress of 渟中倉太玉敷天皇 (reading unconfirmed), she ascended the throne after the death of Emperor Sushun.

figures.name: Prince Umayado no Toyotomimi (廐户豐聰耳皇子)
figures.role: Prince Umayado. He became Crown Prince and regent and, after the establishment of the cap ranks, composed the Seventeen-Article Constitution.

figures.name: The Great Minister Umako no Sukune (大臣馬子宿禰)
figures.role: Great Minister. Together with the Crown Prince he was ordered to promote the Three Treasures. His son 善徳臣 (reading unconfirmed) became temple administrator of Hōkō-ji.

figures.name: Eji (慧慈)
figures.role: A monk of Koguryŏ. He came in the 3rd year, became the Crown Prince's teacher, and lived at Hōkō-ji.

figures.name: Esō (慧聰)
figures.role: A monk of Paekche. Together with Eji he was regarded as a pillar of the Three Treasures.

figures.name: 境部臣 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: The commander-in-chief who attacked Silla in the 8th year to rescue Mimana.

figures.name: Prince Kume (來目皇子)
figures.role: He became General for Attacking Silla but fell ill, and died in Tsukushi in the 11th year.

figures.name: 當麻皇子 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Elder brother of Prince Kume. He became general in his place but turned back because of his wife's death.

figures.name: Kanroku (觀勒)
figures.role: A monk of Paekche. He presented calendars, books of astronomy and geography, and books of 遁甲 (reading unconfirmed) and occult arts.

figures.name: Hata no Kawakatsu (秦造河勝)
figures.role: He received the Crown Prince's Buddha image and built 蜂岡寺 (reading unconfirmed).

compare.where: Kojiki, Part 3, final section — section on Empress Suiko (豐御食炊屋比賣命 (reading unconfirmed))
compare.text: The Kojiki gives Empress Suiko's palace only as the 小治田宮 (reading unconfirmed). The Nihon Shoki says that she ascended the throne at the Toyura Palace and moved to the Oharida Palace in the 10th month of the 11th year.

compare.where: Kojiki, Part 3 — entry on the empresses, consorts and children in the section on Emperor Kinmei
compare.text: In the Kojiki, "豐御氣炊屋比賣命" appears among the children born to Emperor Kinmei by 岐多斯比賣 (reading unconfirmed), daughter of the Great Minister Iname no Sukune. The Nihon Shoki makes her a middle daughter of 天國排開廣庭天皇 (reading unconfirmed) and the full younger sister of 橘豊日天皇 (reading unconfirmed), and records her childhood name as Princess Nukatabe, but this childhood name could not be confirmed in the Kojiki.

compare.where: Kojiki, Part 3 — entry on the empresses, consorts and children in the section on Emperor Yōmei
compare.text: In the section on Emperor Yōmei, the Kojiki only gives the name "上宮之厩戶豐聰耳命" among his children; for his becoming Crown Prince and regent, or for the twelve cap ranks and the Seventeen-Article Constitution, no corresponding entries could be confirmed in the Kojiki.

suiko-2.title: Empress Suiko, the Envoys to the Great Tang, and the Death of the Crown Prince of the Upper Palace
suiko-2.lead: The 13th to the 36th years of Empress Suiko record the completion of the jōroku (sixteen-foot) Buddha images, the dispatch of Ono no Imoko to the Great Tang and the arrival of Pei Shiqing, negotiations with Silla and Mimana, and the compilation of the Tennōki (Record of the Emperors) and Kokki (Record of the Country). After Prince Umayado no Toyotomimi and the Great Minister of the Island (嶋大臣) passed away and the offices of Sōjō and Sōzu were established, the empress left words to Prince Tamura and Prince Yamashiro no Ōe and died.

points.text: In the 7th month of the 15th year, Ono no Omi Imoko, of the rank Greater Propriety, was sent to the Great Tang, and in the 4th month of the 16th year the Tang envoy Pei Shiqing came to Tsukushi together with Imoko. Imoko reported that the letter of the Tang emperor had been stolen from him in Paekche; the ministers said he should be exiled, but the empress pardoned him.

In the 9th month of the 16th year, when Pei Shiqing returned home, Imoko was again sent with him as ambassador, and the empress sent a letter beginning "東天皇敬白西皇帝". At this time eight students and student monks in all were also sent to Tang.

In the 2nd month of the 29th year, Prince Umayado no Toyotomimi passed away at the Ikaruga Palace, and people lamented, "The sun and moon have lost their light, and heaven and earth have crumbled." It is written that the Koguryŏ monk Eji vowed that he would surely die on the 5th day of the 2nd month of the following year and meet the Crown Prince in the Pure Land, and that he died on that day.

In the 28th year, the Crown Prince and the Great Minister of the Island deliberated together and compiled the Tennōki and Kokki, as well as the fundamental records (本記) of the Omi, Muraji, Tomo-no-Miyatsuko, Kuni-no-Miyatsuko, the hundred and eighty be (部) and the common people.

In the 32nd year, prompted by an incident in which a monk struck his grandfather with an axe, Kanroku was made Sōjō and 鞍部徳積 (reading unconfirmed) was made Sōzu to supervise the monks and nuns. A survey in the 9th month recorded forty-six temples, 816 monks and 569 nuns.

For Empress Suiko, the Kojiki records that she ruled the realm for thirty-seven years and that her tomb was at 大野岡上 (reading unconfirmed) and was later moved to the 科長大陵 (reading unconfirmed). In the Nihon Shoki, the empress died in the 3rd month of the 36th year and, in accordance with her last edict, was buried in the tomb of Prince Takeda.

story.text: In the 4th month of the 13th year, the empress, together with the Crown Prince, the Great Minister, the princes and the ministers, made a vow and began making two jōroku (sixteen-foot) Buddha images, one of bronze and one of embroidery, and Kuratsukuri no Tori was made the craftsman for the images. Hearing of this, 大興王 (reading unconfirmed), king of the country of Koguryŏ, sent three hundred ryō of gold as tribute. In the 10th month, the Crown Prince took up residence at the Ikaruga Palace. In the 4th month of the 14th year, the jōroku bronze image was completed and was to be placed in the golden hall of Gangō-ji, but the image was taller than the door of the hall; when the workmen discussed breaking the door, Tori's excellent skill made it possible to bring it in without breaking the door. From this year, Buddhist feasts came to be held at every temple on the 8th day of the 4th month and the 15th day of the 7th month. In the 5th month, citing the services of his grandfather Shiba Tatto, his father 多須那 (reading unconfirmed) and his aunt 嶋女 (reading unconfirmed), and his present service as well, the empress gave Tori the rank of Greater Benevolence and twenty chō of paddy fields in 坂田郡 (reading unconfirmed), Ōmi Province, and Tori built 金剛寺 (reading unconfirmed) on those fields for the empress.

In the 7th month of the 14th year, at the empress's request, the Crown Prince lectured on the Śrīmālā Sutra over three days, and in this year he also lectured on the Lotus Sutra at the 岡本宮 (reading unconfirmed) palace, so the empress gave the Crown Prince one hundred chō of paddy fields in Harima Province, which the Crown Prince donated to Ikaruga-dera. In the 2nd month of the 15th year, the 壬生部 (reading unconfirmed) was established, and, citing how the emperors of her ancestral line had revered the gods of heaven and earth and worshiped the mountains and rivers, the empress issued an edict that the ministers should wholeheartedly worship the gods of heaven and earth. Some days later, the Crown Prince and the Great Minister led the officials in worshiping the gods of heaven and earth. In the 7th month, Ono no Omi Imoko, of the rank Greater Propriety, was sent to the Great Tang, with 鞍作福利 (reading unconfirmed) as interpreter. In the winter of this year, the 高市池 (reading unconfirmed), 藤原池 (reading unconfirmed) and other ponds were made in the province of Yamato (倭国), a great canal was dug at 栗隈 (reading unconfirmed) in Yamashiro Province, and miyake estates were established in each province.

In the 4th month of the 16th year, Imoko returned from the Great Tang, and the Tang envoy Pei Shiqing and twelve attendants arrived in Tsukushi following Imoko. It is recorded that in Tang, Imoko was called 蘇因高 (reading unconfirmed). In the 6th month, the envoys arrived at the port of Naniwa and were lodged in a new guesthouse, but Imoko reported that the letter given him by the Tang emperor had been stolen from him in Paekche, and the ministers said he should be exiled. The empress pardoned Imoko, saying it would not be good if this were heard by the guests from a great country. In the 8th month, Pei Shiqing presented the Tang emperor's letter at court; the princes, royal relatives and ministers wore gold hair ornaments (髻華) on their heads and garments of brocade, purple, embroidery and the like. In the 9th month, when Pei Shiqing returned home, Imoko was sent with him as ambassador and 吉士雄成 (reading unconfirmed) as vice-envoy; the empress sent a letter saying, "The Emperor of the East respectfully addresses the Emperor of the West," and eight students and student monks were also sent.

In the 4th month of the 17th year, ten Paekche monks including 道欣 (reading unconfirmed) and seventy-five lay people, who had met a storm on their way to the land of Wu (呉国), arrived at the port of 葦北津 (reading unconfirmed) in Higo Province; while they were being sent back, eleven of the monks asked to stay and lived at Gangō-ji. In the 9th month, Imoko returned from the Great Tang, but the interpreter 福利 (reading unconfirmed) did not return. In the 3rd month of the 18th year, the king of Koguryŏ presented the monks Donchō and 法定 (reading unconfirmed); Donchō knew the Five Classics and was also able to make pigments, paper and ink, and water mills (碾磑). In the 10th month, envoys from Silla and Mimana arrived at the capital and stated the purpose of their mission at court, and the Great Minister stood up to listen. In the 2nd month of the 20th year, the Imperial Lady Dowager (皇太夫人) 堅塩媛 (reading unconfirmed) was reburied in the 檜隈大陵 (reading unconfirmed) tomb and eulogies were offered; in this year 路子工 (reading unconfirmed), who had come from Paekche, built the form of Mount Sumeru and a Wu-style bridge (呉橋) in the southern courtyard, and Mimashi transmitted the gigaku dance.

In the 12th month of the 21st year, at 片岡 (reading unconfirmed) the Crown Prince gave food and drink to a starving man lying by the road, and took off his own garment and laid it over him. After the man died and was buried, the Crown Prince, saying that he had been no ordinary person, had the grave opened; there was no corpse, and only the garment lay folded on top of the coffin, so the people of the time said that it is truly so that a sage knows a sage. In the 6th month of the 22nd year, Inukami no Kimi Mitasuki and 矢田部造 (reading unconfirmed) were sent to the Great Tang, and the two returned in the 9th month of the 23rd year. In the 11th month of the 23rd year, the Koguryŏ monk Eji returned to his country. In the 8th month of the 26th year, Koguryŏ reported that it had defeated an army of three hundred thousand of Emperor Yang of Sui and presented captives, drums and wind instruments, and other things. In the 28th year, the top of the 檜隈陵 (reading unconfirmed) tomb was covered with gravel, and the Crown Prince and the Great Minister of the Island compiled the Tennōki, the Kokki and other records.

In the 2nd month of the 29th year, Prince Umayado no Toyotomimi passed away at midnight at the Ikaruga Palace; the old grieved as if they had lost a beloved child, and the young as if they had lost a loving father and mother. The prince was buried in the 磯長陵 (reading unconfirmed) tomb, and Eji of Koguryŏ held a Buddhist feast and vowed that he would surely die on the 5th day of the 2nd month of the following year and meet the Crown Prince in the Pure Land, and he died on that day. In the 31st year, because Silla attacked Mimana, a large army under 境部臣雄摩侶 (reading unconfirmed) and others was sent out without waiting for the envoys' reply; Silla asked to surrender, but the Great Minister regretted having sent the army so early. In the 4th month of the 32nd year, an incident occurred in which a monk struck his grandfather with an axe; on Kanroku's memorial, all but the wicked monk were pardoned, and Kanroku was made Sōjō and 鞍部徳積 (reading unconfirmed) Sōzu to supervise the monks and nuns. In the 10th month, the Great Minister asked to have 葛城県 (reading unconfirmed) made his own fief, but the empress refused, saying that later generations would say a foolish woman had ruled the realm and lost that district. In the 5th month of the 34th year, the Great Minister, son of Iname no Sukune, passed away; it is recorded that he was called the Great Minister of the Island (嶋大臣) because he had built a small island in the pond in the garden of his house beside the Asuka River.

In the 34th year, long rains continued from the 3rd month to the 7th month, the realm suffered a great famine, and robbery and theft occurred frequently. In the 2nd month of the 36th year, the empress fell ill, and in the 3rd month there was a solar eclipse. The empress summoned Prince Tamura and admonished him not to speak lightly about the heavenly throne, and she instructed Prince Yamashiro no Ōe that, since he was still young, even if he desired it in his heart he should not voice it but should wait for the words of the ministers. The next day the empress died at the age of seventy-five and was given temporary enshrinement in the southern courtyard. In the 9th month the funeral rites began, and, in accordance with her last edict that, because the five grains had not ripened and the people were starving, no tomb should be built for a lavish burial and she should instead be buried in the tomb of Prince Takeda, she was buried in the tomb of Prince Takeda.

quotes.note: The Emperor of the East respectfully addresses the Emperor of the West (the opening of the letter sent to the Tang emperor).
The sun and the moon have lost their light, and heaven and earth have crumbled (words of the people lamenting the Crown Prince's death).
It is true that a sage knows a sage.
A foolish woman ruled the realm and promptly lost that district (the judgment of later generations that the empress feared).

figures.name: 豊御食炊屋姫天皇 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Empress Suiko. She died at seventy-five in the 3rd month of the 36th year and was buried in the tomb of Prince Takeda.

figures.name: Prince Umayado no Toyotomimi (廐户豐聰耳皇子)
figures.role: The Crown Prince of the Upper Palace (上宮太子). He lectured on the Śrīmālā Sutra and the Lotus Sutra, compiled the Tennōki and Kokki, and passed away at the Ikaruga Palace in the 29th year.

figures.name: The Great Minister of the Island (嶋大臣)
figures.role: Great Minister. Son of Iname no Sukune. He compiled the Kokki and other records together with the Crown Prince, and passed away in the 34th year.

figures.name: Kuratsukuri no Tori (鞍作鳥)
figures.role: The craftsman of the jōroku Buddha images. He brought the image into the golden hall without breaking the door, and was granted the rank of Greater Benevolence.

figures.name: Ono no Omi Imoko (小野臣妹子)
figures.role: Of the rank Greater Propriety. He was sent to the Great Tang and in Tang was called 蘇因高 (reading unconfirmed).

figures.name: Pei Shiqing (裴世清)
figures.role: An attendant for guests (掌客) of the Tang office 鴻臚寺 (reading unconfirmed). He came to the court together with Imoko and presented the Tang emperor's letter.

figures.name: Inukami no Kimi Mitasuki (犬上君御田鍬)
figures.role: He was sent to the Great Tang in the 22nd year and returned the following year.

figures.name: Donchō (曇徴)
figures.role: A monk of Koguryŏ. He knew the Five Classics and made pigments, paper and ink, and water mills (碾磑).

figures.name: Eji (慧慈)
figures.role: A monk of Koguryŏ and the Crown Prince's teacher. It is written that after returning to his country he heard of the Crown Prince's death and died on that day the following year.

figures.name: Kanroku (觀勒)
figures.role: A monk of Paekche. He submitted a memorial asking for the pardon of the monks and nuns, and became the first Sōjō.

figures.name: Prince Tamura (田村皇子)
figures.role: The prince whom the empress, on her sickbed, admonished not to speak lightly about the heavenly throne.

figures.name: Prince Yamashiro no Ōe (山背大兄)
figures.role: The person whom the empress, on her sickbed, instructed to wait for the words of the ministers.

compare.where: Kojiki, Part 3, final section — section on Empress Suiko (豐御食炊屋比賣命 (reading unconfirmed))
compare.text: The Kojiki records her reign as thirty-seven years. The Nihon Shoki says that the empress died at seventy-five in the 3rd month of the 36th year.

compare.where: Kojiki, Part 3 — end of the section on Empress Suiko (tomb)
compare.text: The Kojiki places her tomb at 大野岡上 (reading unconfirmed) and records that it was later moved to the 科長大陵 (reading unconfirmed). The Nihon Shoki says that, in accordance with her last edict, she was buried in the tomb of Prince Takeda.

compare.where: Kojiki, Part 3 — section on Empress Suiko (the last entry of the Kojiki)
compare.text: The section on Empress Suiko in the Kojiki ends with only her palace, the length of her reign and her tomb; for the envoys to the Great Tang, the arrival of Pei Shiqing, and the death of the Crown Prince of the Upper Palace, no corresponding entries could be confirmed in the Kojiki.

variants.name: One version says (一云)
variants.text: Concerning the attire on the day Pei Shiqing was received, the main text says that brocade, purple, embroidery, woven fabric and figured silks of five colors were used for the garments, but one version says that the colors of the garments all followed the colors of the caps.

jomei.title: Emperor Jomei — The Ministers’ Debate over the Succession, and the Great Palace and Great Temple of Kudara
jomei.lead: Empress Suiko died without naming a successor, and Soga no Emishi and the ministers debated whether to enthrone Prince Tamura or Prince Yamashiro no Ōe; Prince Tamura took the throne. His reign records the coming and going of envoys with Tang, Paekche and Koguryŏ, a campaign against the Emishi, and the building of a great palace and a great temple beside the Kudara River (百済川), and he died at the Kudara Palace (百済宮) in his 13th year.

points.text: In the 36th year of Empress Suiko the empress died, but no successor had been decided. Soga no Emishi gathered the ministers at his house, presented her last words, and asked whether Prince Tamura or Prince Yamashiro no Ōe should be enthroned. The ministers were divided between those who backed Prince Tamura and those who backed Prince Yamashiro no Ōe.

Prince Yamashiro no Ōe gave a detailed account of the words he had heard directly from the empress on her sickbed and protested that they differed from the last words reported by the ministers. 境部摩理勢 (reading unconfirmed), who backed Prince Yamashiro no Ōe, refused to follow Emishi; troops were sent against him, and he was killed together with his son.

In the first month of the 1st year, the Great Minister and the high officials presented the imperial seal to Prince Tamura; the prince declined once and then took the throne that same day. The text records that in the first month of the 2nd year he made Princess Takara (宝皇女) his empress, and that she bore Prince Katsuragi (葛城皇子; the emperor who reigned at the Ōmi Ōtsu Palace), Princess Hashihito (間人皇女) and Prince Ōama (大海皇子; the emperor who reigned at the Kiyomihara Palace).

In the eighth month of the 2nd year, 犬上君三田耜 and 薬師恵日 (readings unconfirmed) were sent to Great Tang. In the eighth month of the 4th year the Tang envoy 高表仁 (reading unconfirmed) came escorting 三田耜, and in the tenth month he was welcomed at Naniwa Harbor (難波津) with thirty-two ships. 高表仁 and his party went home in the first month of the 5th year.

In the seventh month of the 11th year the emperor ordered a great palace and a great temple to be built beside the Kudara River (百済川); the people of the west were made to build the palace and the people of the east the temple, and in the twelfth month a nine-storied pagoda was erected beside the Kudara River. The emperor moved to the Kudara Palace (百済宮) in the tenth month of the 12th year and died there in the tenth month of the 13th year.

The text records that the place of temporary enshrinement (mogari, 殯) was north of the palace and was called the “Great Mogari of Kudara” (百済大殯), and that on this occasion the crown prince, Prince 開別 (開別皇子, reading unconfirmed), then sixteen years old, delivered the eulogy (shinobigoto, 誄).

story.text: Emperor Jomei (息長足日廣額天皇) was a grandson of Emperor Bidatsu (渟中倉太珠敷天皇) and a son of Prince 彦人大兄 (彦人大兄皇子, reading unconfirmed); his mother was Princess 糠手姫 (糠手姫皇女, reading unconfirmed). After the crown prince 豊聡耳尊 (reading unconfirmed) died in the 29th year of Empress Suiko (豊御食炊屋姫天皇), no crown prince had been appointed; the empress died in the third month of her 36th year, and even after the funeral rites were completed in the ninth month the succession had not been settled.

The Great Minister Soga no Emishi feared that if he decided alone the ministers would not follow him, so after consulting 阿倍麻呂臣 (reading unconfirmed) he invited the ministers to his house. 阿倍臣 presented the late sovereign’s last words, according to which the sovereign on the sickbed had spoken to Prince Tamura and to Prince Yamashiro no Ōe in turn, and asked whom they should make sovereign. 大伴鯨連 (reading unconfirmed) and others backed Prince Tamura, 許勢臣大摩呂 (reading unconfirmed) and others backed Prince Yamashiro no Ōe, and 蘇我倉摩呂臣 (reading unconfirmed) withheld his answer. Because the ministers could not agree, Emishi withdrew without being able to settle the matter.

Prince Yamashiro no Ōe, who was at the Ikaruga Palace (斑鳩宮), heard of this debate and sent messengers to ask the views of Emishi, his uncle. Emishi had them answer that he had only told the ministers of the late sovereign’s testament and that it was not his own private opinion. Prince Yamashiro no Ōe stated that he had been called to the sick sovereign’s bedside and had received words on great matters of state directly, and that the sovereign had told him that Emishi was concerned about him; he repeatedly asked to learn the true content of the testament.

境部摩理勢 (reading unconfirmed) backed Prince Yamashiro no Ōe and would not give way. He tore down the huts at the site where the tomb of the 嶋大臣 (reading unconfirmed) was being built, withdrew to the Soga estate house (田家), and then moved to the palace of Prince 泊瀬 (泊瀬王, reading unconfirmed) at Ikaruga. Prince Yamashiro no Ōe admonished 摩理勢 to go along with the ministers. When Prince 泊瀬 died of illness, 摩理勢 lost his refuge, and he was strangled together with his son 阿椰 (reading unconfirmed) by troops that Emishi sent against him. 毛津 (reading unconfirmed) also hid in a nunnery, then fled into Mount Unebi (畝傍山) and took his own life in the mountains.

In the first month of the 1st year, the Great Minister and the high officials presented the imperial seal to Prince Tamura; the prince declined, but because the ministers pressed him strongly he took the throne that same day. In the first month of the 2nd year he made Princess Takara his empress, and 法提郎媛 (reading unconfirmed), daughter of the Soga 嶋大臣 (reading unconfirmed), bore Prince Furuhito (古人皇子). In this year envoys came from Koguryŏ and Paekche; in the eighth month 犬上君三田耜 and 薬師恵日 (readings unconfirmed) were sent to Great Tang, and in the tenth month the emperor moved to the Okamoto Palace (岡本宮) beside the hill of Asuka.

In the 3rd year people of 掖玖 (reading unconfirmed) came and submitted, and King 義慈 (reading unconfirmed) of Paekche sent Prince 豊章 (reading unconfirmed) as a hostage. In the 4th year the Tang envoy 高表仁 (reading unconfirmed) came escorting 三田耜, and the student monks 霊雲 and 僧旻 (readings unconfirmed) and others returned with him. In the 8th year all those who had violated palace women (采女) were punished, and in the sixth month the Okamoto Palace burned and the emperor moved to the 田中宮 (reading unconfirmed). In the 9th year, in the campaign against the rebellious Emishi, the general 上毛野君形名 (reading unconfirmed) was surrounded, but his wife gave him wine to drink and encouraged him, and had the women twang their bowstrings, so the soldiers rallied and defeated the Emishi.

In the seventh month of the 11th year the emperor ordered a great palace and a great temple to be built beside the Kudara River; in the twelfth month a nine-storied pagoda was erected, and he went to the hot-spring palace (温湯宮) in Iyo. In the 12th year he had 恵隠 (reading unconfirmed) expound the Sutra of Immeasurable Life (無量寿経), welcomed 清安 and 高向漢人玄理 (readings unconfirmed), who had returned from Tang, and in the tenth month moved to the Kudara Palace. In the tenth month of the 13th year the emperor died at the Kudara Palace; the temporary enshrinement was held north of the palace, and the crown prince, Prince 開別 (reading unconfirmed), then sixteen years old, delivered the eulogy.

quotes.note: The words with which Prince Tamura, presented with the imperial seal, declined once, saying that he did not have the ability to bear the great affairs of the state.
Words that Prince Yamashiro no Ōe cites as an admonition the former sovereign left to his children before dying. It means: do nothing evil, and practice what is good.
In the 9th year, when a large star streaked across the sky with a sound, 僧旻 (reading unconfirmed) said, “It is not a shooting star but a heavenly dog (天狗); its barking voice is like thunder.”
The record that, in building the great palace and the great temple beside the Kudara River, the people of the west were made to build the palace and the people of the east the temple.

figures.name: Emperor Jomei (息長足日廣額天皇; Prince Tamura, 田村皇子)
figures.role: Son of Prince 彦人大兄 (reading unconfirmed); the emperor who took the throne after the ministers’ debate.

figures.name: Soga no Emishi (蘇我蝦夷)
figures.role: As Great Minister he gathered the ministers and steered the debate toward making Prince Tamura the successor.

figures.name: Prince Yamashiro no Ōe (山背大兄王)
figures.role: A prince living at the Ikaruga Palace who set out the last words he himself had heard and pressed Emishi for an answer.

figures.name: 境部摩理勢 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Backed Prince Yamashiro no Ōe and defied Emishi; he was killed together with his son.

figures.name: Princess Takara (寶皇女)
figures.role: Became empress in the 2nd year and bore Prince Katsuragi, Princess Hashihito and Prince Ōama.

figures.name: 犬上君三田耜 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Sent to Great Tang in the 2nd year; he returned in the 4th year, escorted by the Tang envoy 高表仁 (reading unconfirmed).

figures.name: 高表仁 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: An envoy of Great Tang who escorted 三田耜 to Naniwa Harbor and went home in the 5th year.

figures.name: 上毛野君形名 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: General in the campaign against the Emishi in the 9th year; with his wife’s encouragement he turned a losing situation around.

figures.name: 僧旻 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: A student monk who returned from Tang and gave his opinions on shooting stars and comets.

figures.name: 開別皇子 (reading unconfirmed; also Prince Katsuragi, 葛城皇子)
figures.role: Son of the emperor and Princess Takara; at sixteen he delivered the eulogy at his father’s temporary enshrinement.

kogyoku.title: Empress Kōgyoku — The Fall of the Royal House of the Upper Palace and the Killing of Soga no Iruka
kogyoku.lead: The empress of Emperor Jomei took the throne. Iruka, son of the Great Minister Soga no Emishi, seized control of the government, and in the 2nd year he destroyed Prince Yamashiro no Ōe and others at Ikaruga. In the sixth month of the 4th year, Prince Naka-no-Ōe, Nakatomi no Kamako and others cut Iruka down in the Great Audience Hall (大極殿), and the empress yielded the throne to Prince Karu.

points.text: In the eleventh month of the 2nd year, Soga no Iruka sent troops to attack Prince Yamashiro no Ōe and others at Ikaruga. The prince rejected a plan to raise troops in the eastern provinces, saying he did not want the people to suffer for his sake alone, and took his own life at Ikaruga-dera (斑鳩寺) together with his consorts, children and younger kinsmen.

In the sixth month of the 4th year, at the ceremony where the memorial of the Three Han (三韓) was read aloud, Prince Naka-no-Ōe, together with 佐伯連子麻呂 and 葛城稚犬養連網田 (readings unconfirmed), cut down Iruka before the empress in the Great Audience Hall. Prince Naka-no-Ōe told the empress that Iruka had been destroying the imperial family and was trying to overturn the imperial throne.

The next day, Soga no Emishi and others, who were about to be put to death, burned the Tennōki (天皇記), the Kokki (国記) and their treasures, but 船史恵尺 (reading unconfirmed) pulled out the Kokki as it was about to burn and presented it to Prince Naka-no-Ōe. The day after that, the empress yielded the throne to Prince Karu and made Prince Naka-no-Ōe crown prince.

Nakatomi no Kamako became close to Prince Naka-no-Ōe after picking up and handing back the shoe that had come off the prince’s foot during a ball game (打毱) under the zelkova tree at Hōkō-ji (法興寺), and the two worked out their plans on the way to and from Master 南淵 (南淵先生, reading unconfirmed), under whom they studied the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius (周孔). Kamako also advised that the daughter of Soga no Kurayamada no Maro (蘇我倉山田麻呂) be made Prince Naka-no-Ōe’s consort.

In the seventh month of the 1st year, neither the prayers taught by the village priests (祝部) nor the Soga Great Minister’s rotating reading of Mahayana sutras at the temples brought rain; but in the eighth month, when the empress bowed to the four directions and prayed to Heaven on the upper reaches of the river at 南淵 (reading unconfirmed), thunder and rain continued for five days, and the people praised her as “the Emperor of Perfect Virtue” (至徳天皇).

In this year (the 1st year), Emishi set up an ancestral shrine at 高宮 (reading unconfirmed) in Katsuragi and performed the dance of eight rows (八佾). He mobilized people from all over the country to build twin tombs (the Great Tomb and the Lesser Tomb) for himself and Iruka at 今来 (reading unconfirmed), even putting to work the people of the 乳部 (reading unconfirmed) of the Upper Palace (上宮). 上宮大娘姫王 (reading unconfirmed) was deeply angered at this.

story.text: Empress Kōgyoku (天豊財重日足姫天皇) was a granddaughter of Prince 押坂彦人大兄 (押坂彦人大兄皇子, reading unconfirmed) and a daughter of Prince 茅渟 (茅渟王, reading unconfirmed), and she became empress in the 2nd year of Emperor Jomei. She took the throne in the first month of the 1st year and kept Soga no Emishi on as Great Minister, but his son Iruka took charge of the government himself, and his power surpassed his father’s. From the same month, Paekche envoys reported that their country was in great disorder and that members of the royal family such as 翹岐 (reading unconfirmed) had been banished to an island, and Koguryŏ envoys also reported that the minister 伊梨柯須彌 (reading unconfirmed) had killed the king. 翹岐 was lodged at the house of 阿曇山背連 (reading unconfirmed) and was entertained by the Soga Great Minister.

In the seventh month of the 1st year, in response to a drought, the ministers, following the teaching of the village priests (祝部), killed cattle and horses to worship the gods of the shrines, moved the markets, and prayed to the river god (河伯), but without effect. The Soga Great Minister proposed reading Mahayana sutras in rotation at the temples to pray for rain; in the south court of the Great Temple (大寺), images of buddhas and bodhisattvas and of the Four Heavenly Kings were set up and the Great Cloud Sutra (大雲経) and other sutras were read, but only a little rain fell, and the reading was stopped. On the first day of the eighth month, when the empress bowed to the four directions and looked up to Heaven in prayer on the upper reaches of the river at 南淵 (reading unconfirmed), thunder rolled and heavy rain fell for five days; the people cried out “ten thousand years” (万歳) and called her “the Emperor of Perfect Virtue” (至徳天皇).

In the ninth month the empress called up laborers from Ōmi and Koshi to build a great temple, and ordered timber and labor to be gathered from the provinces from Tōtōmi in the east to Aki in the west in order to build palace buildings by the twelfth month. Several thousand Emishi from the Koshi frontier came over and submitted. In the twelfth month the funeral of Emperor Jomei was held and he was buried at 滑谷崗 (reading unconfirmed), and the empress moved to the Oharida Palace (小墾田宮). In this year Emishi set up an ancestral shrine at 高宮 (reading unconfirmed) in Katsuragi and performed the dance of eight rows (八佾), and built twin tombs for himself and Iruka at 今来 (reading unconfirmed), even putting to work the people of the 乳部 (reading unconfirmed) of the Upper Palace (上宮), so that 上宮大娘姫王 (reading unconfirmed) lamented in anger.

In the fourth month of the 2nd year the empress moved to the new Itabuki Palace (板蓋宮) in Asuka. In the ninth month Emperor Jomei was buried at the 押坂陵 (reading unconfirmed), and 吉備嶋皇祖母命 (reading unconfirmed) died. In the tenth month Emishi, who was ill and did not attend court, secretly gave Iruka the purple cap, treating him as though he held the rank of Great Minister. Iruka plotted on his own to set aside the princes of the Upper Palace and to make Furuhito no Ōe (古人大兄) emperor, and around this time a children’s song (童謡) was sung.

In the eleventh month Iruka sent 巨勢徳太臣 and 土師娑婆連 (readings unconfirmed) to attack Prince Yamashiro no Ōe and others at Ikaruga. The servant 三成 (reading unconfirmed) and others fought them off, and the prince threw a horse’s bones into his sleeping chamber and fled to Mount Ikoma (膽駒山) with his consorts, children and younger kinsmen. 三輪文屋君 (reading unconfirmed) urged that if they raised troops on the basis of the 乳部 (reading unconfirmed) in the eastern provinces they would certainly win, but the prince refused, saying he did not want the people to suffer for his sake alone. The princes returned to Ikaruga-dera and, surrounded by troops, took their own lives together with their consorts, children and younger kinsmen. When Emishi heard of this, he cursed Iruka’s foolishness.

In the first month of the 3rd year, Nakatomi no Kamako was appointed Head of the Office of Divinities (神祇伯) but declined and withdrew to 三嶋 (reading unconfirmed). Later he became close to Prince Naka-no-Ōe at a ball game, and they consulted again and again on the way to and from Master 南淵 (reading unconfirmed), under whom they studied the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius. On Kamako’s advice, the daughter of Soga no Kurayamada no Maro became Prince Naka-no-Ōe’s consort. In the seventh month 大生部多 (reading unconfirmed), from beside the 不尽河 (reading unconfirmed) in the eastern provinces, urged people to worship an insect as the god of Tokoyo (常世神), and many threw away their wealth, so Hata no Kawakatsu (秦造河勝) of 葛野 (reading unconfirmed) struck 多. In the eleventh month Emishi and Iruka built their houses side by side on Amakashi Hill (甘檮崗) and equipped them with stockades and armories.

In the sixth month of the 4th year, Prince Naka-no-Ōe revealed to Kurayamada no Maro (倉山田麻呂臣) the plan to have him read the memorial of the Three Han. On the day the empress came out to the Great Audience Hall, while the memorial was being read, Prince Naka-no-Ōe, 子麻呂 (reading unconfirmed) and others cut Iruka down, and Prince Naka-no-Ōe set out Iruka’s crimes before the empress. Prince Naka-no-Ōe entered Hōkō-ji and made ready, and at the words of 高向臣国押 (reading unconfirmed), the 漢直 (reading unconfirmed) and others on Emishi’s side dispersed. The next day Emishi and others burned the Tennōki, the Kokki and their treasures, and 船史恵尺 (reading unconfirmed) pulled out the Kokki and presented it to Prince Naka-no-Ōe. The day after that, the empress yielded the throne to Prince Karu and made Prince Naka-no-Ōe crown prince.

quotes.note: The words of Prince Yamashiro no Ōe: is it not the mark of a true man to give up his own life, rather than fight, in order to make the country secure?
Prince Naka-no-Ōe’s appeal to the empress that 鞍作 (reading unconfirmed; that is, Iruka) had wiped out the imperial family and was about to overturn the imperial throne.
The record that Prince Naka-no-Ōe and Nakatomi no Kamako studied the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius under Master 南淵 (reading unconfirmed).
Rain fell after the empress’s prayer, and the people cried out “ten thousand years” and praised her as “the emperor whose virtue is supreme.”

figures.name: Empress Kōgyoku (天豐財重日足姫天皇; partial reading: 重日 = ikashihi, from the original text’s reading note 伊柯之比)
figures.role: Empress of Emperor Jomei; she took the throne after her husband’s death and yielded it to Prince Karu in the 4th year.

figures.name: Soga no Iruka (蘇我臣入鹿), also called 鞍作 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Son of Emishi; he seized control of the government and destroyed Prince Yamashiro no Ōe and others, but was cut down in the Great Audience Hall.

figures.name: Soga no Emishi (蘇我大臣蝦夷)
figures.role: As Great Minister he built an ancestral shrine and twin tombs, and the day after Iruka’s death he burned the Tennōki and the Kokki.

figures.name: Prince Yamashiro no Ōe (山背大兄王)
figures.role: A prince of the Upper Palace (上宮); attacked by Iruka’s troops, he took his own life together with his family at Ikaruga-dera.

figures.name: Prince Naka-no-Ōe (中大兄)
figures.role: Plotted with Nakatomi no Kamako and others and cut Iruka down; he became crown prince when the throne was handed on.

figures.name: Nakatomi no Kamako (中臣鎌子連)
figures.role: Drew close to Prince Naka-no-Ōe and advanced the plan to strike down Iruka; in the Great Audience Hall he stood by with bow and arrows to help.

figures.name: Soga no Kurayamada no Maro (蘇我倉山田麻呂臣)
figures.role: Gave his daughter to Prince Naka-no-Ōe as consort, and read aloud the memorial of the Three Han in the Great Audience Hall.

figures.name: 佐伯連子麻呂 and 葛城稚犬養連網田 (readings unconfirmed)
figures.role: Were given swords and cut Iruka down in the Great Audience Hall.

figures.name: Furuhito no Ōe (古人大兄)
figures.role: The prince whom Iruka meant to make emperor; on seeing Iruka’s death he shut himself up in his private palace.

figures.name: 船史惠尺 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Pulled out the Kokki that Emishi and the others had set on fire and presented it to Prince Naka-no-Ōe.

figures.name: 國勝吉士水鷄 (reading unconfirmed; partial reading: 水鷄 = kuhina, from the original text’s reading note 倶比那)
figures.role: Named as envoy to Paekche in the second month of the 1st year.

variants.name: A certain text says (或本云)
variants.text: The main text names the commanders who attacked Prince Yamashiro no Ōe as 巨勢徳太臣 and 土師娑婆連 (readings unconfirmed), but a certain text names them as 巨勢徳太臣 and 倭馬飼首 (reading unconfirmed).

variants.name: A certain text says (或本云)
variants.text: Concerning the rain after the empress’s prayer, a certain text records that it rained for five days and the nine grains (九穀) ripened well.

variants.name: A certain text says (或本云)
variants.text: The main text says that the place to which the empress moved in the twelfth month of the 1st year was the Oharida Palace, but a certain text says it was a temporary palace in the south court of the Eastern Palace (東宮).

variants.name: A certain text says (或本云)
variants.text: Attached to the record of the burial at the 押坂陵 (reading unconfirmed) in the ninth month of the 2nd year, a certain text records that Emperor Jomei was called “the 高市 Emperor” (高市天皇, reading unconfirmed).

variants.name: An old text says (舊本云)
variants.text: Concerning the record that in the first month of the 4th year the cries of monkeys were heard in various places but no monkeys were seen, the old text says that this was an omen that in this year the capital would be moved to Naniwa and the Itabuki Palace would become a ruin. The main text says that people of the time called them messengers of the Great Deity of Ise (伊勢大神).

kotoku-1.title: Emperor Kōtoku’s Accession and the Taika Reform Edict
kotoku-1.lead: Upon Empress Kōgyoku’s abdication, Prince Karu took the throne; he made Prince Naka-no-Ōe crown prince and Nakatomi no Kamako Inner Minister (内臣), and changed the era name to Taika. In the 1st year of Taika came the dispatch of governors to the eastern provinces, the installation of a bell and a box (鍾 and 匱), Furuhito no Ōe’s plot and its suppression, and the move of the capital to Naniwa; in the first month of the 2nd year the Reform Edict (改新之詔) was proclaimed, followed by edicts on the treatment of the governors, on simple burials and other matters.

points.text: In the first month of the 2nd year of Taika the Reform Edict was proclaimed, setting out four articles: abolishing the 子代 people, the 屯倉 granaries, the 部曲 people and the 田荘 estates, and granting sustenance fiefs (食封) instead; establishing the capital, the Home Provinces (畿内), provincial governors, district officials, post horses and so on; beginning household registers, tax registers and the law for allotting and reclaiming rice land (班田収授); and abolishing the old labor levies and introducing a levy on rice land (田之調).

In the sixth month of the 4th year of Empress Kōgyoku, the empress wished to pass the throne to Prince Naka-no-Ōe, but on Nakatomi no Kamako’s advice Prince Naka-no-Ōe put forward his uncle, Prince Karu. Prince Karu tried to yield to Furuhito no Ōe, but Furuhito no Ōe said he would become a monk and enter Yoshino, and shaved his head at Hōkō-ji, so Prince Karu took the throne.

On the day of accession, Empress Kōgyoku was given the title 皇祖母尊, Prince Naka-no-Ōe was made crown prince, Abe no Uchimaro (阿倍内麻呂臣) Minister of the Left, Soga no Kurayamada no Ishikawa no Maro (蘇我倉山田石川麻呂臣) Minister of the Right, Nakatomi no Kamako Inner Minister, and 僧旻 and 高向史玄理 (readings unconfirmed) National Scholars (国博士). Beneath a great zelkova tree they swore a covenant between sovereign and subjects, and the year was renamed the 1st year of Taika.

In the eighth month of the 1st year of Taika, governors were appointed to the eastern provinces and elsewhere and made to compile household registers and survey the rice fields, and they were forbidden to take bribes or to try cases in the provinces to which they were assigned. On the same day a bell (鍾) and a box (匱) were installed at court so that, if the handling of a complaint was delayed, the complainant could strike the bell.
In the third month of the 2nd year of Taika, the crown prince, stating that only the sovereign can unify the realm and employ the people, presented 524 persons of the 入部 and 181 屯倉 granaries.

An edict of the third month of the 2nd year of Taika, stating that the people were being impoverished by tomb building, fixed the size of tombs and the number of laborers for each rank, from princes and above down to commoners, and banned old customs such as temporary enshrinement (殯), following the dead in death, and placing treasures in tombs.

story.text: Emperor Kōtoku (天万豊日天皇) was the younger brother of Empress Kōgyoku by the same mother; he is described as a man who revered the Buddhist law, made light of the way of the gods (神道), and was fond of Confucianism. In the sixth month of the 4th year of Empress Kōgyoku, the empress wished to pass the throne to Prince Naka-no-Ōe, but Nakatomi no Kamako advised that, since his elder brother Furuhito no Ōe was still living, taking the throne would go against the modesty proper to a younger brother, and recommended putting forward his uncle, Prince Karu. Prince Karu declined again and again and tried to yield to Furuhito no Ōe, but Furuhito no Ōe said he would become a monk and practice the Buddhist way at Yoshino, shaved his head at Hōkō-ji and put on a monk’s robe (袈裟), so Prince Karu took the throne.

On the day of accession the title 皇祖母尊 was presented to Empress Kōgyoku; Prince Naka-no-Ōe was made crown prince, Abe no Uchimaro Minister of the Left and Soga no Kurayamada no Ishikawa no Maro Minister of the Right; Nakatomi no Kamako was given the 大錦 cap and made Inner Minister; and 僧旻 and 高向史玄理 (readings unconfirmed) were made National Scholars. Some days later the emperor, the 皇祖母尊 and the crown prince gathered the ministers beneath a great zelkova tree and swore to the gods of heaven and earth that the sovereign would not govern with a double policy and that the subjects would not be of two minds toward the court, and the 4th year of Empress Kōgyoku was renamed the 1st year of Taika.

In the seventh month, Princess Hashihito (間人皇女), daughter of Emperor Jomei, was made empress, and 小足媛 (reading unconfirmed; mother of Prince Arima), daughter of the Great Minister 阿倍倉梯麻呂 (reading unconfirmed), and 乳娘 (reading unconfirmed), daughter of the Great Minister Soga no Yamada no Ishikawa no Maro (蘇我山田石川麻呂), were made consorts. Koguryŏ, Paekche and Silla presented tribute, and the Paekche envoy also presented the tribute of Mimana (任那). The Great Minister Ishikawa no Maro petitioned that the gods of heaven and earth should first be worshipped and pacified before matters of government were discussed, and envoys were sent to Owari and Mino to levy offerings for the gods.

In the eighth month, governors were appointed to the eastern provinces and elsewhere and ordered, among other things, to compile household registers and survey the rice fields, not to judge offenses in their provinces or take bribes, and to collect weapons in armories. On the same day a bell and a box were installed at court to set up a system for receiving complaints, and rules were also fixed for the status of children born between free people and slaves. Monks and nuns were also gathered at the Great Temple (大寺); after an account of how things had gone since the Buddhist law was transmitted, ten masters (十師) were appointed and the actual state of the temples was investigated.

In the ninth month, Prince Furuhito (古人皇子) plotted rebellion with 蘇我田口臣川堀 (reading unconfirmed) and others, but one of the conspirators, 吉備笠臣垂 (reading unconfirmed), turned himself in to Prince Naka-no-Ōe, and Prince Naka-no-Ōe sent troops to strike down Prince 古人大市 (古人大市皇子, reading unconfirmed) and the others. In the same month envoys were sent to the provinces to record the numbers of people, and powerful men were forbidden to take land as private property and sell it to the people. In the twelfth month the emperor moved the capital to Nagara-Toyosaki in Naniwa (難波長柄豊碕).

In the first month of the 2nd year, when the New Year ceremonies were over, the Reform Edict was proclaimed. The first article abolished the 子代 people, the 屯倉 granaries, the 部曲 people and the 田荘 estates and granted sustenance fiefs (食封); the second organized the capital and established the Home Provinces (畿内), provincial governors, district officials, barriers and forts (関塞), border guards (防人), post horses and transmission horses (駅馬, 伝馬) and so on; the third began household registers, tax registers and the law for allotting and reclaiming rice land, and made fifty households one village (里); and the fourth abolished the old labor levies and fixed a levy on rice land (田之調) and other levies.

In the second month, in response to remonstrances from the people placed in the box, labor levies at various places were stopped. In the third month the merits and faults of each of the eastern governors were made clear one by one through the reports of the court-assembly envoys (朝集使) and the penalties were announced, and the crown prince presented 524 persons of the 入部 and 181 屯倉 granaries. An edict was also issued that fixed tomb regulations by rank and banned customs such as following the dead in death and forcing people to perform purifications (祓除). In the eighth month it was proclaimed that the 品部 groups would be abolished and their people made people of the state, and in the ninth month the scholar 高向黒麻呂 (that is, 玄理; reading unconfirmed) was sent to Silla to make it send hostages, and the tribute of Mimana was discontinued.

quotes.note: The opening words of the covenant beneath the great zelkova tree. It means: as heaven covers and earth supports, so the way of the sovereign is one alone.
The opening of the first article of the Reform Edict. It means: abolish the 子代 people and the 屯倉 granaries in various places that the sovereigns of former times established.
The opening of the third article of the Reform Edict. It means: for the first time make household registers, tax registers, and the law for allotting and reclaiming rice land.
Words the crown prince gave as his reason for presenting the 入部 and the 屯倉. It means: just as there are not two suns in the sky, there are not two kings in a country.

figures.name: Emperor Kōtoku (天萬豐日天皇; Prince Karu, 輕皇子)
figures.role: Younger brother of Empress Kōgyoku by the same mother; he took the throne upon her abdication and changed the era name to Taika.

figures.name: Prince Naka-no-Ōe (中大兄)
figures.role: Became crown prince on the day of accession, ordered the attack on Furuhito no Ōe, and presented the 入部 and the 屯倉.

figures.name: Nakatomi no Kamako (中臣鎌子連)
figures.role: Recommended putting Prince Karu on the throne; on the day of accession he was given the 大錦 cap and made Inner Minister.

figures.name: Furuhito no Ōe (古人大兄), also called 古人大市皇子 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Declined the throne, became a monk and entered Yoshino, but in the ninth month was struck down as having plotted rebellion.

figures.name: Abe no Uchimaro (阿倍内麻呂臣), also called 阿倍倉梯麻呂 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Became Minister of the Left on the day of accession; his daughter 小足媛 (reading unconfirmed) became a consort.

figures.name: Soga no Kurayamada no Ishikawa no Maro (蘇我倉山田石川麻呂臣)
figures.role: Became Minister of the Right on the day of accession and petitioned that the gods be worshipped before matters of government were discussed.

figures.name: 沙門旻法師 and 高向史玄理 (readings unconfirmed)
figures.role: Made National Scholars on the day of accession. 玄理 was sent to Silla in the ninth month of the 2nd year.

figures.name: Princess Hashihito (間人皇女)
figures.role: Daughter of Emperor Jomei; she became empress in the seventh month of the 1st year of Taika.

figures.name: 吉備笠臣垂 (reading unconfirmed; partial reading: 垂 = shidaru, from the original text’s reading note 之娜屢)
figures.role: Had taken part in Prince Furuhito’s plot but turned himself in to Prince Naka-no-Ōe.

figures.name: 難波癬龜 (reading unconfirmed; partial reading: 癬龜 = kubikame, from the original text’s reading note 俱毘柯梅)
figures.role: One of the subordinates of the eastern governors whose faults were pointed out.

variants.name: A certain text says (或本云)
variants.text: The main text says that 吉備笠臣垂 (reading unconfirmed) turned himself in to Prince Naka-no-Ōe, but a certain text says that he turned himself in to Great Minister Abe and Great Minister Soga, confessing that he had been a companion in the rebellion of the prince of Yoshino.

variants.name: A certain text says (或本云)
variants.text: A certain text gives a specific account: on the thirtieth day of the eleventh month, Prince Naka-no-Ōe had 阿倍渠曾倍臣 and 佐伯部子麻呂 (readings unconfirmed) lead thirty soldiers to attack Furuhito no Ōe; they cut down Furuhito no Ōe and his son, and his consorts and concubines took their own lives.

variants.name: A certain text says (或本云)
variants.text: Another such text simply records that in the eleventh month 吉野大兄王 (reading unconfirmed) rebelled and was put to death when the matter came to light; the month differs from the ninth month given in the main text.

variants.name: A certain text says (或本云)
variants.text: The main text says that in the ninth month envoys were sent to the provinces to take charge of weapons, but a certain text says that from the sixth to the ninth month envoys were sent to the provinces in all four directions and gathered weapons of various kinds.

variants.name: A certain text says (或本云)
variants.text: Concerning the record of the emperor going to the 子代 Detached Palace (子代離宮) in the first month of the 2nd year, a certain text says that the 子代屯倉 (reading unconfirmed) at the village of 狭屋部 (reading unconfirmed) in Naniwa was pulled down and a temporary palace built.

kotoku-2.title: Emperor Kōtoku — The Cap-Rank System, the Death of Ishikawa no Maro, the Hakuchi Era and the Naniwa Palace
kotoku-2.lead: Covers the period from the 3rd year of Taika to the 5th year of Hakuchi: the organization of cap ranks and of the official system, the death of the Minister of the Right Soga no Kurayamada no Ishikawa no Maro, the change of era name after a white pheasant was presented, the completion of the Nagara-Toyosaki Palace in Naniwa, and the dispatch of envoys to Tang. In the 4th year of Hakuchi the crown prince moved with the 皇祖母尊, Empress Hashihito and others to the riverside temporary palace at Asuka (飛鳥河辺行宮) in Yamato (倭), and in the 5th year the emperor died at the Naniwa Palace.

points.text: In the third month of the 5th year of Taika, 蘇我日向 (reading unconfirmed) falsely told the crown prince that his half-brother, the Minister of the Right Soga no Kurayamada no Ishikawa no Maro, harbored rebellious intentions, and the minister took his own life at Yamada-dera (山田寺) after swearing that he “would not resent his lord.” Later, among his property were found items labeled “the crown prince’s documents” and “the crown prince’s things,” and the crown prince, realizing that the minister’s heart had been pure, regretted what had happened.

In the second month of the 1st year of Hakuchi, the governor of 穴戸 (reading unconfirmed) presented a white pheasant, and after the Lord of Paekche (百済君) and monks were asked about its origins it was judged an auspicious omen. The emperor issued an edict proclaiming a general amnesty throughout the realm and changing the era name to Hakuchi.

In the 3rd year of Taika a system of caps in seven colors and thirteen grades was established; in the second month of the 5th year it was changed to nineteen grades of caps, from 大織 to 立身, and the scholars 高向玄理 and 僧旻 (readings unconfirmed) were made to establish the eight ministries and the hundred offices.

In the 4th year of Hakuchi the crown prince asked to move to the Yamato capital (倭京), but the emperor did not allow it. The crown prince took the 皇祖母尊, Empress Hashihito, the emperor’s younger brother (皇弟) and others and moved to the riverside temporary palace at Asuka in Yamato, and the high officials and all the hundred officials followed. The emperor, resentful, wished to abandon the throne and sent a poem to Empress Hashihito.

In the fifth month of the 4th year of Hakuchi, the ambassador 吉士長丹 (reading unconfirmed) and his party and the ambassador 高田首根麻呂 (reading unconfirmed) and his party were sent to Great Tang in two ships, and in the second month of the 5th year the supervising envoy (押使) 高向玄理 (reading unconfirmed) and others were also sent. 玄理 died in Tang, and 吉士長丹 and his party returned in the seventh month of the 5th year and were rewarded.

In the tenth month of the 5th year of Hakuchi, the crown prince, hearing of the emperor’s illness, went to the Naniwa Palace with the 皇祖母尊, Empress Hashihito and others, and the emperor died in his main chamber (正寝). In the twelfth month he was buried at the 大坂磯長陵 (reading unconfirmed), and the crown prince, escorting the 皇祖母尊, moved to the riverside temporary palace in Yamato (倭河辺行宮).

story.text: In the 3rd year of Taika the 小郡 (reading unconfirmed) was demolished and a palace built there, and rules of etiquette were set: holders of rank were to line up outside the south gate at the hour of the tiger (寅), bow twice in the courtyard at sunrise, and withdraw on hearing the bell at the hour of the horse (午). Someone remonstrated that the craftsman 倭漢直荒田井比羅夫 (reading unconfirmed) had mistakenly had ditches dug and had exhausted the people; the emperor said this was his own fault and stopped the work that same day. In the twelfth month the crown prince’s palace burned. In this year a system of caps in seven colors and thirteen grades was established; 金春秋 (reading unconfirmed) of Silla came escorting 高向黒麻呂 (reading unconfirmed) and others and became a hostage; and the 渟足 stockade (渟足柵, reading unconfirmed) was built and stockade households (柵戸) were placed there.

In the second month of the 4th year of Taika, student monks were sent to Koguryŏ, Paekche and Silla, and Great Minister Abe invited the fourfold Buddhist assembly (四衆) to Shitennō-ji (四天王寺) and enshrined four Buddhist images inside the pagoda. In the fourth month the old caps were abolished, but the Ministers of the Left and Right still wore the old caps. In this year the 磐舟 stockade (磐舟柵, reading unconfirmed) was put in order to guard against the Emishi, and people from Koshi and Shinano were selected and for the first time placed there as stockade households.

In the second month of the 5th year of Taika, nineteen grades of caps were established, and 高向玄理 and 僧旻 (readings unconfirmed) were made to establish the eight ministries and the hundred offices. In the third month the Minister of the Left, Great Minister Abe, died. 蘇我日向 (reading unconfirmed) falsely told the crown prince that the Minister of the Right Soga no Kurayamada no Ishikawa no Maro was plotting rebellion. When the emperor sent troops against him, the minister fled to Yamada-dera in Yamato, refused the plan of his eldest son 興志 (reading unconfirmed) to meet the attack, swore before the Buddha hall that he would not resent his lord, and took his own life; his wife, children and others died with him. Afterwards, items marked as being for the crown prince were found among his property and the crown prince regretted what had happened; 日向 was made Governor-General of Tsukushi (筑紫大宰帥), and people of the time asked whether this was a hidden banishment.

The minister’s daughter 造媛 (reading unconfirmed), a consort of the crown prince, grieved that her father had been cut down by 物部二田造塩 (reading unconfirmed), and died; when the crown prince lamented, 野中川原史満 (reading unconfirmed) presented two poems to him. In the fourth month 巨勢徳陀古臣 (reading unconfirmed) was made Minister of the Left and 大伴長徳連 (reading unconfirmed) Minister of the Right. In this year the king of Silla sent 金多遂 (reading unconfirmed) as a hostage.

In the second month of the 1st year of Hakuchi, 草壁連醜経 (reading unconfirmed), governor of 穴戸 (reading unconfirmed), presented a white pheasant. The Lord of Paekche and the monks cited ancient precedents from China and the example of a white deer in Koguryŏ, among others, and judged it an auspicious omen; at court, with the Ministers of the Left and Right and the hundred officials lined up, the palanquin bearing the pheasant was brought forward before the throne. The emperor delivered an edict saying that auspicious omens are the result of subjects serving with sincerity, proclaimed a general amnesty throughout the realm, and changed the era name to Hakuchi. In the tenth month, gifts were given to those whose tombs had been destroyed and to those who had been moved to make room for the palace site, and work began on sixteen-foot (丈六) embroidered images and other works.

In the third month of the 2nd year of Hakuchi the sixteen-foot embroidered images and other works were completed. On the last day of the twelfth month more than 2,100 monks and nuns were invited to the 味経宮 (reading unconfirmed) to read the complete Buddhist canon (一切経), and the emperor moved from the 大郡 (reading unconfirmed) to the new palace, which was named the Nagara-Toyosaki Palace in Naniwa (難波長柄豊碕宮). In this year Silla’s tribute envoys arrived in Tsukushi wearing Tang clothing and were sent back, and the Great Minister 巨勢 (reading unconfirmed) petitioned that Silla should be attacked. In the 3rd year the allotment of rice land was completed, household registers were made with fifty households forming one village, and in the ninth month construction of the palace was finished.

In the fifth month of the 4th year of Hakuchi, the ambassador 吉士長丹 and his party and the ambassador 高田首根麻呂 and his party (readings unconfirmed) were sent to Great Tang in two ships, and the emperor visited the sick monk 旻 (reading unconfirmed). In this year the crown prince asked to move the capital to the Yamato capital but was refused; he took the 皇祖母尊, Empress Hashihito and others to the riverside temporary palace at Asuka, and the hundred officials followed, so the emperor, resentful, wished to abandon the throne and sent a poem to Empress Hashihito. In the first month of the 5th year Nakatomi no Kamatari (中臣鎌足連) was given the purple cap, and in the second month the supervising envoy 高向玄理 (reading unconfirmed) and others were sent to Tang, but 玄理 died there. In the tenth month the emperor died in his main chamber; in the twelfth month he was buried at the 大坂磯長陵 (reading unconfirmed), and the crown prince, escorting the 皇祖母尊, moved to the riverside temporary palace in Yamato.

quotes.note: The emperor said that it was his own fault for listening to the deception of 比羅夫 (reading unconfirmed) and having useless ditches dug, and he stopped the work that same day.
The vow Great Minister Ishikawa no Maro made before the Buddha hall at the end. It means: however many times I am reborn, I will not resent my lord.

Words of the edict: because the auspicious omen of a white pheasant has appeared in the province of 穴戸 (reading unconfirmed), a general amnesty is proclaimed throughout the realm and the era name is changed to Hakuchi.
When 蘇我日向 (reading unconfirmed), who had made the false accusation, was appointed Governor-General of Tsukushi, people of the time said, “Is this a hidden banishment?”

figures.name: Emperor Kōtoku (天萬豐日天皇)
figures.role: Organized the cap ranks and the official system at Naniwa, changed the era name to Hakuchi, and died at the Naniwa Palace in the 5th year of Hakuchi.

figures.name: Crown Prince Naka-no-Ōe (皇太子, 中大兄)
figures.role: Believed the false accusation against Ishikawa no Maro and later regretted it; in the 4th year of Hakuchi he moved to Yamato with the 皇祖母尊 and others.

figures.name: Soga no Kurayamada no Ishikawa no Maro (蘇我倉山田麻呂大臣; 石川麻呂)
figures.role: Minister of the Right; falsely accused, he took his own life at Yamada-dera.

figures.name: 蘇我臣日向 (reading unconfirmed; courtesy name 身刺)
figures.role: Falsely accused his half-brother Ishikawa no Maro, and was later made Governor-General of Tsukushi.

figures.name: 蘇我造媛 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Daughter of Ishikawa no Maro and consort of the crown prince. She died grieving over her father’s death.

figures.name: 野中川原史滿 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Presented two poems to the crown prince as he mourned the death of 造媛 (reading unconfirmed).

figures.name: 金春秋 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: A high minister (上臣) of Silla who in the 3rd year of Taika came escorting 高向黒麻呂 (reading unconfirmed) and others and was made a hostage.

figures.name: 草壁連醜經 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: As governor of 穴戸 (reading unconfirmed) he presented the white pheasant and was rewarded.

figures.name: 高向史玄理 (reading unconfirmed; also called 黒麻呂)
figures.role: As a scholar he took part in establishing the eight ministries and the hundred offices; in the 5th year of Hakuchi he went to Tang as supervising envoy and died there.

figures.name: 吉士長丹 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Ambassador to Tang in the 4th year of Hakuchi; he returned in the 5th year, was rewarded, and was granted the surname 呉 (reading unconfirmed).

figures.name: 中臣間人連老 (reading unconfirmed; partial reading: 老 = oyu, from the original text’s reading note 於喻)
figures.role: A member of the embassy to Tang in the 5th year of Hakuchi.

figures.name: Empress Hashihito (間人皇后)
figures.role: Moved to Yamato with the crown prince and others in the 4th year of Hakuchi, and was sent a poem by the emperor.

variants.name: A certain text (或本)
variants.text: A certain text records that in the seventh month of the 5th year of Hakuchi the monk 旻 (reading unconfirmed) lay ill at 阿曇寺 (reading unconfirmed), and that the emperor visited him, took his hand and said, “If the master dies today, I too will die tomorrow.” The main text says that the emperor visited 旻’s quarters in the fifth month of the 4th year.

variants.name: A certain text (或本)
variants.text: Concerning the first ship of the embassy to Tang in the 4th year of Hakuchi, a certain text adds the student monks 知辨 and 義徳 and the student 坂合部連磐積 (readings unconfirmed).

variants.name: A certain text says (或本云)
variants.text: The main text says that in the second month the supervising envoy 高向史玄理 (reading unconfirmed), of 大錦上 rank, was sent, but a certain text says that in summer, in the fifth month, the supervising envoy 高向玄理, of 大花下 rank, was sent, and it also gives the rank of the secretary (判官) 書直麻呂 (reading unconfirmed) as 小山下.

variants.name: A certain text says (或本云)
variants.text: A certain text records that in this emperor’s reign the three kingdoms of Koguryŏ, Paekche and Silla sent envoys every year to present tribute.

saimei.title: Empress Saimei — Her Second Reign, Prince Arima, and the Western Expedition to Aid Paekche
saimei.lead: This book records the seven years in which Empress Saimei (天豐財重日足姬天皇), who had once reigned as Empress Kōgyoku, took the throne again at the Itabuki Palace in Asuka after the death of Emperor Kōtoku, years marked by the building of palaces and canals, expeditions against the Emishi and the 肅慎 (reading unconfirmed), and the affair of Prince Arima. When Paekche was overthrown by Tang and Silla in the 6th year, she decided to send aid and set out for Tsukushi herself; the book goes on to her death at the Asakura Palace in the seventh month of the 7th year.

points.text: Empress Saimei (天豐財重日足姬天皇) yielded the throne to Emperor Kōtoku (天萬豐日天皇) in the 4th year of her reign (改元四年) and was called “皇祖母尊”; after his death she took the throne again at the Itabuki Palace in Asuka in the first month of the 1st year.

In the eleventh month of the 4th year, the caretaker official (留守官) Soga no Akae spoke to Prince Arima of the “three failings” of the empress’s government; the prince plotted, was then arrested, was questioned by the crown prince at the hot springs of Ki (紀温湯), and was strangled at 藤白坂 (reading unconfirmed).

In the ninth month of the 6th year a Paekche envoy reported the destruction of Paekche by Tang and Silla, and in the tenth month 鬼室福信 (reading unconfirmed) asked for aid and for the return of Prince 豐璋 (reading unconfirmed), so the empress issued an edict deciding to send aid, and in the twelfth month she had weapons prepared at the Naniwa Palace.

In the first month of the 7th year she set out westward in the imperial ship and, after the 石湯 temporary palace at 熟田津 and the 磐瀨 temporary palace at 娜大津 (readings unconfirmed), moved to the Asakura no Tachibana no Hironiwa Palace (朝倉橘廣庭宮), but in the seventh month she died at the Asakura Palace.

It is recorded again and again that from the 4th to the 6th year the fleet of Abe no Omi (阿倍臣; Abe no Hikita no Hirafu, 阿倍引田臣比羅夫) subdued the Emishi of 齶田, 渟代, 津輕 (readings unconfirmed) and other places, and fought the 肅慎 (reading unconfirmed).

There are two “certain texts” (或本) concerning Prince Arima’s plot; they relate that the rebellion was divined by drawing lots (短籍), and that a plan was made to burn the palace and seize 牟婁津 (reading unconfirmed).

story.text: Empress Saimei (天豐財重日足姬天皇) first married Prince 高向 (高向王, reading unconfirmed) and bore Prince 漢 (漢皇子, reading unconfirmed), and later married Emperor Jomei (息長足日廣額天皇) and bore two sons and one daughter. She became empress and took the throne after her husband’s death, but in the sixth month of the 4th year of her reign (改元四年) she yielded the throne to Emperor Kōtoku (天萬豐日天皇) and was called 皇祖母尊. When Emperor Kōtoku died, she took the throne again at the Itabuki Palace in Asuka in the first month of the 1st year. In the fifth month of this year, it is said, a figure that looked like a Tang man, riding a dragon and wearing a blue oiled hat, flew from Mount Katsuragi (葛城嶺) to Mount Ikoma (膽駒山), and then from the pine ridge of Sumiyoshi (住吉松嶺) away to the west. In winter the Itabuki Palace burned and the empress moved to the Kawara Palace in Asuka (飛鳥川原宮).

In the 2nd year a palace site was chosen anew at Okamoto in Asuka and a palace was built, named the Later Okamoto Palace in Asuka (後飛鳥岡本宮). A wall was built around the peak of 田身嶺 (reading unconfirmed), and beside two zelkova trees on its summit a tower (観) was built, called the Twin Zelkova Palace (兩槻宮), or the Heavenly Palace (天宮). She also had water engineers dig a canal from west of Mount Kagu (香山) to Mount Isonokami (石上山), and had stones carried on two hundred boats to build stone walls on the hill east of the palace, so people slandered it as “the Canal of the Mad Mind” (狂心渠) and lamented the great labor and expense. The Yoshino Palace was also built, but the Okamoto Palace suffered a fire. In the 3rd year an image of Mount Sumeru (須彌山) was made west of Asuka-dera and the Ullambana assembly (盂蘭瓮会) was held, and people of the country of 覩貨邏 (reading unconfirmed) who had drifted ashore in Tsukushi were entertained.

In the ninth month of the 3rd year, Prince Arima feigned madness, went to the 牟婁 hot springs (牟婁温湯, reading unconfirmed) and praised the place, so the empress wished to go there. When her grandson Prince 建 (建王, reading unconfirmed) died at the age of eight in the fifth month of the 4th year, the empress grieved deeply, composed poems, and ordered that he be buried together with her in her own tomb. In the tenth month, while she was away on an excursion to the hot springs of Ki, Soga no Akae told Prince Arima of three failings of the empress: building storehouses and gathering the people’s wealth, digging canals and wasting public provisions, and carrying stones by boat to build a hill. The prince plotted in the upper room of Akae’s house, but his armrest (脇息, called 夾膝) broke of its own accord, and taking this as an ill omen they swore to each other and stopped. That night Akae had 物部朴井連鮪 (reading unconfirmed) surround the prince’s house; the prince was sent to the hot springs of Ki, answered the crown prince’s questioning by saying that “only Heaven and Akae know,” and was strangled at 藤白坂 (reading unconfirmed).

In the fourth month of the 4th year, Abe no Omi led a fleet of 180 ships against the Emishi, and the Emishi of 齶田 and 渟代 (readings unconfirmed) surrendered. 恩荷 (reading unconfirmed), an Emishi of 齶田, swore that they carried bows and arrows to get meat to eat and not to turn them against the government army, and he received a rank and appointment as district chief. In the third month of the 5th year Abe no Omi again gathered and entertained the Emishi of 飽田, 渟代, 津輕 and 膽振鉏 (readings unconfirmed), and set up an administrative office at 後方羊蹄 (reading unconfirmed). In the third month of the 6th year he attacked the land of the 肅慎 (reading unconfirmed) with two hundred ships and invited them to trade, but no peace was made; they fought at the stockade on 弊賂辨嶋 (reading unconfirmed), and 能登臣馬身龍 (reading unconfirmed) was killed in battle. In the fifth month a Mount Sumeru was made beside the Isonokami pond (石上池) and forty-seven people of the 肅慎 were entertained.

In the seventh month of the 5th year, 坂合部連石布 and 津守連吉祥 (readings unconfirmed) were sent to Tang and showed Emishi men and women from Michinoku (道奥) to the Tang Son of Heaven. According to the Record of 伊吉連博德 (伊吉連博德書, reading unconfirmed) quoted in the main text, 石布’s ship was driven by contrary winds to an island in the southern sea called 爾加委 (reading unconfirmed) and destroyed by the islanders, while 吉祥’s ship reached 越州 (reading unconfirmed) and went up to the capital. The Son of Heaven asked the envoys about the well-being of the emperor (天皇) and about the kinds of Emishi and how they lived, and the envoys answered that, in order of distance, there were three kinds: the 都加留 (reading unconfirmed), the “rough Emishi” (麤蝦夷) and the “tame Emishi” (熟蝦夷). Later they were nearly punished because of slander by a follower of 韓智興 (reading unconfirmed), but escaped through a petition by 博德; the following year, on the grounds that there was to be “a matter of government east of the sea” (海東之政), they were confined in the Western Capital, and they were finally released only after Paekche had been subdued.

In the ninth month of the 6th year a Paekche envoy came and reported that in the seventh month Silla had brought in Tang forces and overthrown Paekche, that the king and his ministers had all been captured, and that 鬼室福信 (reading unconfirmed) and others had gathered the scattered troops and were holding the royal city. In the tenth month 福信 presented more than a hundred Tang prisoners and asked for aid, and for Prince 豐璋 (reading unconfirmed), who was serving in Japan (日本), to be welcomed back as ruler of the country. Saying that helping a country in danger is a way of long standing, the empress ordered aid to be sent, and in the twelfth month she went to the Naniwa Palace and had weapons prepared. For this year the text records events that were taken as omens that the relief army would be defeated: the stern and bow of a ship built in Suruga province changed places of their own accord at night, and in Shinano province (科野国) swarms of flies flew toward the west.

In the first month of the 7th year the imperial ship headed west; on the 大伯 sea (大伯海, reading unconfirmed) Princess 大田 (大田姬皇女, reading unconfirmed) gave birth to a girl, who was named Princess 大伯 (大伯皇女). The empress stopped at the 石湯 temporary palace at 熟田津 in Iyo (readings unconfirmed), and in the third month entered the 磐瀨 temporary palace at 娜大津 (readings unconfirmed) and renamed the place 長津 (reading unconfirmed). In the fifth month she moved to the Asakura no Tachibana no Hironiwa Palace, but because trees of the Asakura shrine (朝倉社) had been cut down to build the palace, the god was angered and destroyed the hall, will-o’-the-wisps (鬼火) were seen in the palace, and many of those serving close to her fell ill and died. In the seventh month the empress died at the Asakura Palace; in the eighth month, when the crown prince moved the mourning to the 磐瀨 palace, it is said that a demon (鬼) wearing a great hat watched the funeral rites from the top of Mount Asakura. The funeral party returned to Naniwa by sea, and in the eleventh month the temporary enshrinement was held at Kawara in Asuka (飛鳥川原).

quotes.note: The words with which people slandered the canal dug from Mount Kagu to Mount Isonokami, calling it “the canal of a mad mind” and saying that the labor of more than thirty thousand people had been wasted.
Prince Arima’s answer when asked the reason for the rebellion. It means: “Heaven and Akae know. I understand nothing at all.”

A passage from the edict ordering aid for Paekche. It means: requests for troops and appeals for aid have been heard of since ancient times, and to support a country in danger and restore a line that has been cut off is the constant way.
The record that the crown prince made a water clock (漏剋) for the first time and let the people know the time.

figures.name: Empress Saimei (天豐財重日足姬天皇)
figures.role: Empress of Emperor Jomei (息長足日廣額天皇); after once yielding the throne, she took it again at the Itabuki Palace in Asuka. The sovereign of this book.

figures.name: The crown prince (皇太子)
figures.role: The empress’s son (called 天命開別天皇 in the chronicle of Emperor Tenji); he questioned Prince Arima, made the water clock, and escorted the empress’s funeral to Naniwa.

figures.name: Prince Arima (有間皇子)
figures.role: A prince who was arrested for plotting rebellion after being drawn in by Soga no Akae, and was strangled at 藤白坂 (reading unconfirmed).

figures.name: Soga no Akae (蘇我赤兄臣)
figures.role: As caretaker official he told Prince Arima of the empress’s three failings, and that same night had the prince’s house surrounded and reported to the empress.

figures.name: Abe no Hikita no Hirafu (阿倍引田臣比羅夫)
figures.role: As governor of Koshi (越国守) he led a fleet, subdued the Emishi, and fought the 肅慎 (reading unconfirmed).

figures.name: 建王 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: The empress’s grandson, who died at the age of eight; the empress composed poems and grieved deeply.

figures.name: 伊吉連博德 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: A member of the embassy to Tang; his record, the 伊吉連博德書, is quoted as a note in the main text, and through a petition he escaped punishment brought on by slander in Tang.

figures.name: 鬼室福信 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: A Paekche official of 佐平 rank who, after Paekche’s fall, gathered troops and held the royal city, presented Tang prisoners, and asked for aid and for the return of Prince 豐璋 (reading unconfirmed).

figures.name: 大田姬皇女 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Gave birth to a girl while the westbound imperial ship was on the 大伯 sea (reading unconfirmed); the child was named Princess 大伯 (大伯皇女).

variants.name: A certain text says (或本云)
variants.text: The main text says the plot was laid in the upper room of Akae’s house, but this certain text relates that Prince Arima drew lots (短籍) with Soga no Akae (蘇我臣赤兄), 鹽屋連小戈, 守君大石 and 坂合部連藥 (readings unconfirmed) to divine the matter of rebellion.

variants.name: A certain text says (或本云)
variants.text: It says that Prince Arima set out a specific plan: first burn the palace, seize 牟婁津 (reading unconfirmed) with five hundred men, and cut off Awaji province with a fleet; and that someone admonished him that at nineteen he was not yet an adult. It records that even when the leg of his table broke for no reason he did not abandon the plot, and that he was finally put to death.

variants.name: A certain text says (或本云)
variants.text: It relates that Abe no Hikita no Hirafu returned from fighting the 肅慎 (reading unconfirmed) and presented forty-nine captives (the main text’s entry for the third month of the 5th year records that he gathered and feasted the Emishi).

variants.name: A certain text says (或本云)
variants.text: The main text says the empress moved to the Asakura no Tachibana no Hironiwa Palace in the fifth month, but this certain text says she moved to the Asakura Palace in the fourth month.

variants.name: A certain text says (或本云)
variants.text: It places in the year 辛酉 (the 7th year) the settling, on newly cultivated fields in Ōmi province, of the 106 Tang prisoners presented by 福信 (reading unconfirmed). The main text records the presentation in the tenth month of the 6th year and says they were placed in Mino province, and the compilers state that, since this had already been recorded under the year 庚申, they keep this only as a note.

tenji.title: Emperor Tenji — Hakusukinoe and the Move of the Capital to Ōmi
tenji.lead: After the death of Empress Saimei, the crown prince ruled without formally ascending the throne (称制) and continued the effort to aid Paekche; this book records how, after his defeat by the Tang fleet at Hakusukinoe (白村江) in the eighth month of the 2nd year, he strengthened the defenses with border guards (防人), beacons (烽), the Water Fortress (水城) and castles.
