It covers the move of the capital to Ōmi in the 6th year, his accession in the 7th year, the appointment of Prince Ōtomo as Grand Chancellor (太政大臣) in the 10th year, and the Crown Prince (東宮; the Imperial Younger Brother, 大皇弟) taking holy orders and entering Yoshino, up to the emperor’s death at the Ōmi Palace in the twelfth month.

points.text: In the eighth month of the 2nd year, the Japanese (日本) fleet fought the Tang fleet at Hakusukinoe; attacking without regard to the conditions, it was caught from left and right, many drowned, and it was defeated. King 豐璋 (reading unconfirmed) of Paekche fled to Koguryŏ, and in the ninth month the fortress of 州柔 (州柔城, reading unconfirmed) surrendered to Tang.

After the defeat, in this year (the 3rd year), guards (防) and beacons (烽) were placed on Tsushima and Iki and in Tsukushi, and in Tsukushi a great embankment was built to hold water and was named the “Water Fortress” (水城). In the 4th year castles were built in Nagato province, and two castles, 大野 and 椽 (readings unconfirmed), in Tsukushi.

In the second month of the 3rd year the emperor ordered the Imperial Younger Brother (大皇弟) to reform the cap ranks into twenty-six grades, granted great swords, small swords, and shields, bows and arrows to the clan heads (氏上), and fixed the 民部 and 家部.

In the third month of the 6th year the capital was moved to Ōmi, but the people did not want the move; many remonstrated indirectly, there were many children’s songs (童謡), and fires were frequent. The crown prince took the throne in the first month of the 7th year (a certain text says he took the throne in the third month of the 6th year).

In the tenth month of the 8th year, the emperor visited the ailing Inner Minister Fujiwara (藤原内大臣) and sent the Imperial Younger Brother to confer on him the Great Woven Cap (大織冠) and the rank of Great Minister, and to grant him the surname Fujiwara. The Inner Minister died the next day.

In the first month of the 10th year Prince Ōtomo became Grand Chancellor. In the tenth month, when the ailing emperor wished to entrust affairs after his death to the Crown Prince (東宮), the Crown Prince asked that they be entrusted instead to the Empress (大后) and Prince Ōtomo (大友王), took holy orders, and entered Yoshino. The emperor died at the Ōmi Palace in the twelfth month.

story.text: Emperor Tenji (天命開別天皇) was the heir (太子) of Emperor Jomei (息長足日廣額天皇), and his mother was Empress Saimei (天豐財重日足姬天皇). He became crown prince in the 4th year of his mother’s reign, and when his mother died in the seventh month of the 7th year, he wore mourning clothes and governed without ascending the throne (称制). The crown prince moved to the 長津宮 palace (reading unconfirmed) to receive news of military affairs overseas, and in the eighth month sent 阿曇比邏夫連 (reading unconfirmed), Abe no Hikita no Hirafu (阿倍引田比邏夫臣) and others to aid Paekche. In the ninth month he conferred the Woven Cap (織冠) on Prince 豐璋 (reading unconfirmed) of Paekche, married him to the younger sister of 多臣蔣敷 (reading unconfirmed), and had 狹井連檳榔 and 秦造田來津 (readings unconfirmed) escort him to his home country with an army of more than five thousand. When 豐璋 entered the country, 鬼室福信 (reading unconfirmed) welcomed him and entrusted all the affairs of the state to him.

In the first month of the 1st year, 福信 was given a hundred thousand arrows, seed rice and other goods. In the third month Tang and Silla attacked Koguryŏ, and at Koguryŏ’s request Japan stationed commanders at the fortress of 疏留 (疏留城, reading unconfirmed). In the fifth month 阿曇比邏夫連 (reading unconfirmed) escorted 豐璋 and others to Paekche with a fleet of 170 ships, conveyed the imperial command and had 豐璋 succeed to the kingship, and gave 福信 a golden tablet (金策), stroking his back in praise. In the twelfth month 豐璋 and 福信 discussed moving to 避城 (reading unconfirmed), saying that 州柔 (reading unconfirmed) was far from the fields and its land was poor; 朴市田來津 (reading unconfirmed) alone remonstrated that 避城 was too close to the enemy, but he was not heeded.

In the second month of the 2nd year, Silla burned the four southern provinces of Paekche and took strategic places, so 避城 (reading unconfirmed) was too close to the enemy to live in, and, just as 田來津 had said, they returned to 州柔 (reading unconfirmed). In the third month 上毛野君稚子 (reading unconfirmed) and others led 27,000 men against Silla, and in the sixth month took the two fortresses of 沙鼻 and 岐奴江 (readings unconfirmed). In the same month 豐璋 suspected 福信 of harboring rebellious intentions, seized him and had him beheaded. In the eighth month the Tang commanders drew up 170 warships at Hakusukinoe, and the Japanese fleet had the worst of the first engagement. The next day the Japanese commanders and the king of Paekche advanced, saying, “If we compete to be first, the enemy will surely retreat,” but they were caught from left and right by the Tang army and defeated; many fell into the water and died, 田來津 too was killed, and 豐璋 fled by boat to Koguryŏ. When the fortress of 州柔 surrendered in the ninth month, the people of Paekche said, “The name of Paekche ends today,” and set out for Japan with the Japanese fleet from the fortress of 弖禮 (弖禮城, reading unconfirmed).

In the second month of the 3rd year the emperor ordered the Imperial Younger Brother to set the cap ranks at twenty-six grades, and to fix the clan heads (氏上) and the 民部 and 家部. In the fifth month 郭務悰 (reading unconfirmed) and others, envoys of 劉仁願 (reading unconfirmed), the garrison commander in Paekche (百済鎮将), arrived. In this year guards and beacons were placed on Tsushima and Iki and in Tsukushi, and the Water Fortress was built in Tsukushi. In the second month of the 4th year Empress Hashihito (間人大后) died; the official ranks of Paekche were examined and the rank 小錦下 was conferred on 鬼室集斯 (reading unconfirmed), and more than four hundred Paekche men and women were settled in 神前 district (神前郡, reading unconfirmed) in Ōmi province. In the eighth month Paekche officials of 達率 rank and others were made to build castles in Nagato province and at 大野 and 椽 (readings unconfirmed) in Tsukushi, and in the ninth month 劉德高 (reading unconfirmed) and others came from Tang. In winter of the 5th year more than two thousand Paekche men and women were settled in the eastern provinces.

In the second month of the 6th year, Empress Saimei (天豐財重日足姬天皇) and Princess Hashihito (間人皇女) were buried together in the 小市岡上陵 (reading unconfirmed), and the crown prince told the ministers that, following his mother’s words, he would not impose on the people the labor of building a stone burial chamber (石槨). In the third month the capital was moved to Ōmi, but the people did not want it; many remonstrated, there were many children’s songs, and fires broke out frequently by day and by night. In the eleventh month the castles of 高安 in Yamato (倭国), 屋嶋 in Sanuki province and 金田 in Tsushima province (readings unconfirmed) were built. In the first month of the 7th year the crown prince took the throne, and in the second month he made 倭姬王 (reading unconfirmed), daughter of Prince Furuhito no Ōe, his empress and took four consorts (嬪). The text records that among their children Princess Uno (鸕野皇女) and Princess 阿陪 (阿陪皇女, reading unconfirmed) later ruled the realm, and that Prince Iga (伊賀皇子), son of 伊賀采女宅子娘 (reading unconfirmed), was later called Prince Ōtomo.

In the fifth month of the 7th year, the emperor went hunting on 蒲生野 (reading unconfirmed), accompanied by the Imperial Younger Brother, the princes, the Inner Minister and the ministers. In the tenth month the Tang commander-in-chief 英公 (reading unconfirmed) destroyed Koguryŏ. In this year the monk 道行 (reading unconfirmed) stole the Kusanagi sword (草薙剣) and tried to flee to Silla, but lost his way in wind and rain on the road and came back. In the eighth month of the 8th year the emperor climbed the peak of 高安 (高安嶺, reading unconfirmed) and discussed repairing the castle, but gave it up out of consideration for the people’s weariness. In the tenth month, when he visited the ailing Inner Minister Fujiwara, the Inner Minister asked that his funeral be kept simple; the emperor sent the Imperial Younger Brother to confer on him the Great Woven Cap, the rank of Great Minister and the surname Fujiwara, but the Inner Minister died the next day.

In the second month of the 9th year household registers were compiled, and robbers and vagrants were cracked down on. In the middle of the night in the fourth month Hōryū-ji burned down, and not a single building was left. In the first month of the 10th year Prince Ōtomo was made Grand Chancellor, Soga no Akae (蘇我赤兄臣) Minister of the Left and 中臣金連 (reading unconfirmed) Minister of the Right, and the cap ranks and laws were put into effect. In the fourth month the water clock (漏剋) that the emperor had made himself when he was crown prince was set on a new platform and struck the hours for the first time. In the ninth month the emperor fell ill, and in the tenth month he summoned the Crown Prince (東宮) and entrusted him with affairs after his death, but the Crown Prince declined and asked that they be entrusted to the Empress (大后) and Prince Ōtomo (大友王); he shaved his head on the spot, became a monk (沙門), and entered Yoshino. In the eleventh month Prince Ōtomo and five senior ministers, holding censers before the woven Buddha image in the inner palace, swore to obey the emperor’s commands, and in the twelfth month the emperor died at the Ōmi Palace and was laid in temporary enshrinement in the new palace.

quotes.note: The scene at the battle of Hakusukinoe in which the Japanese army was defeated: many fell into the water and drowned, and the ships could not even turn around.
The record that in this year (the 3rd year), guards (防) and beacons (烽) were placed on Tsushima and Iki, in Tsukushi and elsewhere.
It means that the people did not want the move of the capital to Ōmi, and that many remonstrated indirectly and there were also many children’s songs about it.
The record that the ailing Inner Minister was given the Great Woven Cap and the rank of Great Minister, and was granted the surname Fujiwara.

figures.name: Emperor Tenji (天命開別天皇)
figures.role: Heir of Emperor Jomei (息長足日廣額天皇). After his mother’s death he governed without ascending the throne and pressed on with the aid to Paekche; he moved the capital to Ōmi and took the throne in the 7th year.

figures.name: The Imperial Younger Brother (大皇弟)
figures.role: The emperor’s younger brother and Crown Prince (東宮). He was ordered to reform the cap ranks; at the emperor’s sickbed he declined to take charge of affairs after the emperor’s death, took holy orders, and entered Yoshino.

figures.name: 豐璋 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: A Paekche prince who had been serving in Japan; he was given the Woven Cap and became king of Paekche, but he beheaded 福信 (reading unconfirmed) and fled to Koguryŏ after the defeat at Hakusukinoe.

figures.name: 鬼室福信 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: A Paekche official of 佐平 rank. He welcomed 豐璋 and entrusted the government to him, but was suspected of rebellious intentions and beheaded by 豐璋.

figures.name: 朴市田來津 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: A Japanese commander who escorted 豐璋 (reading unconfirmed). He remonstrated against the move to 避城 (reading unconfirmed), and was killed at Hakusukinoe after slaying dozens of men.

figures.name: Inner Minister Fujiwara (藤原內大臣)
figures.role: A senior minister who, on his sickbed in the tenth month of the 8th year, was given the Great Woven Cap, the rank of Great Minister and the surname Fujiwara, and died the next day.

figures.name: Prince Ōtomo (大友皇子)
figures.role: Son of 伊賀采女宅子娘 (reading unconfirmed), also called Prince Iga (伊賀皇子); he became Grand Chancellor in the first month of the 10th year and, together with the senior ministers, swore to obey the emperor’s commands.

figures.name: Soga no Akae (蘇我赤兄臣)
figures.role: After serving as Commander of Tsukushi (筑紫率), he became Minister of the Left in the first month of the 10th year and took the oath together with Prince Ōtomo.

figures.name: 郭務悰 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: A man who came repeatedly, as an envoy of 劉仁願 (reading unconfirmed), the garrison commander in Paekche, and as an envoy of the Tang state.

figures.name: 倭姬王 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Daughter of Prince Furuhito no Ōe; she was made empress in the second month of the 7th year.

variants.name: A certain text says (或本云)
variants.text: The main text says that the crown prince took the throne in the first month of the 7th year, but a certain text says he took the throne in the third month of the 6th year (丁卯).

variants.name: A certain text says (或本云)
variants.text: It names the daughter of the Great Minister Soga no Yamada no Ishikawa no Maro (蘇我山田石川麻呂大臣) not as 遠智娘 but as 茅渟娘 (readings unconfirmed), and gives the children she bore as Princess 大田 (大田皇女) and Princess 娑羅羅 (娑羅羅皇女) (readings unconfirmed); the main text gives Princess 大田, Princess Uno (鸕野皇女) and Prince 建 (建皇子, reading unconfirmed).

variants.name: A certain text says (或本云)
variants.text: The main text says that the Crown Prince, the Imperial Younger Brother (東宮太皇弟), proclaimed the enforcement of the cap ranks and laws, but a certain text says that Prince Ōtomo issued the proclamation.

variants.name: A certain text says (或本云)
variants.text: The main text says that the emperor fell ill in the ninth month, but a certain text says the eighth month.

variants.name: The 日本世記 (reading unconfirmed) and an inscription (碑)
variants.text: The main text gives no age for Inner Minister Fujiwara, but the 日本世記 (reading unconfirmed), quoted in a note, says that he died at his private residence at the age of fifty, while the inscription quoted after it says fifty-six.

tenmu-jo.title: Prince Ōama’s Retreat to Yoshino and the Jinshin War
tenmu-jo.lead: This book gathers into one account the year in which Prince Ōama, younger brother of Emperor Tenji (天命開別天皇) by the same mother, declined at his brother’s sickbed to take charge of affairs after his death, took holy orders and entered Yoshino, and then, in the sixth month of the 1st year, went out to the eastern provinces, secured Fuwa (不破), and fought the army of the Ōmi court. It describes events up to Prince Ōtomo hanging himself after his defeat at Seta in the seventh month, and the emperor, back in the Yamato capital (倭京) in the ninth month, moving to the Asuka Kiyomihara Palace.

points.text: The Crown Prince (Prince Ōama), whom Emperor Tenji (天命開別天皇) on his sickbed asked to take charge of affairs after his death, declined, asking that the realm be entrusted to the empress and that Prince Ōtomo be made heir; that same day he took holy orders, handed over his private weapons to the government, and entered Yoshino.

In the fifth month of the 1st year, the emperor heard that the Ōmi court, claiming to be building an imperial tomb, was having laborers in Mino and Owari carry weapons; in the sixth month he sent 村國連男依 (reading unconfirmed) and others to Mino to block the Fuwa road (不破道), and he himself left Yoshino and entered the eastern provinces.

Beside the 跡太川 river (reading unconfirmed) in 朝明 district (朝明郡, reading unconfirmed), the emperor bowed toward Amaterasu-Ōmikami (天照大神) from afar; he sent Prince Takechi (高市皇子) to Fuwa to oversee military affairs, and at the temporary palace at 野上 (reading unconfirmed) he handed over all military affairs to Prince Takechi.

In the seventh month, the army of 村國連男依 (reading unconfirmed) and others advanced by way of 息長横河, 鳥籠山 and 安河 (readings unconfirmed) and broke the Ōmi lines at Seta; Prince Ōtomo hid at 山前 (reading unconfirmed) and hanged himself, and his head was presented before the camp at the Fuwa palace.

In Yamato, 大伴連吹負 (reading unconfirmed) seized the camp west of Asuka-dera and became a general; he was once defeated at Nara Hill (乃楽山), but after the battles at Taima (当麻) and at the 箸陵 tomb (reading unconfirmed) he drove back the Ōmi army. During this time Kotoshironushi-no-Kami (事代主神) and other deities possessed the chief of Takechi district (高市郡大領) and announced that they would protect the government army, and after the war these deities were raised in rank (品).

Kokugakuin University’s database of kami names introduces the view that the status of Kotoshironushi-no-Kami was established in the reign of Emperor Tenmu, or took shape around that reign, on grounds that include the resemblance between the words spoken by Kotoshironushi-no-Kami in this possession in the seventh month of the 1st year of the Tenmu chronicle and the words of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami (大国主神) in the transfer of the land in the Kojiki.

story.text: Emperor Tenmu (天渟中原瀛真人天皇) was the younger brother of Emperor Tenji (天命開別天皇) by the same mother; his childhood name was Prince Ōama (大海人皇子). As he grew up he was brave, and he was versed in astronomy and in 遁甲. He took Princess Uno (菟野皇女), daughter of Emperor Tenji, as his principal consort, and became Crown Prince in the 1st year of Emperor Tenji. In winter, in the tenth month of the 4th year (the tenth month of the 10th year in the chronicle of Emperor Tenji), when he was summoned by the gravely ill emperor, the messenger 蘇賀臣安麻侶 (reading unconfirmed) secretly told him to be careful what he said, so the Crown Prince suspected a hidden plot. When the emperor tried to hand the great task over to him, the Crown Prince declined on the grounds of his frequent illness, asked that the realm be entrusted to the empress and that Prince Ōtomo be made heir, and that same day took holy orders and handed his private weapons over to the government. When he went into the Yoshino Palace, the Ministers of the Left and Right and others saw him off as far as Uji (菟道), and someone said, “They have put wings on a tiger and let it loose.” At Yoshino the Crown Prince told his attendants (舎人) that those who wished to serve and make a name for themselves should go back, and half of them stayed.

In the twelfth month Emperor Tenji died. In the third month of the 1st year, the emperor’s death was announced to 郭務悰 (reading unconfirmed) and the other Tang envoys in Tsukushi; they put on mourning clothes, raised their voices in lament three times, and bowed toward the east. In the fifth month 朴井連雄君 (reading unconfirmed) reported that in Mino and Owari laborers had been assigned on the pretext of building an imperial tomb and that each had been made to carry weapons; there were also reports that lookouts had been posted at various places from the Ōmi capital to the Yamato capital, and that the bridge-keepers at Uji were stopping the transport of food for the attendants of the Imperial Younger Brother (皇大弟). The emperor had it looked into and learned that it was true, and said that he had given up the throne to keep himself safe, but that he could not silently let himself be destroyed. In the sixth month the emperor sent 村國連男依, 和珥部臣君手 and 身毛君廣 (readings unconfirmed) hurrying to Mino and ordered 多臣品治 (reading unconfirmed), steward of the bath-estate (湯沐令) in 安八磨 district (reading unconfirmed), to raise troops and block the Fuwa road.

On the day 甲申, the emperor asked 高坂王 (reading unconfirmed), one of the caretaker officials, for the post-station bells (駅鈴) but could not get them; he sent 大分君惠尺 (reading unconfirmed) to Ōmi to summon Prince Takechi and Prince Ōtsu (大津皇子), and he himself set out for the eastern provinces without even waiting for a carriage. The empress followed in a palanquin, and Prince Kusakabe (草壁皇子), Prince Osakabe (忍壁皇子), some twenty attendants and some ten ladies-in-waiting (女孺) accompanied them from the start. The party passed through 菟田 and 甘羅村 (readings unconfirmed) and at midnight burned the post station at 隱 (reading unconfirmed); before reaching 横河 (reading unconfirmed) they saw a black cloud spreading across the sky, and the emperor himself took up a divination board (式) and divined, saying that it was a sign that the realm would be split in two, but that he would win the realm. At 積殖山口 (reading unconfirmed) in Iga, Prince Takechi joined them, and at Suzuka the governors of Ise and others came to him and blocked the Suzuka mountain road with five hundred soldiers. Through thunder and rain they reached the Mie district office (三重郡家), where they burned one house to warm those who were freezing.

On the morning of the day 丙戌, beside the 跡太川 river (reading unconfirmed) in 朝明 district (reading unconfirmed), the emperor bowed toward Amaterasu-Ōmikami from afar. Prince Ōtsu arrived, and word came from 村國連男依 (reading unconfirmed) that the Fuwa road had been blocked with three thousand soldiers from Mino. The emperor sent Prince Takechi to Fuwa to oversee military affairs and had him raise the armies of the Tōkai and Tōsan regions (東海, 東山). At the Ōmi court the ministers were alarmed, and Prince Ōtomo sent messengers to the eastern provinces, the Yamato capital, Tsukushi and Kibi to raise troops, but 當摩公廣嶋 (reading unconfirmed), governor of Kibi, was killed, and 栗隈王 (reading unconfirmed), the governor (大宰) of Tsukushi, did not move his troops, giving as his reason the need to guard against foreign enemies. On the day 丁亥 the emperor entered Fuwa, and the governor of Owari came over to his side, bringing twenty thousand soldiers. At 野上 (reading unconfirmed) Prince Takechi told the emperor that, relying on the emperor’s spirit (霊), he would lead the commanders and attack; the emperor took his hand, stroked his back, and handed over all military affairs to him.

In the seventh month the emperor sent 紀臣阿閉麻呂 (reading unconfirmed) and others with tens of thousands of men from Ise toward Yamato, and 村國連男依 (reading unconfirmed) and others with tens of thousands from Fuwa toward Ōmi, and had them put red markings on their clothing so they could tell friend from foe. On the Ōmi side, beside the 犬上川 river (reading unconfirmed), 山部王 (reading unconfirmed) was killed by his own side and the army fell into disorder; 蘇賀臣果安 (reading unconfirmed) stabbed himself in the neck and died, and 羽田公矢國 (reading unconfirmed) surrendered with his kin. 男依 and the others won at 息長横河, at 鳥籠山 and on the shore of 安河 (readings unconfirmed), and on the day 辛亥 they reached Seta. West of the bridge lay the great camp of Prince Ōtomo and his ministers; the commander 智尊 (reading unconfirmed) had cut the middle of the bridge and laid a plank across it, but 大分君稚臣 (reading unconfirmed), wearing two layers of armor, crossed the plank, cut the rope, and charged into the camp, and the Ōmi army collapsed. Prince Ōtomo fled, then hid at 山前 (reading unconfirmed) and hanged himself, and on the day 乙卯 his head was presented before the camp at the Fuwa palace.

In Yamato, 大伴連吹負 (reading unconfirmed) conspired with the caretaker official 坂上直熊毛 (reading unconfirmed) and others; pretending that Prince Takechi had arrived, he scattered the troops in the camp west of Asuka-dera and cut down 穗積臣百足 (reading unconfirmed). 吹負 was appointed general, but he was defeated at Nara Hill (乃樂山) by the Ōmi commander 大野君果安 (reading unconfirmed), and at 倉歷 (reading unconfirmed), 田中臣足麻呂 (reading unconfirmed), attacked at night by 田邊小隅 (reading unconfirmed), barely escaped by means of the password “金” (metal). After being pressed by the army of 壹伎史韓國 (reading unconfirmed), which came from Kawachi, 吹負 met the army of 置始連菟 (reading unconfirmed) at 墨坂 (reading unconfirmed) and regained his strength; he defeated 韓國’s army beside the 葦池 pond (reading unconfirmed) at Taima, and ordered that, since the aim was to strike down the chief culprits, the common people were not to be killed indiscriminately. On the Upper Road (上道), 三輪君高市麻呂 and 置始連菟 (readings unconfirmed) inflicted a great defeat on the Ōmi army at the 箸陵 tomb (reading unconfirmed), and after that the Ōmi army no longer came.

Before this, 高市縣主許梅 (reading unconfirmed), chief of Takechi district, suddenly became unable to speak; three days later he was possessed by deities who named themselves Kotoshironushi-no-Kami of the Takechi shrine (高市社) and the 生靈神 of the 身狹社 shrine (readings unconfirmed), and they told him to offer horses and weapons at the tomb of Emperor Jinmu (神日本磐余彥天皇) and said they would protect the government army. The god of 村屋 (reading unconfirmed) also announced that an army would come by the Middle Road (中道), and since everything happened as foretold, the ranks of the three deities were raised after the war. In the eighth month Prince Takechi pronounced the crimes of the Ōmi ministers: eight who had committed grave crimes were given the ultimate penalty, the Minister of the Right 中臣連金 (reading unconfirmed) was beheaded at 淺井田根 (reading unconfirmed), the Minister of the Left Soga no Akae (蘇我臣赤兄) and others were banished, and the rest were pardoned. In the ninth month the emperor passed through Kuwana, Suzuka, 阿閉 (reading unconfirmed) and Nabari, entered the 嶋宮 palace (reading unconfirmed) in the Yamato capital, and moved to the Okamoto Palace. In this year a palace was built south of the Okamoto Palace, and in winter he moved into it; this is called the Asuka Kiyomihara Palace (飛鳥淨御原宮).

quotes.note: The words of the Crown Prince when he declined to take charge of affairs. It means: “Today I will take holy orders, and I wish to perform meritorious deeds for Your Majesty.”
Words someone spoke on seeing off the Crown Prince on his way to Yoshino. It means: “They have put wings on a tiger and let it loose.”
The record that on the way to the eastern provinces, beside the 跡太川 river (reading unconfirmed) in 朝明 district (reading unconfirmed), he bowed toward Amaterasu-Ōmikami from afar.
An order issued to the army by 大伴連吹負 (reading unconfirmed). It means that the troops were raised not to kill the common people but to strike down the chief culprits.

figures.name: Prince Ōama (大海人皇子)
figures.role: Younger brother of Emperor Tenji (天命開別天皇) by the same mother, and Crown Prince. He took holy orders and entered Yoshino, went out to the eastern provinces in the 1st year, and defeated the army of the Ōmi court. The sovereign of this book.

figures.name: Princess Uno (菟野皇女)
figures.role: Daughter of Emperor Tenji, made the emperor’s principal consort.

figures.name: Prince Takechi (高市皇子)
figures.role: Crossed 鹿深 (reading unconfirmed) and joined the emperor at 積殖山口 (reading unconfirmed); he oversaw military affairs at Fuwa, was given full charge of military affairs by the emperor at 野上 (reading unconfirmed), and after the war pronounced the crimes of the Ōmi ministers.

figures.name: Prince Ōtsu (大津皇子)
figures.role: Summoned from Ōmi by 大分君惠尺 (reading unconfirmed), he passed through the Suzuka barrier and joined the emperor in 朝明 district (reading unconfirmed).

figures.name: Prince Ōtomo (大友皇子)
figures.role: As the central figure of the Ōmi court he had troops raised in the eastern provinces, the Yamato capital, Tsukushi and Kibi, but he was defeated at Seta and hanged himself at 山前 (reading unconfirmed).

figures.name: 村國連男依 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: The commander who raised troops in Mino and blocked the Fuwa road, and later led tens of thousands into Ōmi and won at Seta.

figures.name: 大伴連吹負 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Seized the camp west of Asuka-dera in Yamato and became a general; despite defeats, he drove back the Ōmi army.

figures.name: 大分君稚臣 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: The brave warrior who crossed the plank on the Seta bridge, charged into the Ōmi camp, and broke the Ōmi army.

figures.name: 栗隈王 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Governor (大宰) of Tsukushi. Even on receiving the Ōmi court’s orders, he did not move his troops, giving as his reason the need to guard against foreign enemies.

figures.name: 高市縣主許梅 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Chief of Takechi district, through whom Kotoshironushi-no-Kami and the 生靈神 (reading unconfirmed), possessing him, announced among other things that they would protect the government army.

tenmu-ge-1.title: Emperor Tenmu’s Accession and the Yoshino Covenant
tenmu-ge-1.lead: Gathers the records from Emperor Tenmu’s accession at the Asuka Kiyomihara Palace in his 2nd year through his 9th year. Year by year it records the posthumous granting of ranks to those who served with merit in the year 壬申, the worship of the gods and Buddhist ceremonies, exchanges with Silla, Koguryŏ and 耽羅 (reading unconfirmed), the princes’ covenant at Yoshino, and the vow to found Yakushi-ji.

points.text: In the second month of the 2nd year, the emperor had officials set up an altar platform (壇場) and took the throne at the Asuka Kiyomihara Palace. He made his principal consort empress; the text records that the empress bore Prince Kusakabe (草壁皇子尊), and then lists his consorts and wives and their princes and princesses.

In the fifth month of the 8th year, at the Yoshino Palace, the emperor had the empress and Prince Kusakabe, Prince Ōtsu, Prince Takechi, Prince Kawashima (河嶋皇子), Prince Osakabe (忍壁皇子) and Prince 芝基 (芝基皇子, reading unconfirmed) swear to help one another and not to quarrel. Saying that he would cherish these children of different mothers as though they had been born of one mother, the emperor embraced the six princes.
Records recur in which, when people who had served in the war of the year 壬申 died, they were posthumously given ranks for their merit (坂本財臣, 紀臣阿閉麻呂, 物部雄君連, 村国連雄依 and others; readings unconfirmed).

Worship of the gods: in the 2nd year Princess 大来 (大来皇女, reading unconfirmed) was made to live in the abstinence palace (斎宮) at 泊瀬 (reading unconfirmed) so that she could serve at the shrine of Amaterasu-Ōmikami (天照大神宮), and in the tenth month of the 3rd year she was sent to the Ise shrine (伊勢神宮). From the fourth month of the 4th year, records of worship of the wind god of Tatsuta (龍田) and the 大忌 deity of Hirose (広瀬) appear almost every year.

Buddhist ceremonies: in the 2nd year the copying of the complete Buddhist canon (一切経) began at Kawara-dera (川原寺), and in the 6th year a great vegetarian feast (大斎) was held at Asuka-dera and the complete canon was read. In the eleventh month of the 9th year Yakushi-ji was founded for the first time for the sake of the empress’s illness, and a hundred monks were ordained.

In the second month of the 4th year an edict declared that the 部曲 granted to the clans in the year 甲子 were abolished, and that the mountains, marshes, forests and fields that had been granted to imperial princes, princes, ministers and temples were taken back. In the fourth month of the same year, fishing and hunting devices were restricted and the eating of the meat of cattle, horses, dogs, monkeys and chickens was forbidden.

story.text: In the first month of the 2nd year a banquet was given for the ministers. In the second month the emperor took the throne at the Asuka Kiyomihara Palace and made his principal consort empress. In the third month a white pheasant was presented from Bingo province and a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the realm, and at Kawara-dera scribes were gathered and the copying of the complete canon began. In the fourth month, so that Princess 大来 (reading unconfirmed) could serve at the shrine of Amaterasu-Ōmikami, she was first made to live in the abstinence palace at 泊瀬 (reading unconfirmed). In the fifth month an edict declared that those entering service for the first time should first serve as great attendants (大舎人), and that women too would be allowed to serve if they wished.

In the intercalary sixth month of the 2nd year, Silla sent envoys to congratulate the emperor on his accession and envoys to offer condolences on the death of the previous emperor. A prince of 耽羅 (reading unconfirmed) also came with tribute, and in the eighth month the 耽羅 envoys were given court rank for the first time. In the twelfth month gifts were given to the Nakatomi (中臣), the 忌部 (reading unconfirmed), the shrine officials, and the district officials of Harima and Tanba and others who had served at the Great Thanksgiving (大嘗), and the head of the office for building the Great Temple of Takechi (高市大寺) was appointed.

In the third month of the 3rd year it was reported from Tsushima that silver had been produced for the first time, and the governor was given rank. In the eighth month Prince Osakabe was sent to Isonokami Shrine (石上神宮) to polish the sacred treasures with oil, and it was ordered that the treasures that the various houses had deposited in the divine storehouse (神府) be returned to their descendants. In the tenth month Princess 大来 (reading unconfirmed) set out from the abstinence palace at 泊瀬 for the Ise shrine.

In the first month of the 4th year a star-observation platform (占星台) was built for the first time. In the second month the abolition of the 部曲 and other measures were proclaimed, and in the fourth month the emperor had the wind god of Tatsuta and the 大忌 deity of Hirose worshipped, and fixed restrictions on fishing, hunting and eating meat. In the 5th year there was a great drought in summer; though prayers were offered to the gods and to the Buddha, no rain fell and the people starved. In the eighth month a great purification (大祓) was held in all four directions and an amnesty reducing punishments was issued. In this year the emperor intended to place the capital at 新城 (reading unconfirmed) and let the fields there go to waste, but in the end he did not make it the capital.

In the sixth month of the 6th year the emperor issued an edict to the 東漢直 (reading unconfirmed) and others in which he reproached them for the crimes they had committed in the past, but pardoned them out of great mercy so that their clan would not die out. In the eighth month a great vegetarian feast was held at Asuka-dera and the complete canon was read, and imperial princes, princes and high officials were each permitted to have one person enter holy orders. In spring of the 7th year an abstinence palace was built on the upper reaches of the river at 倉梯 (reading unconfirmed) to worship the gods of heaven and earth, but just before the departure in the fourth month Princess 十市 (十市皇女, reading unconfirmed) died suddenly in the palace, the excursion was cancelled, and the gods were not worshipped. In the twelfth month of the 7th year a great earthquake struck Tsukushi; the ground split and many houses collapsed.

In the third month of the 8th year the emperor paid homage at the tomb of the Later Okamoto Emperor (後岡本天皇) at 越智 (reading unconfirmed). In the fifth month, at the Yoshino Palace, he made a covenant with the empress and the six princes, and when they returned to the palace the six princes together bowed to the emperor. In the tenth month, saying that bad people were numerous in the towns because princes and high officials overlooked them, he issued an edict that high and low should correct one another, and he also fixed the dress of monks and nuns. In the eleventh month barriers were set up for the first time on Mount Tatsuta and on Mount 大坂 (大坂山, reading unconfirmed), and an outer wall (羅城) was built at Naniwa.

In the fourth month of the 9th year it was decided that, except for two or three great state temples, government offices would not administer temples. In the fifth month the Golden Light Sutra (金光明経) was expounded for the first time in the palace and at the temples. In the seventh month a branch of the zelkova tree west of Asuka-dera broke off of its own accord, and Prince 舎人 (舎人王, reading unconfirmed) died. In the eleventh month, when the empress fell ill, the emperor made a vow for her sake and founded Yakushi-ji for the first time, and had a hundred monks ordained, and the empress recovered. In the same month the emperor also fell ill, but as soon as a hundred monks were ordained he recovered.

quotes.note: The accession record: he took the imperial throne at the Asuka Kiyomihara Palace.
The emperor’s words at the Yoshino covenant. He says that he will cherish the princes born of different mothers as though they were children of the same mother.
The record of silver produced in Tsushima, which states that this was the first time silver had been produced in the land of Yamato (倭国).
The record that a vow was made for the empress’s illness and Yakushi-ji was founded for the first time.

figures.name: Prince Kusakabe (草壁皇子尊)
figures.role: Son of the empress. At the Yoshino covenant he was the first to step forward and take the oath.

figures.name: Prince Ōtsu (大津皇子)
figures.role: Son of Princess 大田 (大田皇女, reading unconfirmed). One of the six princes who joined the Yoshino covenant.

figures.name: Prince Takechi (高市皇子)
figures.role: Son of 尼子娘 (reading unconfirmed). He joined the Yoshino covenant, and in the 9th year was sent to offer condolences on the death of a monk of Asuka-dera and to visit the ailing Prince 舎人 (reading unconfirmed).

figures.name: 大來皇女 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: A princess who purified herself at the abstinence palace at 泊瀬 (reading unconfirmed) in order to serve at the shrine of Amaterasu-Ōmikami, and set out for the Ise shrine in the tenth month of the 3rd year.

figures.name: 十市皇女 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Daughter of Nukata no Ōkimi (額田姫王). In the fourth month of the 7th year, just before the excursion to the abstinence palace, she died suddenly in the palace.

figures.name: Prince Osakabe (忍壁皇子)
figures.role: A prince who was sent to Isonokami Shrine in the 3rd year and polished the sacred treasures.

variants.name: One version says (一云)
variants.text: The main text records 金薩儒 (reading unconfirmed) and others of Silla as envoys sent to offer condolences on the death of the previous emperor. A small note attached there reads “一云，調使” (“one version says: tribute envoys”), which shows that there was also a tradition that regarded these envoys as envoys bringing tribute (調).

tenmu-ge-2.title: Emperor Tenmu — Compiling the Codes and the Imperial Chronicles, and His Death
tenmu-ge-2.lead: Gathers the records from the 10th year of Emperor Tenmu to his death in the 1st year of Shuchō (朱鳥). The making of codes (律令) and the recording and fixing of the Imperial Chronicles (帝紀) go forward, together with institutional measures such as the eight kabane (八色之姓) and new court ranks; the book ends with the emperor’s illness and death and the eulogies delivered at his temporary enshrinement.

points.text: In the second month of the 10th year, the emperor and empress, in the Great Audience Hall (大極殿), issued an edict to the imperial princes, princes and ministers declaring that codes (律令) would be established and the laws and regulations revised. On the same day Prince Kusakabe (草壁皇子尊) was made crown prince and put in charge of government affairs.

In the third month of the 10th year, the emperor had twelve people, including Prince Kawashima (川嶋皇子) and Prince Osakabe (忍壁皇子), record and fix the Imperial Chronicles (帝紀) and the various matters of high antiquity. 中臣連大嶋 and 平群臣子首 (readings unconfirmed) took up the brush themselves and wrote the record.

In the tenth month of the 13th year the clan titles (族姓) were reformed and the eight kabane were created: 真人, 朝臣, 宿禰, 忌寸, 道師, 臣, 連 and 稲置. After that, 真人 (thirteen clans), 朝臣 (fifty-two clans), 宿禰 (fifty clans) and 忌寸 (eleven clans) were granted one after another.

In the 1st year of Shuchō, when divination was performed about the emperor’s illness, it was found to be a curse of the Kusanagi sword (草薙剣), so that same day the sword was sent to the Atsuta shrine (熱田社) in Owari province. In the seventh month it was ordered that all affairs of the realm, great or small, be reported to the empress and the crown prince; the era name was changed to Shuchō, and the palace was named the Asuka Kiyomihara Palace.

In the ninth month of the 1st year of Shuchō, the emperor, his illness not cured, died in the main palace. A temporary enshrinement palace (殯宮) was built in the south court, and the text records that during the mourning Prince Ōtsu plotted rebellion against the crown prince.

In the first month of the 14th year the names of the court ranks were changed and the number of grades increased: twelve grades of the 明 and 浄 ranks were established for princes, and forty-eight grades of 正, 直, 勤, 務, 追 and 進 for ministers. Prince Kusakabe was given the rank 浄広壱, Prince Ōtsu 浄大弐, and Prince Takechi 浄広弐.

story.text: In the first month of the 10th year, the Home Provinces and the other provinces were made to repair the shrines of the heavenly and earthly deities (天社, 地社). In the second month the emperor and empress declared in the Great Audience Hall that codes would be established, and Prince Kusakabe was made crown prince. In the third month the Imperial Chronicles and the various matters of high antiquity were recorded and fixed, and in the fourth month ninety-two articles of prohibitions (禁式) were laid down, fixing rules for what people could wear. In the fifth month the spirits of the imperial ancestors were worshipped, and in the seventh month a great purification was held throughout the realm. In the eighth month the envoys sent to 多禰 Island (多禰嶋, reading unconfirmed) presented a map of the land of 多禰 and reported on how its people lived.

In the third month of the 11th year, 三野王 (reading unconfirmed) and others were sent to 新城 (reading unconfirmed) to view the lay of the land, with the intention of placing the capital there. 境部連石積 (reading unconfirmed) and others were made to create a new script (新字), one work in forty-four scrolls. The sustenance households of imperial princes and below were abolished and returned to the state, and in the fourth month men and women alike were ordered to tie up their hair. In the seventh month many Hayato (隼人) came and presented local products, and the Ōsumi Hayato and the 阿多 Hayato (reading unconfirmed) wrestled (相撲) at court, the Ōsumi Hayato winning. In the ninth month it was ordered that the practices of bowing on the knees and crawling be abolished and the standing bow of the Naniwa court (難波朝庭) be used.

In the first month of the 12th year a three-legged sparrow presented from Tsukushi was shown to the ministers; an edict declared that in the emperor’s reign auspicious signs from heaven appeared again and again every year, and an amnesty and a remission of taxes and labor followed. In the second month Prince Ōtsu took part in hearing state affairs for the first time. In the third month the monastic offices of 僧正, 僧都 and 律師 were filled; in the fourth month an edict ordered that copper coins be used and silver coins not be used, but a few days later another edict said the use of silver should not be stopped. In the twelfth month envoys were sent around to divide the boundaries of the provinces, but this was not settled that year; and an edict declared that capitals and palaces would be built in two places, and that first a capital would be placed at Naniwa.

In the second month of the 13th year, 広瀬王 (reading unconfirmed) and others were sent to the Home Provinces to divine a site suited to a capital, and 三野王 (reading unconfirmed) and others were sent to Shinano to view the lay of the land. In the third month the emperor toured the capital and fixed the site of the palace. In the intercalary fourth month, declaring that the essential thing in government is military affairs, he ordered civil and military officials to keep weapons and horses and to practice riding and the use of troops. In the tenth month the eight kabane were created, and on a night that month a great earthquake struck: mountains collapsed, the hot spring of Iyo was buried, and more than 500,000 頃 of fields in Tosa province sank into the sea. In the twelfth month 土師宿禰甥 (reading unconfirmed) and others who had stayed in Tang returned by way of Silla.

In the first month of the 14th year the names and grades of the court ranks were changed. In the third month an edict ordered every household in the provinces to make a Buddhist shrine (仏舎) and to place a Buddhist image and sutras in it for worship. In the seventh month the colors of court dress for each rank were fixed. In the ninth month, because the emperor was unwell, sutras were read for three days at Daikan Daiji (大官大寺), Kawara-dera and Asuka-dera. In the eleventh month a rite of summoning the soul (招魂) was performed for the emperor.

In the first month of the 1st year of Shuchō, a fire that started in the Treasury (大蔵省) at Naniwa burned down all the palace buildings. In the fifth month the emperor first became unwell, and the Medicine Buddha Sutra (薬師経) was expounded at Kawara-dera. In the sixth month divination about his illness pointed to a curse of the Kusanagi sword, and the sword was sent to the Atsuta shrine. In the seventh month affairs of the realm were made to be reported to the empress and the crown prince, the era name was changed to Shuchō, and the palace was named the Asuka Kiyomihara Palace. The princes and ministers made images of Kannon (観世音) for the emperor and had many monks ordained to pray for his recovery.

In the ninth month the imperial princes and those below gathered at Kawara-dera and made vows for the emperor’s illness, but the emperor died in the main palace without recovering. A temporary enshrinement palace was built in the south court, and the text records that during the mourning Prince Ōtsu plotted rebellion against the crown prince. Afterwards monks and nuns wailed in the courtyard of the temporary enshrinement, and ministers in turn delivered eulogies on the affairs of the 壬生, the princes, the palace household (宮内), the 大政官, the 法官 and others. Finally 百済王良虞 (reading unconfirmed) and the provincial chieftains (国造) also delivered eulogies, and various songs and dances were performed.

quotes.note: The emperor’s words saying that he now wished to establish codes and revise the rules of law.
The record that he had the Imperial Chronicles and the various matters of high antiquity recorded and fixed.
The record that the eight kabane were created and the many clan titles of the realm were reorganized.
When divination was performed about the emperor’s illness, it was found to be a curse of the Kusanagi sword.

figures.name: Prince Kusakabe (草壁皇子尊)
figures.role: Made crown prince in the second month of the 10th year and put in charge of government affairs.

figures.name: Prince Ōtsu (大津皇子)
figures.role: Took part in hearing state affairs for the first time in the second month of the 12th year; the text records that at the temporary enshrinement of Emperor Tenmu he plotted rebellion against the crown prince.

figures.name: Prince Kawashima (川嶋皇子)
figures.role: Was ordered, together with Prince Osakabe and others, to record and fix the Imperial Chronicles and the various matters of high antiquity.

figures.name: 中臣連大嶋 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Together with 平群臣子首 (reading unconfirmed), took up the brush himself and recorded the Imperial Chronicles and other matters.

figures.name: 平群臣子首 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Together with 中臣連大嶋 (reading unconfirmed), took up the brush himself and recorded the Imperial Chronicles and other matters.

figures.name: Prince Takechi (高市皇子)
figures.role: Given the rank 浄広弐 in the first month of the 14th year; in the first month of the 1st year of Shuchō he answered correctly in a question-and-answer session and was rewarded.

variants.name: Some say (或曰)
variants.text: The main text records that in the eighth month of the 11th year something fire-colored, like a consecration banner (灌頂幡), drifted north across the sky and was seen in every province. According to “some say,” it entered the sea of Koshi.

variants.name: Some say (或曰)
variants.text: The main text says that fire broke out from the Treasury at Naniwa and burned down all the palace buildings. According to “some say,” it was a fire from the house of 阿斗連薬 (reading unconfirmed) that spread to the palace, and only the Office of the Armory (兵庫職) did not burn.

variants.name: Some say (或曰)
variants.text: The main text says that lightning flashed and thunder sounded in the south, and the storehouse of the Ministry of Popular Affairs (民部省) holding the 庸 tax burned. According to “some say,” the fire started at the palace of Prince Osakabe and spread to the Ministry of Popular Affairs.

jito-1.title: Empress Jitō — Rule before Enthronement, and Accession
jito-1.lead: Gathers the records of Empress Jitō’s background and of how, after the death of Emperor Tenmu, she took charge of government and then took the throne in the first month of the 4th year. Among the events recorded are Prince Ōtsu’s rebellion, the death of Prince Kusakabe, the funeral of Emperor Tenmu, the distribution of the code (令), and the appointment of Prince Takechi as Grand Chancellor.

points.text: When Emperor Tenmu (天渟中原瀛真人天皇) died in the ninth month of the 1st year of Shuchō, the empress came to court and took charge of government (臨朝称制). In the first month of the 4th year, 物部麻呂朝臣 (reading unconfirmed) set up the great shield, 中臣大嶋朝臣 (reading unconfirmed) read the words of blessing of the heavenly deities (天神寿詞), and 忌部宿禰色夫知 (reading unconfirmed) presented the sacred sword and mirror (神璽), and the empress took the imperial throne.

In the tenth month of the 1st year of Shuchō, Prince Ōtsu’s rebellion was discovered, and the prince was ordered to die at his house at 訳語田 (reading unconfirmed) (he was twenty-four). His consort, Princess 山辺 (山辺皇女, reading unconfirmed), ran there with her hair disheveled and her feet bare and died with him, and it is said that all who saw it wept.

Of Prince Ōtsu the main text records that he was of fine bearing and excellent speech, that he was loved by Emperor Tenji (天命開別天皇), that he was fond of learning and writing, and that the flourishing of poetry and rhapsodies (詩賦) began with Ōtsu.

At the temporary enshrinement palace of Emperor Tenmu, the crown prince led the high officials and the hundred officials in wailing again and again, and the Hayato and the Emishi also delivered eulogies. In the eleventh month of the 2nd year, after a eulogy recounting the order in which the imperial ancestors had succeeded to the throne, the emperor was buried at the 大内陵 (reading unconfirmed). In the fourth month of the following year, the 3rd, the crown prince, Prince Kusakabe (草壁皇子尊), died.

In the sixth month of the 3rd year a code (令), one work in twenty-two scrolls, was distributed to the government offices, and in the ninth month of the 4th year an edict ordered that household registers be made according to the household statutes (戸令). In the seventh month of the 4th year Prince Takechi was made Grand Chancellor (太政大臣) and 丹比嶋真人 (reading unconfirmed) Minister of the Right; in the tenth month Prince Takechi, and in the twelfth month the empress herself, went to view the palace site at Fujiwara (藤原).

In the tenth month of the 4th year, the empress issued an edict praising 大伴部博麻 (reading unconfirmed). 博麻 had been taken prisoner by the Tang army in the war to aid Paekche, had sold himself so that his comrades could return home, and had remained in a foreign land for thirty years, so he was given rank, rice land and other rewards.

story.text: Empress Jitō (高天原広野姫天皇) had the childhood name Princess Uno no Sarara (鸕野讃良皇女); she was the second daughter of Emperor Tenji (天命開別天皇), and her mother was 遠智娘 (reading unconfirmed). In the 3rd year of 天豊財重日足姫天皇 (Empress Kōgyoku, later Empress Saimei) she became a consort of Emperor Tenmu (天渟中原瀛真人天皇), and in the 1st year of Emperor Tenji she bore Prince Kusakabe at the Ōtsu Palace. In the tenth month of the 10th year of Emperor Tenji she followed Emperor Tenmu, who had taken holy orders, into Yoshino, avoiding the suspicion of the court. In the sixth month of the 1st year of Emperor Tenmu she fled with him to the eastern provinces and settled their plans, and in the seventh month Prince Ōtomo was struck down. In the 2nd year she became empress, and it is said that she helped the emperor and often gave her views on government.

In the ninth month of the 1st year of Shuchō Emperor Tenmu died, and the empress took charge of government. In the tenth month Prince Ōtsu’s rebellion was discovered, and more than thirty people whom the prince had deceived were also arrested. The prince was ordered to die at his house at 訳語田 (reading unconfirmed), and his consort Princess 山辺 (reading unconfirmed) died with him. The empress pardoned his followers, saying they had had no choice, banishing only 礪杵道作 (reading unconfirmed) to Izu and moving the Silla monk 行心 (reading unconfirmed) to a temple in Hida. In the eleventh month Princess 大来 (大来皇女, reading unconfirmed), who had been serving at the shrine of the god of Ise (伊勢神祠), returned to the capital.

Through the 1st and 2nd years, records of wailing, eulogies and offerings (奠) at the temporary enshrinement palace follow one after another. People from Koguryŏ and Silla who had come over and submitted were settled in Hitachi, 下毛野 (reading unconfirmed) and Musashi and given rice land. In the ninth month the Silla prince 金霜林 (reading unconfirmed) came; informed in Tsukushi of the emperor’s death, he put on mourning clothes, bowed toward the east, and wailed. In the tenth month the crown prince, leading the high officials, the hundred officials and people of the provinces, began building the 大内陵 (reading unconfirmed).

In the seventh month of the 2nd year, because of drought, a great rain ritual (大雩) was held, and when the Paekche monk 道蔵 (reading unconfirmed) was made to pray for rain, rain fell across the realm before the morning was out. In the eleventh month the crown prince led the high officials, the hundred officials and the guests from the various foreign lands (諸蕃) in wailing at the temporary enshrinement palace, and the ministers each delivered eulogies on how their ancestors had served. The Emishi too delivered eulogies, bearing tribute, and after 当麻真人智徳 (reading unconfirmed) delivered a eulogy on the order in which the imperial ancestors had succeeded to the throne, the emperor was buried at the 大内陵 (reading unconfirmed).

In the first month of the 3rd year the empress went to the Yoshino Palace. In the fourth month the crown prince, Prince Kusakabe, died. In the fifth month the empress had the Silla condolence envoys told that, because among other things the envoy’s rank was lower than before and there was only one ship, their tribute and gifts would be sealed and returned. In the sixth month the Office for Selecting Good Words (撰善言司) was set up, and a code, one work in twenty-two scrolls, was distributed to the government offices. In the intercalary eighth month she ordered that household registers be made this winter, that vagrants be brought under control, and that one quarter of each province’s men be selected as soldiers and trained in military arts.

In the first month of the 4th year the empress took the throne. In the fourth month the way of granting rank according to officials’ years of service and the colors of court dress were fixed, and in the seventh month the high officials and the hundred officials wore the new court dress for the first time. In the same month Prince Takechi was made Grand Chancellor and 丹比嶋真人 (reading unconfirmed) Minister of the Right, and appointments in the eight ministries and the hundred offices were changed. In the tenth month 大伴部博麻 (reading unconfirmed) was praised, and Prince Takechi viewed the palace site at Fujiwara. In the eleventh month, by imperial order, the 元嘉 and 儀鳳 calendars (元嘉暦, 儀鳳暦) were used for the first time, and in the twelfth month the empress herself went to Fujiwara to view the palace site.

quotes.note: After the emperor’s death, the empress, without taking the throne, came to court and took charge of government.
An assessment of Prince Ōtsu: the flourishing of poetry and rhapsodies (詩賦) began with him.
The sacred sword and mirror, the divine tokens, were presented to the empress, and the empress took the imperial throne.
The empress’s words praising him for honoring the court, loving the country, and showing his loyalty by selling himself.

figures.name: Princess Uno no Sarara (鸕野讚良皇女)
figures.role: The childhood name of Empress Jitō. Second daughter of Emperor Tenji (天命開別天皇), she became the empress of Emperor Tenmu (天渟中原瀛真人天皇).

figures.name: Prince Ōtsu (皇子大津)
figures.role: Third son of Emperor Tenmu. His rebellion was discovered and he was ordered to die at the age of twenty-four.

figures.name: 皇女山邊 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Consort of Prince Ōtsu. She ran to him at his death and died with him.

figures.name: Prince Kusakabe (草壁皇子尊)
figures.role: As crown prince he led the rites at the temporary enshrinement palace, but he died in the fourth month of the 3rd year.

figures.name: Prince Takechi (皇子高市)
figures.role: Became Grand Chancellor in the seventh month of the 4th year, and in the tenth month went to view the palace site at Fujiwara.

figures.name: 大伴部博麻 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: A soldier (軍丁) who was taken prisoner by Tang in the war to aid Paekche, sold himself so that his comrades could return home, and came back thirty years later.

jito-2.title: Empress Jitō — The Fujiwara Palace and Her Abdication
jito-2.lead: Gathers the records from the 5th year of Empress Jitō to her abdication in the 11th year. A remonstrance over an excursion to Ise, the move to the Fujiwara Palace, repeated excursions to Yoshino, and records of Buddhism and of religious rites follow one another, and in the eighth month of the 11th year she yields the throne to the crown prince, where the Nihon Shoki ends.

points.text: In the second month of the 6th year, when the empress announced that she would make an excursion to Ise in the third month, the Middle Counselor (中納言) 三輪朝臣高市麻呂 (reading unconfirmed) remonstrated that it would interfere with farm work. In the third month he remonstrated again, taking off his cap of rank and offering it up to the court, but the empress did not listen and went to Ise.

In the tenth month of the 5th year the 新益京 capital (reading unconfirmed) was ritually pacified, and in the fifth month of the 6th year the palace site at Fujiwara was ritually pacified, and the new palace was announced at four places: Ise, 大倭 (reading unconfirmed), Sumiyoshi and Kii. In the twelfth month of the 8th year the empress moved to and took up residence in the Fujiwara Palace.
On the first day of the eighth month of the 11th year, the empress made her decision in the palace and yielded the imperial throne to the crown prince. This is the last entry in the Nihon Shoki.
In the eighth month of the 5th year, eighteen clans, including the Ōmiwa (大三輪), Isonokami (石上), Fujiwara (藤原) and Ōtomo (大伴), were made to submit the tomb records (墓記) of their ancestors.
From the 5th year to the 11th year, the empress’s excursions to the Yoshino Palace are recorded every year, several times a year.

Buddhist records: in the 6th year monks were sent to Ōsumi and 阿多 (reading unconfirmed) to transmit Buddhism, and in the 8th year a hundred copies of the Golden Light Sutra (金光明経) were placed in the provinces to be read every first month. In the 11th year, because of the empress’s illness, the high officials and the hundred officials began making Buddhist images, and in the seventh month an eye-opening ceremony was held at Yakushi-ji.

story.text: In the first month of the 5th year, Prince Takechi’s sustenance households were increased to three thousand, and other princes and ministers were also given additional sustenance households. In the second month the empress issued an edict to the high officials telling them to devote themselves to the Buddhist law as in the reign of the previous emperor. In the third month rules were laid down concerning the status of people who had been sold, and in the fourth month concerning lawsuits by slaves. In the sixth month, because long rains had continued since the fourth month, the high officials and the hundred officials were made to abstain from wine and meat and perform repentance (悔過), and sutras were read at the temples. In the eighth month eighteen clans were made to submit their ancestors’ tomb records.

In the ninth month of the 5th year Prince Kawashima (川嶋皇子) died. In the tenth month it was decided that five or more tomb-guardian households (陵戸) should be assigned to the tombs of former emperors, and the 新益京 capital (reading unconfirmed) was ritually pacified. In the eleventh month the Great Thanksgiving (大嘗) was held, and the Head of the Office of Divinities (神祇伯), 中臣朝臣大嶋 (reading unconfirmed), read the words of blessing of the heavenly deities (天神寿詞). In the twelfth month residential land was allotted according to rank, from the Minister of the Right down, and the size of the household.

In the second month of the 6th year, when the empress announced an excursion to Ise, 三輪朝臣高市麻呂 (reading unconfirmed) remonstrated that it would interfere with the farming season, and in the third month he remonstrated again, taking off his cap of rank. The empress did not heed him and went to Ise; she gave caps of rank to the divine districts (神郡) she passed through and to the provincial chieftains (国造) of Iga, Ise and Shima, and exempted them from tribute and labor. In the fifth month the palace site at Fujiwara was ritually pacified, and the new palace was announced at the four places. In the intercalary fifth month the Great Deity of Ise (伊勢大神) addressed the empress concerning the treatment of tribute and labor in Ise province, and monks were sent to Ōsumi and 阿多 (reading unconfirmed) to transmit Buddhism.

In the first month of the 7th year the common people of the realm were made to wear yellow clothing and slaves black clothing. In the third month people were made to plant mulberry, ramie, pears, chestnuts and turnips as a supplement to the five grains. In the ninth month an unrestricted great assembly (無遮大会) was held in the inner palace for the Kiyomihara Emperor (清御原天皇). In the tenth month imperial princes and those below were made to keep armor, swords, bows and arrows and other equipment according to their rank, and the Sutra of Benevolent Kings (仁王経) was expounded in the provinces. In the eleventh month monks were made to taste the water of the sweet spring (醴泉) in 益須 district (reading unconfirmed) in Ōmi province.

In the third month of the 8th year officials of the mint (鋳銭司) were appointed, and because many sick people had been cured by the sweet spring of 益須 district (reading unconfirmed), the district was exempted from tribute and labor. In the fifth month a hundred copies of the Golden Light Sutra were sent to the provinces to be read every first month. In the twelfth month the empress moved to and took up residence in the Fujiwara Palace, and the hundred officials paid their respects at court.

In the third month of the 9th year the Silla prince 金良琳 (reading unconfirmed) came and reported on the affairs of his country, and envoys were sent to 多禰 (reading unconfirmed) to search out the places where the barbarians (蛮) lived. In the fifth month the empress watched the Hayato wrestle beneath the western zelkova tree. In the fourth month of the 10th year, 物部薬 and 壬生諸石 (readings unconfirmed), who had suffered long in the land of Tang, were given rank, rice land and other rewards. In the seventh month the 後皇子尊 (reading unconfirmed) died. In the eighth month 多臣品治 (reading unconfirmed) was given rank in recognition of his merit in following the emperor from the very beginning and in holding the barrier firmly. In the tenth month the Minister of the Right 丹比真人 (reading unconfirmed) was given a palanquin and a staff in consideration of his retirement from office.

In the second month of the 11th year officials such as the Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (東宮大傅) and the Master of the Crown Prince’s Household (春宮大夫) were appointed, and in the third month an unrestricted great assembly was held at the Crown Prince’s palace (春宮). In the sixth month, because of the empress’s illness, sutras were read at the temples of the capital and the Home Provinces, and the high officials and the hundred officials began making Buddhist images. In the seventh month an eye-opening ceremony was held at Yakushi-ji. On the first day of the eighth month the empress made her decision in the palace and yielded the throne to the crown prince.

quotes.note: Words from the remonstrance of 三輪高市麻呂 (reading unconfirmed). It means: in the season of farm work, the imperial carriage must not move.
The empress moved to and took up residence in the Fujiwara Palace.
The empress made her decision in the palace and yielded the throne to the crown prince. The last sentence of the Nihon Shoki.
Eighteen clans were made to submit the tomb records of their ancestors.

figures.name: 三輪朝臣高市麻呂 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Middle Counselor. He remonstrated twice that the excursion to Ise would interfere with the farming season.

figures.name: Prince Takechi (皇子高市)
figures.role: Was given additional sustenance households in the 5th and 6th years and was granted the rank 浄広壱 in the first month of the 7th year.

figures.name: 丹比真人 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Minister of the Right. In the tenth month of the 10th year he was given a palanquin and a staff in consideration of his retirement from office.

figures.name: 中臣朝臣大嶋 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Head of the Office of Divinities. He read the words of blessing of the heavenly deities at the Great Thanksgiving in the eleventh month of the 5th year.

figures.name: 後皇子尊 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Recorded as having died in the seventh month of the 10th year.

figures.name: 物部藥 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Together with 壬生諸石 (reading unconfirmed), he was given rank and other rewards in consideration of his long suffering in the land of Tang.
